en: I have heard, O Venerable One, that it has been thus declared by the Blessed One: "In this world, for some there arises no recognition [of their origin], namely:

'I have come from the eastern direction,' or 'I have come from the southern direction,' or 'I have come from the western direction,' or 'I have come from the northern direction,' or 'I have come from the upward direction,' or 'I have come from the downward direction,' or 'I have come from some other direction or intermediate point. Thus, for some, such knowledge does not exist."
Do I have a self that transmigrates? Do I not have a self that transmigrates? Who was I in the past? Or, having passed away from here, what shall I become after dying here?

Furthermore, one might know through spontaneous intuition, through the instruction of another, or by hearing it from others, as follows: "I have come from the eastern direction; or I have come from the southern direction; or I have come from the western direction; or I have come from the northern direction; or I have come from the upward direction; or I have come from the downward direction; or I have come from some other direction or intermediate direction. Thus, for some, there arises the knowledge: "I have a self that is subject to rebirth, which wanders through all these directions and intermediate directions—from every direction and every intermediate direction—and that is I."
He is one who professes [the existence of] the self, professes [the existence of] the world, professes [the existence of] karma, and professes [the efficacy of] action.
He thinks: "I shall do it myself, I shall cause others to do it, and I shall approve of those who do it.
All such undertakings of action in the world must be fully understood.
Indeed, this person who wanders through these directions or intermediate directions is one who lacks full comprehension;
he traverses all directions and all intermediate directions, enters into various kinds of wombs, and experiences diverse types of sensations.
Regarding this, the Blessed One has proclaimed full comprehension.

Whatever undertakings of action exist in this world—all of them are to be fully understood as being for the sake of honoring, respecting, and venerating this very life, for the purpose of escaping birth and death, and for the sake of warding off suffering. He for whom these undertakings of action in this world have been fully understood is indeed a sage who has comprehended action. Thus I say.

This world is afflicted, decayed, difficult to instruct, and ignorant; it is beset by calamities here and there. Behold how people, being tormented, cause suffering in various ways. There are living beings, distinct and separate, who feel shame [for their actions]. Behold how some, claiming to be "homeless ones" (*anagāra*), professing various doctrines, and engaging in the undertaking of work upon the earth with diverse weapons, inflict violence upon many kinds of living beings by undertaking the weapon of the earth against the earth itself.

In this regard, the Blessed One has proclaimed full comprehension: for the sake of this very life—with its greetings, honors, and worship; for the sake of escaping birth and death; and for the sake of warding off suffering—one either personally undertakes violence against the earth-element, causes others to undertake violence against the earth-element, or approves of others who are undertaking violence against the earth-element.

That is for his own harm; that is for his own delusion. But he who understands this, having heard it from the presence of the Blessed One or from the monks, perceives: "This indeed is a bond; this indeed is delusion; this indeed is death; this indeed is hell. Thus the world is entangled in this [bondage], whereby, through various weapons and the undertaking of work upon the earth, one who undertakes weapons against the earth harms many other kinds of living beings. This I say: some pierce the ankle; some the foot; some the heel; some the knee; some the thigh; some the hip; some the navel; some the belly; some the side; some the back; some the chest; some the heart; some the breast; some the shoulder; some the arm; some the hand; some the finger; some the nail; some the neck; some the jaw; some the lip; some the tooth; some the tongue; some the palate; some the throat; some the cheek; some the ear; some the nose; some the eye; some the eyebrow; some the forehead; some the head; some they kill outright; some they destroy. For one who undertakes weapons here, these undertakings remain unrecognized.

For one who does not undertake violence here, these undertakings have been fully understood. Having understood them, the wise man should neither himself cause violence to the earth-element, nor cause others to cause violence to the earth-element, nor approve of others who are causing violence to the earth-element. He for whom these undertakings involving action toward the earth have been fully understood—he indeed is a sage who has fully understood his karma. Thus I say.
This I say: Just as a mendicant who is straightforward, has entered the religious order, and is free from deceit is described—
having renounced the wavering of those with faith by following that very faith in which he went forth,
the heroes, being humble, have entered the great path.
Having fully understood the world through the authoritative teaching, one is free from fear on all sides.
Regarding this, I say: one should not deny the world, nor should one deny oneself. He who denies the world denies himself; he who denies himself denies the world.

Seeing [this] with shame, some proclaim themselves to be "homeless ones" (*anagāra*), yet they engage in various kinds of weapons for the purpose of water-activity. While engaging in such weapons for water, they harm many other living beings of various forms. Regarding this, the Blessed One has proclaimed full understanding (*pariṇṇā*). For the sake of this very life—for the sake of salutation, honor, and worship, for liberation from birth and death, and as a means to ward off suffering—one personally engages in weapons for water, causes others to engage in weapons for water, or approves of others who are engaging in weapons for water. That leads to one's own harm; that leads to one's own lack of awakening. But he, becoming fully awakened, having heard it from the Blessed One or in the presence of the homeless ones, rises up and understands what ought to be understood. Thus, for some here, knowledge arises.

This indeed is bondage; this indeed is delusion; this indeed is death; this indeed is hell. Thus attached to this world, people, by means of various kinds of weapons through the undertaking of activities that produce [karmic] results, while undertaking weapons that produce results, harm many other living beings of various forms. This I say: there are living beings dependent on water, numerous souls. And here, O worthy ones, among the ascetics, those who live in water have been declared. Observe this weapon thoroughly;
the weapon has been explained separately.
Or else there is taking what is not given.
It is fit for them, it is not fit for them to drink, or for the sake of adornment.
They are struck down by various weapons.
Even in this case, there is no destruction for them.

In this regard, for one who employs weapons, these acts of violence remain uncomprehended; for one who does not employ weapons, these acts of violence become comprehended. Having understood this, the wise man should neither himself employ weapons that cause arising [of karma], nor cause others to employ weapons that cause arising, nor approve of others who employ weapons that cause arising. He for whom these acts of employing weapons that cause arising have been fully comprehended—he indeed is a sage who has comprehended karma. Thus I say.
This I say: one should never deny the world, nor should one deny oneself. He who denies the world denies himself; he who denies himself denies the world.
He who knows the path to the long journey of the world knows the path to the non-path; he who knows the path to the non-path knows the path to the long journey of the world.
This has been seen by the heroes, who are self-restrained, ever striving, and ever heedful.

He who, though established in virtues, is negligent, is indeed called a "staff-bearer" (one who inflicts harm). Having understood this, the wise man should now resolve: "That which I previously did through negligence, I shall not do again."

Seeing them acting thus, some ascetics, feeling ashamed, proclaim themselves as "Anagāras" (homeless ones). Yet, by means of various weapons, through the undertaking of the work of fire, they employ the weapon of fire; and in so employing the weapon of fire, they harm many other kinds of living beings. Regarding this, the Blessed One has proclaimed full understanding: for the sake of this very life—its praise, honor, and worship; for the sake of escaping birth and death; and for the sake of warding off suffering—one personally undertakes the weapon of fire, causes others to undertake the weapon of fire, or approves of others undertaking the weapon of fire. That leads to one's own harm; that leads to one's own lack of enlightenment. Understanding this, having risen up with what is to be grasped, and having heard it from the Blessed One or in the presence of the Anagāras, some here come to know: "This indeed is a bond; this indeed is delusion; this indeed is death; this indeed is hell. Thus the world is entangled in this, whereby, by means of various weapons and through the undertaking of the work of fire, one employs the weapon of fire and harms many other kinds of living beings.

This I say: there are living beings dependent upon the earth, dependent upon grass, dependent upon leaves, dependent upon wood, dependent upon cow dung, and dependent upon husks; there are flying creatures that come together by chance. And indeed, when touched by fire, some undergo a state of distress; those who undergo distress there meet with calamity, and those who meet with calamity there perish.

In this regard, for one who employs the weapon [of violence], these acts of undertaking are not fully understood; for one who does not employ the weapon [of violence] in this regard, these acts of undertaking are fully understood. Having understood this, the wise person should neither himself employ the weapon of fire, nor cause others to employ the weapon of fire, nor approve of others employing the weapon of fire. He for whom these undertakings involving the action of fire are fully understood—he indeed is a sage who has fully understood his actions. Thus I say.

"I shall not do that; being wise, I shall rise above intoxication. Having understood this as freedom from fear, he who does not perform it is one who has transcended; having transcended this, he is called a "homeless one" (anagāra).
Whatever is a quality (*guṇa*) is a whirlpool (*āvarta*); whatever is a whirlpool is a quality.
Looking upward, downward, across, and toward the east, he sees forms; hearing, he hears sounds.
Whether above, below, across, or in the east, one who is infatuated becomes infatuated with forms and also with sounds.
This world is thus described: here, one who is unrestrained and lacking in instruction, repeatedly craving for sensory qualities, is of crooked conduct.
One who is heedless dwells in a household.

Look at those who, feeling ashamed [of their own conduct], claim individually, "We are homeless ascetics," yet engage in this: by means of various kinds of instruments, through the undertaking of work involving vegetation, they, while employing weapons upon vegetation, harm many other living beings of various forms. Regarding this, the Blessed One has indeed proclaimed full understanding: for the sake of this very life—its praise, honor, and worship; for the sake of liberation from birth and death; and for the sake of warding off suffering—one personally undertakes the use of weapons upon vegetation, causes others to undertake the use of weapons upon vegetation, or approves of others undertaking the use of weapons upon vegetation. That leads to one's harm; that leads to one's lack of awakening.

One who understands this should rise up, having grasped what is to be taken up, having heard it from the Blessed One or in the presence of the *anagāras*. Then, some here gain this knowledge: "This indeed is a bond; this indeed is delusion; this indeed is death; this indeed is hell. Thus the world is obsessed with this meaning. For by means of various weapons, through the undertaking of action involving plants, one who undertakes the weapon against plants harms many other kinds of living beings.

I say this: this too is subject to birth, that too is subject to birth; this too is subject to growth, that too is subject to growth; this too possesses consciousness, that too possesses consciousness; this too, when cut, joins together, that too, when cut, joins together; this too requires nutriment, that too requires nutriment; this too is impermanent, that too is impermanent; this too is non-eternal, that too is non-eternal; [this too is unstable, that too is unstable]; this too is subject to accumulation and decay, that too is subject to accumulation and decay; this too is subject to change, that too is subject to change.

In this regard, for one who employs violence, these acts of violence remain unrecognized; for one who does not employ violence, these acts of violence become recognized. Having recognized this, the wise man should neither himself employ violence against plants, nor cause others to employ violence against plants, nor approve of others employing violence against plants. He for whom these acts of violence against plants are fully recognized is indeed a sage who has understood karma. Thus I say.

This I say: there are mobile beings, such as those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, those born from fluids, those born from filth, those born by spontaneous generation, those born from sprouts, and those born by transformation; this is what is called "the cycle of existence" (*saṃsāra*).

For the dull-witted who do not understand, having reflected and scrutinized [this], [one realizes] that for every single living being, for every single creature, for every single soul, and for every single sentient being, there is suffering, lack of peace, and great terror—pain that is not conducive to liberation. Thus I say. Mobile beings tremble in the various directions and intermediate points.
There, in various places, look at those who, being afflicted, torment themselves.

There are living beings that exist separately; see them, O seeker, as they act with restraint. There are some who, proclaiming themselves "homeless ones," engage in the destruction of the mobile-bodied realm with various kinds of weapons. In doing so, while destroying the mobile-bodied realm with weapons, they harm many other kinds of living beings. Regarding this, the Blessed One has indeed proclaimed full understanding: for the sake of this very life—its praise, honor, and worship, for liberation from birth and death, and for the warding off of suffering—one personally engages in the destruction of the mobile-bodied realm with weapons, causes others to engage in the destruction of the mobile-bodied realm with weapons, or approves of others engaging in the destruction of the mobile-bodied realm with weapons. That leads to one's own harm; that leads to one's own lack of awakening. But he, becoming fully awakened, having heard it from the Blessed One or in the presence of the homeless ones, rises up with what is to be understood. Then this knowledge arises in some here: "This is indeed a bond; this is indeed delusion; this is indeed death; this is indeed hell. Thus the world is obsessed, such that by engaging in the destruction of the mobile-bodied realm with various kinds of weapons, while destroying the mobile-bodied realm with weapons, they harm many other kinds of living beings.

I say this: some are driven for their skin; some are driven for their hide; some are driven for their flesh; some are driven for their blood; some are driven for their heart; some are driven for their bile; some are driven for their fat; some are driven for their gall; some are driven for their tail; some are driven for their hair; some are driven for their horn; some are driven for their tusks; some are driven for their fangs; some are driven for their claws; some are driven for their sinews; some are driven for their bones; some are driven for their marrow; some are driven for profit; some are driven for no profit; some are driven because they have harmed me; some are driven because they are harming me; some are driven because they will harm me.

In this regard, for one who employs weapons against living beings, these acts of violence remain unrecognized; for one who does not employ weapons against living beings, these acts of violence become recognized. Having recognized this, the wise person should neither himself employ weapons against the body of mobile creatures, nor cause others to employ weapons against the body of mobile creatures, nor approve of others employing weapons against the body of mobile creatures. He for whom these acts of violence against the body of mobile creatures are fully recognized is indeed a sage who has understood karma. Thus I say.
The Master is capable of revulsion toward existence.

Seeing the reflection [of the self], and knowing it to be for one's own betterment, he who knows the internal knows the external; he who knows the external knows the internal. This is the same for others.
Having attained peace here, the detached do not long for life.

Seeing them acting thus, some ascetics, feeling ashamed, proclaim individually: "We are indeed *anagāras* (homeless ones). Yet, by means of various kinds of weapons, through the undertaking of the activity of air, they inflict injury upon many kinds of living beings while undertaking the weapon of air. Regarding this, the Blessed One has proclaimed full understanding: for the sake of this very life—namely, for the sake of salutation, honor, and worship; for the sake of escaping birth and death; and for the sake of warding off suffering—one personally undertakes the weapon of air, causes others to undertake the weapon of air, or approves of others undertaking the weapon of air. That leads to one's harm; that leads to one's lack of awakening. Understanding this, having risen up with what is to be grasped, and having heard it from the presence of the Blessed One or from the *anagāras*, the knowledge arises in some here: "This is indeed a bond; this is indeed delusion; this is indeed death; this is indeed hell. Thus the world is obsessed, such that by undertaking the weapon of air through the undertaking of the activity of air with various kinds of weapons, it inflicts injury upon many kinds of living beings.

This I say: There are beings that have come together and those that come together by chance; and some, when touched by contact, undergo injury. Those there who undergo injury perish; those there who perish go forth [to rebirth]. For one who employs violence here, these acts of violence remain unrecognized; for one who does not employ violence here, these acts of violence become recognized. Having recognized this, the wise person should not himself employ the weapon of wind, nor should he cause others to employ the weapon of wind, nor should he approve of others employing the weapon of wind. He for whom these acts of employing the weapon of wind are recognized is indeed a sage who has recognized his karma. Thus I say.

Even here, one should know those who, though being instructed, do not delight in right conduct; who, while undertaking [worldly] activities, depart from discipline; led by their own whims and obsessed with them, being attached to such undertakings, they create further bondage.

He who possesses wealth—by means of his own self endowed with all-encompassing wisdom—does not perform sinful karma that ought not to be done, nor does he cause others to do so. Having understood this, the wise man should neither himself initiate violence against the six classes of living beings, nor cause others to initiate violence against the six classes of living beings, nor approve of others initiating violence against the six classes of living beings. He for whom these initiations of violence against the six classes of living beings have been fully understood is indeed a sage who has comprehended karma. Thus I say.
[The Second Chapter – The Conquest of the World]

"That which is a quality (*guṇa*) is a fundamental basis (*mūlasthāna*); that which is a fundamental basis is a quality. Thus, one who is intent on qualities, through great attachment, becomes again and again addicted to worldly life, thinking: "My mother, my father, my brother, my sister, my wife, my sons, my daughters, my grandsons, my friends, kinsmen, relatives, and associates; my separate belongings, my turnings-about, my food, and my clothing"—thus entangled in these things, the world is addicted to worldly life. Worrying day and night, rising up at improper times, intent on acquisition, greedy for wealth, plundering, acting with recklessness, and with a mind fixed upon this [worldly life], the lifespan here for some of these men is indeed short, as follows: [The text continues with the description of various short-lived beings.]

As the discernment of tastes declines, as the discernment of forms declines, as the discernment of odors declines, as the discernment of flavors declines, and as the discernment of tangibles declines—perceiving indeed that [youth] has passed away—one then, at some time, gives rise to a state of delusion.

Even those with whom one dwells—though they were formerly one's own kin and have since passed away—may later pass away even while one is still among them; they are not capable of being your protection or your refuge, nor are you capable of being their protection or their refuge. This [body] is not for laughter, nor for play, nor for pleasure, nor for adornment.
Thus having arisen for the sake of the higher life, and reflecting upon this interval, the wise man should not be negligent for even a moment; for youth and life pass away.

Those who are heedless here in this life are killers, cutters, breakers, plunderers, ravagers, destroyers, and intimidators; thinking "I shall do what has not been done," they imagine themselves secure. Yet those with whom they dwell—even their own kin—may at some time have supported them previously, and they too may later support those kin. They are not capable of being your protection or your refuge, nor are you capable of being their protection or their refuge.

Or, by means of the remnants of what has been eaten, accumulation is made here for the sake of food by some who are undisciplined; then, at some time, diseases arise which [afflict them], or those with whom they dwell—whether their own kin or others—will at some time first abandon them, or they will later abandon those kin, saying: "You are not capable of being our protection or our refuge, nor are you capable of being their protection or their refuge.
Having realized that suffering and pleasure are individual, and having observed that life is indeed fleeting, one should reflect upon this.
O wise one, know the moment!

As long as the discernment of hearing is not lost, as long as the discernment of sight is not lost, as long as the discernment of smell is not lost, as long as the discernment of taste is not lost, and as long as the discernment of touch is not lost—while these various forms of wisdom remain unimpaired—you should properly pursue your own welfare. Thus I say: that wise man who turns away from worldly attachment is liberated in that very moment.

Some, though questioned regarding the lack of [worldly] command, turn back; they are dull-witted, obscured by delusion, thinking, "We shall be without possessions. Having renounced, yet when sensual pleasures are obtained, they pursue them. Through lack of discernment, such sages reflect [on worldly things]; herein lies delusion, again and again, neither on this shore nor on the further shore. Truly, those people are liberated who go to the further shore; loathing greed through non-greed, he does not pursue sensual pleasures when they are obtained.

Having subdued greed and having gone forth, this one who is free from karma knows and sees through inspection; he does not long for [worldly things] and is thus called a "homeless one. But day and night he is consumed by anxiety, rising up at improper times and proper times alike, intent on acquisition, greedy for wealth, seizing things by force, his mind fixed on plunder. Regarding these various matters, he repeatedly employs the use of force—thinking it is for the sake of liberation from evil, or else out of hope—for the strength of his kin, for the strength of his family, for the strength of his relatives, for the strength of his friends, for the strength of his deceased ancestors, for the strength of the gods, for the strength of the king, for the strength of thieves, for the strength of guests, for the strength of the poor, or for the strength of ascetics. Thus, through such diverse affairs, he employs violence, thinking it is done out of fear, or imagining it will bring release from sin, or driven by expectation.

Having understood this, the wise man should not himself initiate violence for these purposes, nor should he cause another to initiate violence for these purposes, nor should he approve of another who initiates violence for these purposes. This is the path proclaimed by the noble ones, wherein the skillful one shall not be defiled—thus I say.

Sometimes one is born into a high caste, sometimes into a low caste; knowing this—that one is neither deficient nor superior, and should not yearn for anything—who would speak of caste? Who would speak of pride? Or what would a single person covet? Therefore, the wise man should neither rejoice nor be angry. Know the well-being of all living beings.

Being self-restrained and observing these things, he understands them as follows: blindness, deafness, being a beast, being one-eyed, being lame, being hunchbacked, being a eunuch, being leprous, and being crippled. Along with negligence, one wanders through various kinds of wombs and experiences diverse types of sensations.

Not understanding this, they are struck down and repeatedly wander through birth and death. Life is dear to some men here; they claim ownership over fields and lands. Clinging to gold, women, and their attachment to red and white jewels and earrings, they find no austerity, self-restraint, or discipline therein. The fool, desiring to live and prattling on, being deluded, falls into error.
Those people who follow the eternal path do not even long for this.
Having fully understood birth and death, one should practice firmly in the transition [to liberation]. (Āyār. 81)

There is no escaping Time; all living beings cherish life, desire happiness, loathe suffering, detest death, and love to live. Life is dear to all. Having acquired property—whether two-footed or four-footed—and having accumulated it by means of the three types of action (thought, word, and deed), whatever measure of it there may be, whether small or great, he remains attached to it for the sake of enjoyment. Then, at one time, that which has been amassed becomes a vast accumulation of possessions. At another time, his heirs divide it among themselves, or thieves steal it, or kings plunder it, or it is lost, or it perishes, or it is consumed by a fire in his house. Thus, the fool, performing cruel deeds for the sake of another, becomes deluded by that suffering and undergoes a reversal of fortune. This has indeed been proclaimed by the Sage: these people are not able to cross over the flood, nor can they reach the further shore; they do not go to the opposite bank, nor can they reach the end. Having taken up what is to be grasped, he does not remain steadfast in that state; encountering what is contrary, the ignorant man persists in that very position.

For the one who has seen the truth (the Pāsa-ga), there is no rebirth; but the fool, attached to desires and finding them agreeable, being untrained from suffering, suffers and wanders on through the cycle of sufferings—thus I say.

Then, at some time, diseases arise by which those with whom one lives may, at some time, first desert him, or he may later desert them; they are not capable of being your protection or your refuge, nor are you capable of being their protection or their refuge. Knowing that suffering and pleasure are individual, [one realizes]: "Lusts pursue me," as is the case for some men here.

Whatever measure of food he has there, whether small or great, he remains attached to it for the sake of eating. Then, at one time, that which was left over becomes a great accumulation of possessions; yet at another time, his heirs divide it among themselves, or thieves steal it, or kings plunder it, or it perishes, or it is destroyed, or it is consumed by a fire in his house. Thus, the fool, performing cruel deeds for the sake of another, being deluded by that suffering, falls into perversion.

O wise one, having discarded both hope and desire! You yourself must extract that very arrow by which you might exist or not exist. Those people who are shrouded in delusion do not understand this: "The world is overwhelmed by fear. O people, they say: "These are the sources [of suffering]—for the sake of pain, for delusion, for death, for hell, and for rebirth as an animal. Constantly deluded, he does not recognize the Dharma. Or rather, the Hero says: "Heedfulness is the remedy for great delusion; enough with negligence for one who is skilled. Contemplating peaceful death, contemplating the perishable nature [of things], see that it is not enough; enough for you with these!"

Behold this, O sage! It is a great danger; one should not beg for anything at all. He is praised as a hero who does not become despondent regarding acquisitions. If someone does not give him anything, he should not become angry. Having received only a little, he should not disparage it. When refused, he should reflect upon it. You should dwell in accordance with this state of silence (mona). Thus I say.

At night, various kinds of undertakings involving weapons are carried out by people for the sake of their own karmic activities, namely: for themselves, for their sons, daughters, daughters-in-law, kinsmen, nurses, kings, male servants, female servants, laborers, and laborers; for morning meals, separate snacks, midday meals, evening meals, and for the purpose of storing up and accumulating provisions here for the food of certain men.

Having risen [from the world], the homeless one is noble, noble in wisdom, and noble in vision; he perceives the connection [to suffering] and has seen it. He does not buy, nor cause to buy, nor approve of one who buys. Having fully understood all that is foul-smelling (impure), he should wander about free from foul-smell.

Not appearing in the context of buying and selling, he neither buys nor causes to buy, nor approves of one who buys. That monk should know the right time, know strength, know moderation, know weariness, know the moment, know discipline, know his own doctrine, know the doctrines of others, and know the inner state of beings. Not being possessive toward acquisitions, he acts according to the right time and is free from fixed expectations.

Having cut through both [extremes], he goes forth [as a monk], [carrying] a robe, an alms-bowl, a blanket, a broom, a dwelling, and a seat made of straw; he should recognize only these as his requirements.

When food is obtained, the homeless one should not harbor deceitful thoughts. As this has been proclaimed by the Blessed One: he should not be elated by gain, nor should he be dejected by lack of gain; even if much is obtained, he should not store it away; he should withdraw himself from possessiveness. Otherwise, one should observe and avoid [faults]. This is the path proclaimed by the Noble Ones; herein, the skillful one should not be defiled—thus I say.
Sensual pleasures are difficult to transcend; life is difficult to sustain. This person who craves sensual pleasures indeed grieves, suffers, is tormented, and is consumed by fever.

The one with far-reaching vision, the seer of the world, knows the lower portion of the world, knows the upper portion, and knows the middle portion. Having discovered the juncture here among mortals while the world is wandering in attachment, he is the hero praised by the wise: he who releases those who are bound. As it is within, so it is without; as it is without, so it is within. The wise man, through careful examination, perceives the internal parts of the body as putrid and observes them separately as they flow forth.

Having understood this with wisdom, do not indulge in craving; do not direct yourself toward those [objects] in a transverse manner. This man is indeed full of doubt, deceitful, and deluded by his own actions; he commits that [act] again and increases his own greed and enmity. That which is described here is for the sake of its very suppression. He who possesses great faith acts like an immortal, but seeing this suffering and lacking full understanding, he weeps.

Know that which I say: when a wise physician speaks, he is a slayer, a cutter, a piercer, a plunderer, a ravager, and a destroyer; thinking "I shall do what has not been done," he does it even for one who does not desire it. Enough with the company of such a fool, or with the fool who causes him to act. This does not occur to a true renunciant—thus I say. Understanding this as something to be grasped, one should exert oneself; therefore, one should neither commit evil karma nor cause it to be committed.

There may be one who violates any one of these six [precepts]; seeking pleasure, he laments while deluded by his own suffering and falls into perversion. Through his own negligence, he creates for himself a separate destiny (rebirth) in which these living beings are obstructed; this is called "thorough comprehension" (*parijñā*) for the subsiding of karma.

He who abandons the mind that clings to "mine" abandons what is clung to as "mine. He is indeed a sage who has seen the path, for whom there is nothing clung to as "mine. Having understood this, the wise man, having known the world and vomited out the worldly notion, should exert himself with discernment; thus I say. The hero does not tolerate discontent, nor does the hero tolerate contentment; since the hero is undisturbed in mind, therefore the hero does not become attached. (Āyāra 101)
Enduring sounds and touches, the sage, having become weary of the delight in this life, should adopt silence and gnaw away at the body of karma.
The heroes who see all things resort to what is secluded and coarse; such a sage is declared to have crossed over the flood, liberated, and withdrawn from worldly ties. Thus I say. (Āyār. 102)

The sage who is difficult to control through improper instruction is one who is base, sickly, and talkative; such a person is not praised as a hero. He who transcends the attachment to the world is praised as a hero; this is declared to be the true knowledge. Regarding the suffering that has been proclaimed here for human beings, the experts describe its full comprehension. Having comprehended karma in every respect, he who sees nothing else is one who delights in nothing else; he who delights in nothing else is one who sees nothing else. As it is with the full for some, so it is with the base for others; as it is with the base for some, so it is with the full for others.

Furthermore, even if one kills while not being censured, know that there is no "this is for my welfare" in this matter either; for who is the man, and what is his doctrine? He is the hero praised by the wise, who releases those bound above, below, and in the intermediate directions. Moving with full discernment in every way, he is not smeared by the stain of slaughter. That wise man is a hero who knows how to avoid destruction and seeks release from bondage; indeed, the skillful one is neither bound nor liberated. Having fully understood the world’s attachment—both that which is undertaken and that which is not undertaken, and that which has not been begun and should not be begun—he transcends the worldly convention in every respect.

There is no rebirth for the one who has seen the truth; but the fool, attached to desires and finding them agreeable, being untrained from suffering, remains a sufferer and wanders on through the cycle of sufferings—thus I say.
[The Third Chapter – On Coldness] Those who are asleep are not sages; sages are always awake.

Know that suffering prevails in the world; having understood the nature of the world, one should here become a teacher who has restrained himself. For him, sounds, forms, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations have been fully comprehended.

Such a person—possessed of self-control, knowledge, wisdom, righteousness, and celibacy—understands the world through his insights. He is called a sage, one who knows the Dharma, upright, who has turned away from the stream [of worldly existence], and who thoroughly understands attachment.

Casting off cold and heat, that Nirgrantha endures both aversion and delight; he feels no harshness, being a hero who has transcended wakefulness and enmity. In this way, you shall be liberated from suffering. A man brought low by old age and death—if he is constantly deluded, he does not recognize the Dharma.

Beholding living beings who are afflicted by illness, one should wander about with vigilance. Wise, observe the mantra; knowing that this suffering is born of violent activity (*ārambha*), the deceitful and negligent person enters the womb again. Observing sounds and forms, upright, fearing death, one is liberated from death. Being vigilant regarding sensual pleasures and ceased from evil deeds, the hero protects himself and is an expert. He who is an expert in the weapon consisting of the various states of rebirth is an expert in the weaponless; he who is an expert in the weaponless is an expert in the weapon consisting of the various states of rebirth. For one without karma, worldly activity (*vavahāra*) does not exist; through karma, the burden is produced, and karma is to be examined.

Having thoroughly examined and abandoned every festival rooted in karma, and being invisible through both extremes [of past and future], the wise man, having understood and known the world, and having vomited out worldly attachment—that wise man should exert himself. Thus I say.
O noble one! Behold birth and growth here; know the well-being of beings by examining them.
Therefore, knowing the triple knowledge to be supreme, the one who sees with completeness does not commit evil. (Āyār. 115)
"Release the bond here from those who live by violence; seeing both [worlds], those greedy for sensual pleasures make their accumulation. Being drenched [in karma], they enter the womb again.
Even having encountered laughter, the killer thinks, 'It is joy. (Āyār. 116)
Enough with association with the fool; it increases one's own enmity. (Āyār.

117) Therefore, having understood the supreme state, the wise one who perceives his own welfare does not commit evil. Having plucked out both the tip and the root, the steadfast one, seeing beyond karma, cuts them off completely. (Āyār. 118)

He is liberated from death—he who has seen the danger, the sage who perceives the world, the supreme seer, living in solitude, tranquil, restrained, disciplined, ever-victorious; he wanders as one awaiting his time. Indeed, much evil karma has been manifested. Therefore, let the wise man establish firm resolve in truth and be moderate; thus he consumes all evil karma. This person indeed possesses many thoughts; he is capable of filling [the world] with slaughter, with affliction, and with possession—of slaughter, affliction, and possession of people; of slaughter, affliction, and possession of the countryside.

Having practiced this matter, some have indeed risen up; therefore, one should not indulge in that second [state], seeing it to be essence-less. Seeing rebirth and death as distinct, O Brahmin, wander as a knower. He neither destroys nor causes to destroy, nor does he approve of one who destroys. Having become indifferent to delight, detached from worldly beings, seeing no pride, he sits still through his evil karmas. The hero, having slain anger and pride, sees the great hell in the snare of greed;
therefore, the hero, abstaining from violence, should cut off the stream, becoming light in his course. (Āyāra 1.2.3)
Having fully understood the bonds and having understood the stream of existence here today, the hero should wander self-controlled.
Having perceived the wrong path here by men, one should not, among living beings, initiate violence against living beings. Thus I say. (Āyār. 124)

Having understood the junction of the world, look both within and without; therefore, one should neither kill nor cause [others] to kill. Since this mutual hesitation and scrutiny leads one not to commit evil karma, what reason could there be for a sage to do so?
Observing equanimity therein, the knower should inspire himself with confidence, never being heedless, regarding that which is supreme and unsurpassed.

The hero, guarding his conduct at all times, should exert himself in the conquest of birth and death. He should proceed with detachment toward forms, whether they be large or small. Having fully understood coming and going, and being invisible to both extremes, he is not cut, not broken, not burned, and not harmed—like gold in the entire world.
Some do not remember what was before; what is his past, or what is his future?
Some men here in this world say that what was in the past for him will be so in the future.

But those who have attained the goal do not perceive the goal as being in the past, nor as being in the future; rather, having shaken off their conceptual constructs and beholding this [truth], the great seers, having drunk it up, destroy [the karmic influx] as they progress. (Āyār. 128–129)

What is sorrow? What is joy? Even in this regard, one should move without grasping; having abandoned all laughter, wandering as one who is restrained and guarded. O men! You alone are your own friend; why do you seek a friend outside?

What one knows as "elevated" (uccālayita), that one should know as "far-extended" (dūrālayita); what one knows as "far-extended," that one should know as "elevated. O man, by grasping yourself alone, you shall thus be released from suffering. O man, recognize only the truth; established in the command of truth, that wise man crosses over Māra. Having taken up the Dharma with fortitude, he perceives what is beneficial.
From both [worlds], for the sake of the life of praise, honor, and worship, some become negligent.
Touched by suffering for the sake of endurance, he does not become agitated; seeing the world, the wise one is liberated from the deceptions of this world and the next. Thus I say.
Having vomited forth anger, pride, deceit, and greed—this is the vision of the seer (pāsa-ka), who has laid down the weapons and made an end of rebirth; his acquisition is like that of a cart-driver.
He who knows the one, knows all; he who knows all, knows the one.

For one who is heedless in every way there is fear; for one who is heedful in every way there is no fear. He who is called "one" is called "many," and he who is called "many" is called "one. Having understood the suffering of the world and having vomited up attachment to the world, the heroes go to the Great Vehicle; they go beyond the further shore and do not long for life.

When discerning one thing, he discerns it separately; when discerning separately, he discerns it as one. The wise person, possessing faith, having understood the world through the teaching, attains fearlessness from all sides. There is violence beyond the other [the self], but there is no non-violence beyond the other.

He who perceives anger perceives pride; he who perceives pride perceives deceit; he who perceives deceit perceives greed; he who perceives greed perceives attachment; he who perceives attachment perceives aversion; he who perceives aversion perceives delusion; he who perceives delusion perceives conception; he who perceives conception perceives birth; he who perceives birth perceives death; he who perceives death perceives hell; he who perceives hell perceives the animal realm; he who perceives the animal realm perceives suffering.

Therefore, the wise man should turn away from anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, aversion, delusion, conception, birth, death, hell, the animal realm, and suffering. This is the vision of the seer (pāsa-ka), who has laid aside the weapons and made an end of worldly existence; for whom the yoke of rebirth has been set aside, there exists no further burden for the seer. There is none. Thus I say.

This I say: all those Arhats and Blessed Ones who have passed away, who are present now, and who will arise in the future—all of them declare thus, speak thus, teach thus, and proclaim thus: "All breaths, all beings, all souls, and all living creatures must not be killed, must not be subjected to violence, must not be imprisoned, must not be tormented, and must not be destroyed. This Dharma is pure, eternal, and everlasting; having understood the world, it has been proclaimed by those possessing knowledge. That is to say: whether they have risen or have not risen, whether they have approached or have not approached, whether they have ceased from violence or have not ceased from violence, whether they possess worldly possessions or are without possessions, whether they are restrained or unrestrained—this is the truth, this is so, and this is declared in this regard.

Having taken that up, one should neither hide it nor cast it aside; having understood the Dharma as it truly is, one should attain detachment through what is seen, and not pursue the search for worldly things.

For whom these [categories] do not exist, how could there be another for him? That which is called "seen," "heard," "sensed," and "cognized" is merely what is being described. Striving and faltering, they fashion birth again and again.
Day and night, the hero who exerts himself is always possessed of wisdom; but the heedless one looks outward. Therefore, you should always exert yourself with vigilance—thus I say.

Those which are influxes (*āsava*) are also outflows (*parissava*); those which are outflows are also influxes. Those which are non-influxes are non-outflows; those which are non-outflows are non-influxes. One who understands these points, having comprehended the world through the teaching, has explained it separately. The Knower (*nāṇī*) instructs here those human beings who have entered the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), who are awakening, and who have attained discernment. Whether they are diligent or negligent, [he teaches] that "this is according to truth," so I say. There is no escape from the mouth of Death. Desires are enticing, crooked, and deceptive; seized by Time, settled in negligence, they fashion their various births one after another.

In this world, some have acquaintances here and there; they experience pleasant sensations resulting from their past lives. One who persists in evil deeds continues to persist in them, while one who does not persist in evil deeds does not continue to persist in them. Some say this, or else the wise say it; some say it, or else the wise say it.

"Whatever recluses and brahmins there may be in the world, they each speak in dispute, saying: 'This has been seen by us, heard by us, thought by us, and known by us; it has been thoroughly scrutinized by us above, below, across, and in all directions—that all breathing things, all beings, all souls, and all creatures must be killed, must be subjected to violence, must be imprisoned, must be tormented, and must be destroyed. Know this: there is no fault in this. This is the speech of the ignoble. Regarding this, those who are noble have spoken thus:"

Whatever you have seen wrongly, whatever you have heard wrongly, whatever you have thought wrongly, whatever you have understood wrongly, and whatever has been poorly scrutinized by you above, below, across, and in all directions—namely, that which you thus declare, thus speak, thus prescribe, and thus teach: "All breathers, all beings, all souls, all living things are to be killed, to be maimed, to be imprisoned, to be tormented, to be destroyed"—know this: there is no fault here; this is the speech of the ignoble.

We, however, declare thus, speak thus, prescribe thus, and explain thus: "All breathers, all beings, all living things, all souls—these must not be killed, nor subjected to violence, nor imprisoned, nor tormented, nor destroyed. Know this: there is no fault in this; this is the word of the Noble Ones (*ārya*). We shall now inquire individually regarding the ancient doctrine and tradition: "O followers of false views (*pāpāduka*), is suffering pleasant for you, or is it unpleasant? To those who have accepted the principle of equanimity, one should say: "For all breathers, all beings, all living things, all souls, suffering is unpleasant, it is lack of peace, it is a great terror. Thus I say.

Go forth beyond this world; look upon all those in the entire world who possess wisdom. Observe those who have laid down the rod of violence toward all beings, who cast off their life-span, men who are self-controlled, upright, and knowers of the Dharma. Having understood that "this suffering is born of worldly undertakings," those who see with perfect vision have spoken thus: "All these practitioners of evil are experts in the full comprehension of suffering. Thus, having comprehended karma in every respect.

In this world, the wise man who desires the command, being free from enmity, should contemplate the self alone; he should shake off the body, emaciate himself, and wither away the self, just as a consuming fire burns up withered wood. Thus, being composed within himself and free from enmity, having cast aside anger, remaining unshakable, and contemplating that this life-span is restricted, let him know suffering both present and future. He experiences various contacts separately and beholds the world in its agitation. Those who have submerged themselves in evil karmas and are without worldly motives—they are declared [to be the ones who have attained peace]. Therefore, one who has attained higher knowledge should not be inflamed by passion; thus I say.

Having abandoned former attachments—whether by agitating, piercing, or crushing—and having left behind tranquility, therefore the hero, free from mental distraction, should always be diligent, self-controlled, composed, and striving. The path of the heroes who proceed without turning back is difficult to follow; having cast off flesh and blood, this man, steadfast and heroic, is declared worthy of being taken as a refuge. Having dwelt in the practice of celibacy, he shakes off the accumulation [of karma]. But those fools, whose senses are not severed and who are mired in the stream of worldly acquisition, whose bonds are unbroken and whose attachments they have not transcended, lack discernment in the darkness; for them there is no attainment through the Teacher’s command. Thus I say.

For whom there is nothing before, after, or in between—how could there be anything for him? He is indeed one possessed of wisdom, a Buddha, who has desisted from violence. Behold those who perceive correctly! Having severed the external stream [of craving], the seer of the state beyond action, having seen that action bears fruit in this world of mortals, the knower of the Vedas then departs.

"O noble ones! Those heroes who are restrained, harmonious, ever-victorious, who perceive the congregation, who have restrained themselves, and who observe the world as it truly is—in the east, west, south, and north—they abide in truth. We shall declare the knowledge of those heroes, who are restrained, harmonious, ever-victorious, who perceive the congregation, who have restrained themselves, and who observe the world as it truly is: Is there any affliction for the one who sees (the truth)? It does not exist. Thus I say.
[The Fifth Chapter – The Essence of the World]

O Āvantī, however many people in this world plunder—whether for a purpose or for no purpose—they plunder only these [sensual pleasures]. Those sensual pleasures are within Māra; since they are within Māra, one is far from them. He who is neither within nor far from them sees it like a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass, blown away, turned over, and driven by the wind. Such is the life of the fool, the dull-witted one who lacks discernment. Committing cruel deeds, the fool, deluded by that suffering, undergoes perversion. Through delusion, he goes from womb to death, again and again in this delusion.

For one who fully understands doubt, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) becomes fully understood; for one who does not fully understand doubt, cyclic existence remains ununderstood. He who is detached should not indulge in what belongs to others. Having done so, the fool, lacking discernment, commits a second folly. [The commentary states: "He who indeed indulges in sensual objects, or having indulged, does not confess it; or being questioned by another, he denies it; or he defames that other person with his own fault or with an even more wicked fault. Having obtained [the opportunity], one should examine it thoroughly from all sides; having returned, one should command [himself] to refrain from such indulgence. Thus I say.

Behold some who are greedy for forms while they are being transformed; here, again and again, there are those in the world who live by violence—those very ones who live by violence. Here too, the fool, while being cooked, delights in evil deeds, thinking that what is no refuge is a refuge. In this regard, for some there is a solitary life; yet he is full of anger, full of pride, full of deceit, full of guile, full of passion, full of fraud, full of cruelty, and full of many schemes. Overpowered by the influx [of karma] and covered by it, he proclaims a doctrine of asceticism while remaining steeped in worldly talk, thinking, "Let no one see me. Constantly deluded through the fault of ignorance and negligence, he does not recognize the Dharma. Alas, O people! You are afflicted and skilled in karma; those who, being devoted to ignorance, claim to have found liberation, merely wander about in the cycle of rebirth. Thus I say.

O Āvantī, who in this world are those who live without undertaking [evil deeds]? Among them, one who restrains himself here and reflects upon that [restraint], perceives: "This is the junction. He who considers this moment to be the opportunity for this physical existence—this is the path proclaimed by the Noble Ones. Having arisen, do not be negligent; knowing that suffering is individual and experience is personal, men here have diverse inclinations, and suffering has been proclaimed as distinct for each. Thus, being non-violent and non-injurious, even when touched by [unpleasant] sensations, he remains undisturbed.

This is declared to be the practice of tranquility (*samiyā-pariyāya*) for those who are not attached to evil deeds; or rather, do physical ailments (*āyaṅkā*) touch them? Thus, the steadfast one should endure such sensations when touched by them. Behold this form (*rūpa*) and this connection (*sandhi*): it was drunk before and it will be drunk after; it is fragile by nature, subject to destruction, unstable, non-eternal, non-permanent, characterized by accumulation and depletion, and subject to transformation. For one who thus reflects, who is focused on a single goal, who is liberated here, and who has desisted from worldly life, there is no further path [of rebirth]. Thus I say.

O Āvantīs, who among people in this world possesses possessions? Whether it be little or much, minute or large, animate or inanimate—one who possesses these very things is one who possesses possessions. This indeed becomes a great fear for some; and having observed what is known in the world, those who do not understand these attachments [suffer].

Knowing that what is well-bound is easy to carry away, those men of supreme vision exert themselves against these very things; for them alone is there celibacy. What has been heard by me and what is realized within myself: release from bondage is here. One who is inwardly restrained, a homeless ascetic, should endure for a long time. See those who are heedless in external things; you, being heedful, should wander on. You should properly practice this silence—so I say.

"O Āvantī, who in this world is truly free from possessions? It is those very ones who are free from possessions. Having heard these words and having listened to the teachings of the wise, a wise person should, with equanimity, follow the Dharma proclaimed by the Noble Ones. Just as a connection here has been severed by me, so too would a connection elsewhere be difficult to sever. Therefore, I say: one should not withhold one's energy.

He who rises first and does not stop later; he who rises first and stops later; and he who neither rises first nor stops later—he too may be such a one who, having fully understood the world, seeks the Beyond."

This is the path proclaimed by the Sage: here, the wise man, desiring the command, free from enmity, striving always in what is consistent before and after, should carefully observe his conduct; having heard [the truth], he should be without desire and without resentment; fight with this alone—what is the use of fighting with external foes?

Indeed, that which is worthy of battle is difficult to find; herein, discernment and detachment have been proclaimed by the wise. Yet the fool, having fallen away, takes delight in various wombs. This is said regarding beauty or even a festival: he alone is the sage who has pierced the path, observing the world otherwise. Having thus fully understood karma, he does not harm, he restrains himself, and he is not shameless. Observing the suffering of each individual, seeking excellence, he does not undertake anything in the whole world. With a single-pointed mind, intent on the quarters [of liberation], wandering with disillusionment, he is dispassionate toward all beings.

He who possesses wealth [of self-mastery], with a soul endowed with all-encompassing wisdom, does not seek from others that evil karma which ought not to be committed. Behold that which is right as silence; behold silence as that which is right. This is not possible for those who are lax, who are distracted by the pursuit of sense-pleasures, whose conduct is crooked, who are heedless, and who dwell in the household life. By practicing silence, the sage shakes off the body of karma. The heroes who see the truth resort to solitude and austerity. Such a sage, having crossed over the stream, is declared to be one who has transcended, is liberated, and is a hero—thus I say.

For a monk who wanders from village to village, there occurs what is ill-done and ill-striven, being undiscerning. Even when addressed with mere words, some young men become angry; and a man who exalts himself is deluded by great delusion. Many obstacles, difficult to overcome again and again, beset one who does not know and does not see. Let this not be so for you; this is the vision of the skillful. With that as his view, that as his refuge, that as his priority, having that as his perception and that as his dwelling, he should wander with self-control, with a mind sheltered, observing the path, watching for those who set fire to it, and he should proceed having seen living beings.

Whether moving forward, moving backward, contracting [the limbs], extending them, turning around, or lying down, at times certain living beings perish through contact with the body of one who is practicing with restrained senses. This results in suffering experienced in this world as a consequence of what has been encountered. Having fully understood that karma produced by intentional activity (*āuṭṭi*), he brings about its separation. Thus, through heedfulness, the knower of the Veda proclaims this separation.

He who sees much, possesses great discernment, is tranquil, self-controlled, composed, and ever-vigilant, having seen [the danger], turns away from himself [of sensual desire]: "What will this person do? For him, women in this world are the supreme delight; this has indeed been proclaimed by the Sage. Even when being assailed by the village-dharmas—whether he should reduce his food intake, whether he should practice fasting, whether he should stand upright, whether he should wander from village to village, or whether he should even cease taking food—he should abandon the thought of women. First come the blows, then the pleasures; first come the pleasures, then the blows. These are quarrels that cause attachment. Having understood this through careful examination, one should command [oneself] to non-indulgence. Thus I say.

One should not be a speaker, nor a listener, nor one who encourages others; one should not be a companion, nor one who performs services for another; guarding one's speech, restrained within oneself, one should always avoid evil. You should dwell in accordance with this state of silence—so I say.

This I say: just as a well-filled water-jar remains on level ground in a sheltered spot, protected [from the sun], it stays there in the midst of coolness; so too, the great seers of the world, who possess wisdom and are awakened, having desisted from all undertakings, perceive correctly and see [the truth]. Desiring the right time, they wander about. Thus I say.
One who is overcome by doubt does not attain concentration; they follow some impulses and do not follow others. How could one not become despondent when following some and not others?
"Only that which has been proclaimed by the Jinas is the truth, free from doubt."

For one who is faithful, well-disposed, and has gone forth together [with others], while thinking "it is peaceful": at times it becomes peaceful; for one thinking "it is peaceful," at times it becomes unpeaceful; for one thinking "it is unpeaceful," at times it becomes unpeaceful; for one thinking "it is unpeaceful," at times it becomes unpeaceful. For one thinking "it is peaceful," whether it be peaceful or unpeaceful, it becomes peaceful through observation (*uvēhā*). For one thinking "it is unpeaceful," whether it be peaceful or unpeaceful, it becomes unpeaceful through observation. Observing, he should say to one who does not observe: "Observe with equanimity (*samiyā*). In this way, the connection (*sandhī*) there is dissolved. Behold the course of one who has risen and one who stands still; even here, in the state of a fool (*bālabhāva*), one should not display oneself.

You yourself are indeed the very one whom you think should be killed; you yourself are indeed the very one whom you think should be oppressed; you yourself are indeed the very one whom you think should be tormented; you yourself are indeed the very one whom you think should be plundered; you yourself are indeed the very one whom you think should be destroyed. Therefore, one who is upright and lives with awakened consciousness should neither kill nor cause to be killed; through self-reflection, one should not desire that which is thought to be "to be killed."

That which is the self is consciousness; that which is consciousness is the self. That by which one knows is the self. With reference to this, through reflection and equanimity, this doctrine of the self has been declared in the course of study. Thus I say. Some, through lack of instruction, remain in a state of stagnation; others, through instruction, are free from stagnation. Let this not be so for you. This is the vision of the wise: having that as their view, that as their conduct, that as their priority, that as their perception, and that as their dwelling.

Having overcome [all things], he saw them; the Lord, being himself unconquered, through non-reliance, he who is not of the external mind should know the proclamation by means of the proclamation, through spontaneous realization, through the explanation of others, or having heard it from the presence of others. A wise man should not overstep the instruction; having thoroughly examined everything in every way with his whole being, and having correctly understood it, having understood that which delights in this world, guarded in his attachments, he should wander as one who delights in [the goal]. Having reached the end of his purpose, the hero should always exert himself according to the scripture; thus I say. Streams flow upward, streams flow downward, and streams flowing crosswise have been explained.
These are the streams that have been explained, by which you see attachment. Observing this whirlpool, the seeker of truth should desist from it here;
having removed the stream, he goes forth. This great one is free from karma; through discernment he knows and sees, and having fully understood coming and going, he does not long for them.

He has transcended the path of birth and death; his passion is extinguished. All sounds cease where no thought-construction (*takkā*) exists, and there the intellect (*maī*) finds no foothold. He knows the state that is without foundation. He is neither long nor short, neither round nor triangular, nor quadrangular, nor circular. He is neither black, nor blue, nor red, nor yellow, nor white. He has neither pleasant nor unpleasant odor; he is neither bitter, nor pungent, nor astringent, nor sour, nor sweet. He is neither hard nor soft, neither heavy nor light, neither cold nor hot, neither oily nor dry. He is neither dark nor bright; he is neither female, nor male, nor otherwise. To him who has full knowledge and perception, no analogy exists. He is a formless being; for that which is without origin, there is no origin.
Neither in sound, nor in form, nor in smell, nor in taste, nor in touch—thus indeed do I say.
[The sixth chapter – Dhuta]

The man who fully awakens among these human beings proclaims it; he for whom all these births have been thoroughly scrutinized on every side. He proclaims that incomparable knowledge to those who have exerted themselves, laid down the rod of violence, attained composure, and possess wisdom—this very path to liberation in this world. Thus do some great heroes strive. Behold some who are failing, lacking self-knowledge. I say this: just as a tortoise whose mind is settled in a lake and whose body is hidden by leaves finds no way out, like a beast trapped in a pen, so too some born into various kinds of families, beings attached to forms, wail piteously; because of their causal attachments (*niyāṇa*), they do not attain liberation. But behold them, born into those families through their own past actions.
A person with dropsy, or one with leprosy, a king’s son, one afflicted by pestilence, one who is one-eyed, one who is sluggish, one who is deformed, and likewise one who is hunchbacked;
one with a protruding belly, one who is mute, one who is emaciated, and one who is sickly. (Āyāra 187)
Epilepsy, lameness, leprosy, and diabetes—these sixteen diseases have been declared in their successive order. Then, indeed, afflictions and unpleasant sensations assail him. (Āyār.

Reflecting upon their death, having understood their rebirth and their passing away, and reflecting upon their various conditions of existence—listen to how it truly is: there are living beings described as being blind in the darkness; they pass through that very state of existence, whether it be real or unreal, and experience high and low sensations. This has been proclaimed by the Awakened Ones. There are living beings dwelling in water, those who feed on flavors, those moving in water, those moving in the air, and those moving through space; these beings cause suffering to other beings. Behold the great terror in this world!

Truly, living beings are full of suffering; young men are obsessed with sensual pleasures. They go to their destruction with this frail, perishable body. He who is afflicted has much suffering; thus the fool is reckless. Having recognized these many diseases, the sick man suffers further distress. Behold, it is not enough! Enough of these torments! O sage, behold this great danger: one should not disregard anyone.

Listen, sirs! Pay close attention, sirs! I shall proclaim the discourse on the daughters. Here indeed, for the sake of their own selves, they were consecrated by various families; they were born, produced, brought forth, fully developed, awakened, and having gone forth in due succession.

"O Great Sage! Lamenting, they say to you who are striving, 'Do not depart! Led by their desires, overcome by passion, and wailing, your kinsmen cry out. But such a sage as you, O kinsmen, cannot be hindered by those from whom you have been utterly detached; no refuge can be found there for you. How indeed could he find delight there? You should always dwell in this knowledge—thus I say."

Having abandoned the world which is afflicted by illusion, having left behind former attachments, and having dwelt in tranquility while practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one may abide or not abide according to the Dharma as it truly is; yet some unrighteous ones do not transcend darkness. They cast aside their robes, alms-bowls, blankets, and brooms, being unable to endure the successive hardships that are difficult to bear. For one who clings to sensual pleasures—whether now or in a moment—their destruction is immeasurable; thus, through these internal sensual desires that fall short of omniscience (*kevala*), they have not crossed over.

Having taken up the Dharma, one should practice with restraint from the very beginning; not clinging, firm, having fully understood all household life, this great sage is intent on his goal. Having transcended attachment in every way, thinking "I have no possessions," he is solitary, thinking "I am alone. Here, striving, restrained, a homeless ascetic, shaven on all sides, wandering about, he who is unclothed and well-dressed [in self-restraint] dwells in moderation regarding food. Whether reviled, struck, or assaulted, whether his hair is pulled out or he is subjected to harsh sounds and tactile sensations, having reflected thus and discerning various other things, he should wander about enduring them. Both those who are modest and those who are shameless—[he remains equanimous toward them both].

Having abandoned all agitation and attained tranquility through equanimity of vision, O Bhagins, those who are described as having the nature of non-returning in this world—those who follow the Dharma taught by me according to my command—are declared here to be the superior speakers among men. Having understood what is to be grasped and having renounced it through the religious life (*pariyāya*), one should practice restraint in this regard. For some here, there is a solitary wandering; among various families, whether pure or impure, he—the wise one—should wander as an alms-seeker, accepting food that is fragrant or foul. And if there, terrifying creatures should distress other living beings, you, being firm when touched by such conditions, should endure them. Thus I say.

Indeed, this is the way for a sage who has always well-proclaimed the Dharma and shaken off worldly attachments: having consumed [all worldly ties], he who wanders unclothed does not think, "My garment is worn out; I shall obtain a garment, I shall obtain thread, I shall obtain a needle, I shall join it, I shall sew it, I shall patch it, I shall mend it, I shall wear it, I shall put it on. Or rather, while striving there, as one unclothed, the touch of grass affects him, the touch of cold affects him, the touch of heat affects him, the touch of gadflies and mosquitoes affects him; he endures various and manifold such touches, being unclothed and perceiving lightness. Austerity becomes fully realized for him, just as it was proclaimed by the Blessed One. Having fully understood that very thing, he should recognize perfect right conduct in every respect and in all ways. Thus, behold how those great heroes, practicing for many long years, endured as steadfast ones.

The arms of those who have attained wisdom become emaciated, and their flesh and blood grow thin; having constructed a bridge and understood [the nature of existence], he is declared to be one who has crossed over, liberated, and restrained. Thus I say.

For a monk who is detached and practicing for a long night, what can discontent cause him to hold back there? When he has risen and is striving, just as that island is unshakeable, so is the Dharma taught by the Teacher. Not longing for sensual pleasures and not transgressing against living beings, those wise ones are truly learned; such is their practice according to the Blessed One. Just as the sun illuminates, so those disciples, day and night, have been instructed in due order—thus I say.

Thus were those disciples taught by day and by night in due succession by those great heroes endowed with wisdom. Having obtained wisdom from them and having abandoned harshness for the sake of tranquility, they dwell in the practice of celibacy, thinking, "We shall not [obey] that command. But having heard [the teaching on] the goal and having reflected upon it, some, being well-disposed, think, "We shall live [accordingly]," and they go forth. Yet others, failing to achieve [self-mastery], burning with desires, greedy and deeply attached, disregarding meditative concentration, they speak harshly even to the Teacher.

Those who possess virtue, observe the fasts, and conduct themselves with restraint, while those who lack virtue and do not follow the vows—these are the second kind of foolishness for the dull-witted.
Those who claim to be practicing self-restraint actually deviate from their conduct and sphere of activity; they are fallen from knowledge and destroyers of right vision.

Some, when being rebuked, violently transform their lives; some, when touched by hardship, turn back for the sake of life itself. Even though they have gone forth, it is as if they have not truly gone forth; for those men are led by the words of fools, and they repeatedly fashion birth again and again. Arising from below and being pierced [by suffering], they boast "I am superior," speaking harshly to the indifferent. They weave a web of old karma or rather, they entangle themselves with new karma. A wise person should understand that Dhamma.

"You are indeed a fool, established in unrighteousness, established in violence, pursuing it, killing, causing to kill, and even approving of those who kill. In this terrible heat, he suffers through his lack of knowledge; thus is he described as despondent and deprived of his true nature. Thus I say."

Thinking, "What shall I do with this person?"—having spoken thus, some abandon their mother and father, as well as their kinsmen and possessions; acting like heroes, they rise up, non-violent, well-restrained, and self-controlled. Yet, behold, some among them, being miserable, fall back from their resolve; enslaved by worldly desires, those cowardly people become destroyers. For some, there arises a sinful reputation. Having become a śramaṇa, one sees others who have gone forth, some possessing [virtues] while others lack them; some bowing down while others do not; some being restrained while others are unrestrained; some being steadfast while others are not. Having fully understood this, the wise and intelligent hero, having achieved his goal, should always exert himself according to the scripture. Thus I say.

Whether in houses or between houses, in villages or between villages, in towns or between towns, in districts or between districts, or in the intervals between villages, towns, and districts, there may be certain people who are plunderers, or perhaps harsh contacts [of suffering] touch him; touched by these contacts, the hero should endure them. With equanimity and right vision, having understood compassion for the world, he should proclaim, analyze, and explain [the truth] to the east, west, north, and south—the sage who is indeed a monk, highly learned, one who has mastered the external scriptures, skilled in examples and reasons, and endowed with the attainment of preaching the Dharma. Having considered the place, the time, and the person—asking, "Who is this man? or "What is his doctrine?"—he should teach when they have risen [to listen] or even when they have not, provided they are desirous of hearing. He should proclaim the Dharma to the mendicant: peace, renunciation, tranquility, nirvana, self-restraint, purity, gentleness, and lightness. Without transgression toward all breathing things, all beings, all souls, and all living creatures, the mendicant should proclaim the Dharma after due consideration.

A monk who proclaims the Dharma should not harm himself, nor should he harm others, nor should he harm other living beings, creatures, or sentient beings. Being one who does not harm and does not cause harm, he becomes like an island that is unassailable for the sake of living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings who are being tormented. Thus he becomes a refuge, a great sage. Thus, having risen, with his self established, free from enmity, immovable yet moving, without possessions, he wanders as an ascetic. Having fully understood the excellent Dharma, possessed of right vision, he is extinguished (parinirvṛta). Therefore, behold attachment! Men gripped by bonds are despondent and distressed by sensual desires. Therefore, one should not shrink away from austerity. He for whom these undertakings have been thoroughly understood in every way and in all respects—those which destroyers do not shrink from—he has vomited out anger, pride, deceit, and greed; he is declared to be contented. Thus I say.

The exertion of the body is declared to be the very front line of battle. Such a sage, indeed, having gone beyond, even while being struck down, standing firm like a plank, brought to his end by time, should await the moment until the dissolution of the body—thus I say.
[The Seventh Chapter – The Faded] [The Eighth Chapter – Liberation]

This I say: toward one who is agreeable or one who is disagreeable, one should not give food, drink, hard food, or soft food; nor clothing, a bowl, a blanket, or a broom; nor should one offer an invitation or perform service—while showing respect for another. Thus I say.

He should certainly know this: whether he obtains food, drink, hard food, or soft food, or clothing, a bowl, or a water-strainer, or whether he does not obtain them, or whether he eats or does not eat; having set out on the path, having departed, reflecting upon the divided Dharma, harmonizing it, moving forward, or turning back, he may offer it, or invite [others], or perform service for another, while remaining unattached—thus I say.

In this world, some individuals are not well-versed in the sphere of right conduct (*ācāra-gocara*).
