Being intent on violence, they follow [this path], killing, causing slaughter, and even approving of those who kill; or else they take what is not given, or they utter various speech-sounds such as: "The world exists" or "the world does not exist"; "the world is eternal" or "the world is non-eternal"; "the world has a beginning" or "the world has no beginning"; "the world has an end" or "the world has no end"; or they speak of "well-done" or "ill-done," "meritorious" or "evil," "virtuous" or "non-virtuous," "liberation" or "non-liberation," "hell" or "no hell. Regarding these things, they proclaim a doctrine of their own while being thus perverted. Know that even in this case, for them, the Dharma is neither well-expounded nor well-proclaimed.

Thus has this been proclaimed by the Blessed One, the swift-attainer, the knower, and the seer; or rather, it concerns the guarding of the sphere of conduct. Thus I say. Sin is everywhere censured; having avoided that very thing, this is declared to be my great detachment (*vivega*). Whether in a village or in a forest—neither in a village nor in a forest—know this to be the Dharma. It was proclaimed by the Brahmin through his wisdom: three stages of life have been described, in which these noble ones, being awakened, have exerted themselves. Those who are free from sinful karmas and without worldly attachments—they are declared [to be the true ascetics].

Above, below, and in all directions everywhere, in every single instance, there is the undertaking of violence against living beings through the instigation of karmic actions. Having fully understood this, the wise man should not himself undertake such violence with these instruments of harm; he should not cause others to undertake such violence with these instruments of harm; nor should he approve of others who are undertaking such violence with these instruments of harm. We feel shame even for those others who undertake such violence with these instruments of harm. Having understood this, the wise man—being fearful of violence—should neither undertake that violence himself, nor any other violence. Thus I say.

Whether that monk should be walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—in a cemetery, in an empty house, in a mountain cave, at the foot of a tree, in a potter’s workshop, or wandering elsewhere anywhere—a householder, having approached that monk, might say: "O venerable ascetic! For your sake, I have procured food, drink, delicacies, or sweets; or clothing, a bowl, a blanket, or a broom—having undertaken [the act], having intended it for you, having bought it, having had it bartered, having taken it by force, having received it as a gift, or having brought it from elsewhere—I provide these things, or I construct a dwelling. O venerable ascetic, please enjoy this and dwell here! The monk should reject that householder, speaking thus: "O venerable householder! I do not accept your word; I do not approve of your word, that for my sake you have procured food, drink, delicacies, or sweets; or clothing, a bowl, a blanket, or a broom—having undertaken [the act], having intended it for me, having bought it, having had it bartered, having taken it by force, having received it as a gift, or having brought it from elsewhere—and that you provide these things or construct a dwelling. O venerable householder, abstain from doing this."

If that monk should walk about, stand, sit, or lie down in a cemetery, or anywhere else while wandering about; and a householder, having approached that monk with a mind directed toward him, should offer food, drink, delicacy, or refreshment, or clothing, a bowl, a blanket, or a broom, or even build a dwelling for him, in order to provide for that monk—if that monk should know this through his own intuition, through the explanation of another, or by hearing it from others: "This householder is indeed building a dwelling for my sake"—then that monk, having reflected upon it, should inform him so that he may desist from it. Thus I say.

Indeed, O monks, whether questioned or unasked, when these painful contacts touch him, he—the wise one—should endure them when touched. He should say: "Kill! Strike! Dig! Cut! Burn! Cook! Pluck! Loot! Act with violence! Seize! Regarding these contacts, the steadfast one should endure them when touched; or else, he should explain the sphere of conduct (*ācāragocara*). Having reflected upon that which is incomparable, or through the restraint of speech, he should properly examine it in due order. Thus has this been proclaimed by the Buddhas to one who is self-restrained and guarded.

One who is of like mind with one who is not of like mind should not give food, drink, hard food, or soft food; nor clothing, nor a bowl, nor a blanket, nor a broom; nor should he offer an invitation, nor perform service for him, even while showing respect. Thus I say. Understand this Dharma as it has been proclaimed by the wise Brahmin: one who is of like mind with one who is of like mind may give food, or [all items up to] perform service for him, even while showing respect. Thus I say.

Even in middle age, some, becoming awakened, have risen up; having heard and attended to the wise, they have listened to the Dharma taught by the Noble Ones with equanimity. Desiring nothing, not transgressing, and not grasping, they do not possess anything. Having laid down the rod toward all beings in this world, they do not commit evil karma against living creatures. This is declared to be my "unbound" state. Knowing the origin and passing away of the world, the one who possesses wisdom understands the light of truth.

Bodies are accumulations of food and are fragile against the hardships [of life]. Behold some who are wasting away with all their senses failing. One who shows compassion toward such a person is one who knows how to dispel the affliction caused by the weapon of worldly attachment. Such a monk is one who knows the right time, knows strength, knows the measure, knows the moment, knows discipline, and knows the doctrine; he does not treat possessions as "mine," he rises at the proper time, makes no vows for the future, and having severed both [extremes], he proceeds toward liberation.

When a householder approaches that monk whose body is trembling from the touch of cold, he should say: "Venerable ascetic! Are the village-distractions not overwhelming you? "Venerable householder! Indeed, the village-distractions do not overwhelm me, but I am unable to endure the touch of the cold. It is not permissible for me to kindle or ignite a fire, or to warm or heat my body, whether by my own means or at the request of others. If another person, upon hearing him speak thus, should kindle or ignite a fire and then warm or heat his body, the monk, having inspected it, should return and command [the householder] not to use it again. Thus I say.

When a monk is provided with three robes and a fourth for his alms-bowl, it does not occur to him: "I shall obtain a fourth robe. He should seek robes that are permissible; he should wear robes that have been formally accepted. He should not wash them, nor dye them, nor wear robes that have been washed and dyed. Without concealing them, wearing even worn-out rags while moving between villages—this indeed is the proper conduct for one who wears robes.

But if he should know thus: "The winter has indeed passed and the summer has arrived," he should discard his worn-out garments; or he may have an inner and outer garment, or a single garment, or be without clothing.

Attaining lightness and having fully realized austerity, he should, having thoroughly understood that which was proclaimed by the Blessed One, recognize it as complete in every way and in all respects.

When a monk thinks, "I am indeed afflicted; I am not capable of enduring the touch of cold," he—being possessed of self-control and with his wisdom fully perfected—should, by means of his own self, turn away from any [unwholesome] action. For that ascetic, it is indeed better to remain solitary. Even there, for him, there comes the right time; even there, he brings about an end [to suffering]. This is a source of freedom from delusion—beneficial, pleasant, appropriate, leading to liberation, and conducive to the goal. Thus I say.

If a monk is provided with two robes sufficient for his feet, it does not occur to him, "I shall seek a third robe. He should seek robes that are permissible; this indeed is the proper conduct for that monk. However, if he should know that winter has passed and summer has arrived, he should discard the worn-out robes. Having discarded the worn-out robes, he may be [clad] with an inner and outer garment, or with a single layer, or with one shoulder-cloth, or even naked. Attaining lightness and practicing austerity, he realizes that which was proclaimed by the Blessed One; having fully understood that very thing, he should recognize it completely in every way. If a monk thinks, "I am afflicted and weak; I am not capable of moving from house to house for the practice of alms-seeking," and while he is speaking thus, another person brings and offers him food, drink, solid food, or delicacies, he should first inform them: "O householder! It is not permissible for me to eat or drink food, drink, solid food, or delicacies that have been brought to me, nor anything else of this kind."

For that monk who has made this resolve: "I shall approve of service being performed for me by fellow monks—whether I am designated or not designated, whether I am ill or not ill"—and who, being himself un-designated, performs service for a designated fellow monk who is ill; or who, having undertaken the vow, will cause it to be brought to him and will approve of what is brought; or who, having undertaken the vow, will cause it to be brought but will not approve of what is brought; or who, having undertaken the vow, will not cause it to be brought but will approve of what is brought; or who, having undertaken the vow, will neither cause it to be brought nor approve of what is brought—thus understanding the Dharma exactly as it has been taught, being peaceful, restrained, and of well-composed conduct, even there he reaches the end of his time. He attains the cessation of suffering therein. This is the source of freedom from delusion, beneficial, pleasant, appropriate, leading to liberation, and conducive to the goal. Thus I say.

If a monk is provided with one garment and a second for the rainy season, it does not occur to him: "I shall seek a second garment. He should not seek a garment that is not permissible to accept; he should wear a garment as it has been formally accepted. This continues until winter or summer has arrived, at which point he should discard the garment when it is worn out. Having discarded the garment when it is worn out—whether he is then without clothing or perceiving the attainment of the goal—he should fully understand the perfection of his practice.

For that monk who has this thought: "I am alone; I have no one belonging to me, nor do I belong to anyone"—thus he should recognize himself as truly alone. As he recognizes this, the attainment of austerity becomes fully realized for him, up until he has so recognized it.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, while eating food, drink, chewables, or delicacies, they should not shift [the food] from the left jaw to the right jaw while tasting it; nor should they shift it from the right jaw to the left jaw while tasting it. By not tasting for pleasure and attaining lightness, austerity becomes fully realized for them. Having thus understood that which has been proclaimed by the Blessed One, one should recognize it as complete in every respect and in all ways.

If a monk should think thus: "I am indeed ill at this time; I must carry this body gradually," he should gradually reduce his food. Having gradually reduced his food and made his afflictions thin, being composed and intent on the plank-like practice, the monk should rise and be fully extinguished.

Having entered a village, city, hamlet, market town, mountain settlement, port, mine, hermitage, inhabited area, trade center, or capital, he should seek out grass. Having sought out the grass, he should take it and go to a secluded spot. Having gone to a secluded spot, he should spread out the grass after repeatedly inspecting and repeatedly sweeping it—ensuring it is free of small insects, free of living beings, free of seeds, free of green plants, free of dew, free of water, and free of earth, mold, and spiderwebs. Having spread out the grass, even at that moment he should remain for only a short time. He is truthful and a speaker of truth; he has crossed over, severed the flow of worldly talk, transcended the world, and is not of the world. Having cast off this fragile body and shaken off various kinds of hardships and afflictions, he remains confident in this [state] which is difficult to practice. Even there, his time comes to an end, leading him toward the goal—thus I say.

If a monk who has lived as a naked ascetic (*acēla*) thinks to himself: "I am able to endure the touch of grass, to endure the touch of cold, to endure the touch of heat, to endure the touch of gadflies and mosquitoes, and to endure various diverse kinds of contacts; however, I am not able to endure the concealment of shame," then it is permissible for him to wear a waist-band (*kaḍibandhaṇa*).

Or else, while striving there, the touch of grass, the touch of cold, the touch of heat, and the touch of gadflies and mosquitoes again afflict him who is naked; he endures various and manifold such touches, being naked and perceiving the attainment of austerity, until he fully understands that which is complete.

If a monk thinks: "I shall indeed bring food, drink, solid food, or delicacy for other monks and give it to them, but I will not enjoy what has been brought"; if a monk thinks: "I shall indeed bring food, drink, solid food, or delicacy for other monks and give it to them, but I will not enjoy what has been brought"; if a monk thinks: "I shall indeed bring food, drink, solid food, or delicacy for other monks but will not give it to them, yet I will enjoy what has been brought."

If a monk thinks thus: "I shall not bring food, drink, solid food, or delicacy for other monks and give it to them, nor shall I partake of what has been brought; yet, with that which is in excess, which is permissible, and which has been properly accepted—whether food, drink, solid food, or delicacy—I shall, if desired, perform service for a fellow-monk; or, with that which is in excess, which is permissible, and which has been properly accepted—whether food, drink, solid food, or delicacy—I shall, if desired, approve of the service being performed for me by fellow-monks," [he should do so] considering it a gain and understanding it as a complete fulfillment of his duty.

If a monk thinks thus: "I am indeed ill at this time; I must carry this body gradually," he should gradually reduce his food. Having gradually reduced his food, having made his passions thin, being composed and intent on the plank-like austerity (phalagāvayaṭṭhī), the monk, having risen and become tranquil, should enter a village or even a capital city. There he should seek grass and spread it out. At that time, he should renounce the body, activity, and movement. He is truthful, a speaker of truth, one who has crossed over, one whose doubts are severed, one who has transcended the worldly state, yet is not attached to it. Having cast off the fragile body, having shaken off various kinds of hardships and afflictions, having endured fear and practiced what is terrifying, there too he reaches the end of his time. That is the making of an end there. This is the source of liberation—beneficial, pleasant, appropriate, leading to the highest good, and conducive to the future. Thus I say.

Having relied upon those stages of gradual liberation which the wise, the steadfast, the powerful, and the intelligent have attained—having understood all that is incomparable—and having known both [aspects] of the Dharma, the awakened ones have reached its further shore. (Āyār. 240)
Through gradual reckoning, he desists from his undertakings.
Having made his passions thin, the monk, taking little food, should endure [hardship].
Now, if the monk should become ill, [he should remain] in the vicinity of food. *Āyār.* 241–242.

One should not long for life, nor should one desire death; one should not be attached even to one's daughter, remaining thus toward both life and death. Being equanimous and seeking the shedding of karma, one should maintain composure. (Āyār. 243)
Having discerned both the internal and the external, one should seek purity within oneself. (Āyār.
244) Whatever means one knows for the exhaustion of one's own life-span, the wise person should quickly practice that very thing during the intervening period. (Āyār. 245)

Whether in a village or in the forest, having inspected a bare patch of ground and knowing it to be free of living beings, the sage should spread out grass. Without food, he should remain steadfast; when touched by hardships there, he should endure them.
One should not associate with humans for too long, even when questioned by them. (Āyār.
247) As for those crawling creatures, as well as those that move above or below, which feed on flesh and blood—one should neither kill nor wipe them away. (Āyār. 248)
Living beings harm the body; one should not move from one's place.
Enduring torments while remaining free from influxes, one should persevere until reaching the end of one’s lifespan, free from bonds. (Āyār. 249)
This is indeed more highly esteemed for one who understands the steadfast [ascetic] (Āyār. 250). This is another duty taught by the Son of the Jñātṛs:
one should abandon, in three ways and of three kinds, the remedy that involves injury to oneself (Āyār. 251).
He should not lie down on green plants; having recognized a bare spot, the wise one should rest there.
When without food and afflicted by hunger, he should endure it there. When his senses fail him, the sage should take food with moderation. *Āyāra 252*
Nevertheless, he is beyond reproach, steadfast and composed.
Whether moving forward or backward, contracting or extending his limbs for the sake of maintaining the body—even in this regard, he remains free from attachment to the insentient. (Āyār. 253–254)

When exhausted by exertion, or when standing in a place that causes fatigue, he should sit down at least for a moment. While sitting, he should restrain his senses until death, which is incomparable. (Āyār. 255)
Having taken up residence in a village, one should not display falsehood. (Āyār.
256) Since danger may arise there, one should not rely upon it; rather, one should lift oneself up from that [danger] and endure all sensations there with equanimity. (Āyār. 257)
And this [practice] would be even more extensive for one who thus maintains it, even when all bodily movements are restrained, so that he does not swerve from his position.
This is the supreme dharma, the exertion in the previously established state. (Āyār. 258)
Having swept [the area] shortly before, O Brahmin, remain standing there.
Having approached a spot free from living beings, one should station oneself there;
one should completely cast off the body, thinking: "No afflictions shall affect my body. (Āyār. 259–260)
"As long as life lasts, there are hardships and obstacles; when the body is destroyed, one who is self-restrained has transcended them—thus should one understand. (Āyār.
261) One should not take delight in fragile things, even if they are numerous, such as sensual pleasures.
One should not indulge in desire or greed, having abandoned that which is of constant splendor. (Āyār.
262) One might be invited by those who offer consolation, but one should not believe in divine illusion.
Having shaken off all pride, the Brāhmaṇa should awaken to this. (Āyār. 263)
Unattached to all things, having reached the further shore of the duration of life, and knowing that supreme endurance is the highest benefit beyond delusion—thus I say. (Āyār. 264)

[The Ninth Chapter – On Austerities (Uvahāṇasuya): I shall speak according to what has been heard, concerning how that venerable ascetic, having risen with resolve, practiced austerities during that winter season, having recently gone forth into homelessness. Āyār. 265.
"I shall not cover myself with this garment during that winter;
rather, I shall cross over until the end of my life. This indeed is his practice in accordance with the Dharma.
(Āyār. 266) For four months and more, many species of living beings come...
They climbed upon his body and dwelt there; having torn it, they harmed him there.
For a year and an additional month, the Blessed One did not leave off his garment while he was unclothed; thereafter, the renunciant, the homeless one, gave up that garment. (Āyār. 267–268)
Or he meditates within, having fixed his gaze upon a human form or a wall;
then many, terrified by his gaze and recoiling, cried out, "He has killed us! He has killed us! (Āyār. 269).
Having understood that women there were mingled with his own kinsmen...
He does not frequent the householders' dwellings; he meditates alone, having entered [into solitude]. (Āyār.

270) Whosoever these householders may be, having abandoned association with them, he meditates; even when questioned, he does not speak back; he goes straight on, he does not turn back—he is upright. (Āyār. 271)

It is not easy for some [to endure] when one does not speak back to those who address them, even though they have previously struck him there with sticks or previously assaulted him— those of little merit. Transcending harsh words that are difficult to endure, the sage exerts himself.

Having set aside dancing and singing, staff-fighting and boxing, at the time of the discourse between the two kinsmen, the son of the Nāgas, free from sorrow, beheld these sublime things; thus did the son of the Jñātas proceed toward the state of no-refuge. (Āyār. 273–274)
Having endured two rainy seasons, he went forth without consuming cold water;
solitary, with his senses restrained, he possessed the vision of the realized truth. (Āyār.
275) [He avoided] the earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, and the air-body.

Having fully understood that there are dewdrops, seeds, green plants, and the bodies of mobile beings everywhere—having recognized these as possessing consciousness and having discerned them—he would avoid them and not wander [among them];
thus, with such awareness, he was the Great Hero. (Āyār. 276–277)

"Or stationary beings may become mobile, and mobile living beings may become stationary; indeed, all beings of every birth-order are fashioned separately by their own karma—such is the view of the ignorant. And the Blessed One thinks thus: 'The ignorant person, possessed of worldly attachments, is surely plundered. (Āyāra 278)
Having understood action in its entirety, the Blessed One rejected that which is evil. (Āyār.

279) The wise one, having comprehended the two-fold [path] and having declared incomparable action, understands the influx of karma through the senses and the influx through speech, as well as activity in its entirety. (Āyār. 280)

One who does not return [to worldly life], who personally pursues the non-performance [of sinful acts], and for whom women have been fully understood as the bringers of all karma—he has seen [the truth].
He should not consume what is prepared for him; he should see with his whole being that it is indeed an act of karma.
Whatever was cooked, O Blessed One, he did not eat; he ate only what was prepared [for him]. (Āyār.
282) He did not wear another’s garment, nor did he eat from another’s vessel.
Having avoided contempt, he went to a communal meal where there was no refuge [from social ties]. (Āyār. 283)
Moderate in food and drink, not greedy for flavors, and free from fixed expectations, the sage should not wipe his eyes nor scratch his body.
Looking but a little to the side, he should look but a little behind him. (Āyār. 284)
Having little speech and being one who does not respond [needlessly], he should wander with circumspection, watching his path. (Āyār.
285) When the cold season has set in, the homeless monk, having cast off that garment, should exert himself by stretching out his arms, and not by leaning upon the shoulders [of others]. (Āyār. 286)
This rule has been proclaimed by the Brahmin, the wise hero, the Kāśyapa, the great seer who was free from all undertakings—thus I say. (Āyār.
287) Regarding his wandering, sitting, and beds, some [of these] have already been explained.

291) The Blessed One does not indulge even in sleep out of habit; rather, rising up, he keeps himself awake, sleeping only slightly and free from fixed expectations. (Āyār. 292)

Those creatures that crawl along, or those birds that fly about; those that roam in the wilderness, village guards with spears in their hands, or the dangers encountered in the village—women and certain men [may cause such obstacles]. (Āyār. 294–295)

Whether pertaining to this world or the next, whether terrifying and of many kinds, or having pleasant and unpleasant odors, and sounds of many kinds—he should always endure these various sensations with equanimity. (Āyār.

While some were teaching, as the cool breezes blew... (Āyār. 299)

O Blessed One, you are free from worldly undertakings; like the open sky, you endure all things, steadfast, having gone forth alone at night. The Blessed One practices with equanimity. This rule has been successively transmitted by the Brahmin who was possessed of wisdom.
"By the hero, the Kāśyapa, the great seer who is free from all undertakings—thus I say. (Āyār.

303) The one who is ever self-controlled should endure the touch of grass, the touch of cold, the touch of heat, and gadflies and mosquitoes; he should endure various kinds of tactile sensations. (Āyār. 304)

Then, practicing the difficult conduct of the Lādhas, they frequented the grounds of fault and the grounds of danger, as well as remote lodgings and secluded seats. Because of the Lādhas, many afflictions befell him; the local people harassed him. (Āyār. 305)
Now, when the alms-food was coarse and local, dogs there would attack it and turn away.
A few people would ward them off;
others, as the dogs were tearing at it and making "chuchuka" sounds, said to the ascetic, "The dogs are biting you! (Āyār. 306–307).
Again, many people in Vajrabhūmi were harsh; taking sticks and clubs, they harassed the ascetics who lived there. Even while living there in this manner, they were previously attacked by dogs. (Āyār.
308) Thus, even while dwelling there, they were beset by dogs.
Being torn apart by dogs, it was difficult to move about there among the Lādhas.
Having laid down the rod toward living beings, the Blessed One, the homeless one, having fully understood them, endured those village-thorns while relinquishing that body. (Āyār. 309–310)
Like an elephant at the head of the battle, that great hero stands firm there;
even thus, among the Lādhas, he may once find a village that was not previously obtained. (Āyār.
311) Approaching, yet making no promise, even before reaching the edge of the village.
Having gone out, they tore him apart, thinking, "From here on, he shall flee! (Āyār.
312). There, having been struck previously with a staff, or with a fist, or with a spear-head, or with a clod of earth, or with a potsherd, many cried out, "Strike! Strike! (Āyār. 313).

Having renounced all, he was humble; the Blessed One endured suffering without making any vows.
Like a hero at the head of a battle, the Blessed One remained there, self-restrained, as that Great Hero endured harsh words, remaining unshakable in his conduct. (Āyār. 315–316)
This rule has been proclaimed by the Brahmin, the wise, the unattached hero, the Kāśyapa, the great seer; thus I say. (Āyār.
317) He practices moderation in food, even when not afflicted by diseases, O Blessed One.
Whether asked or unasked, he does not consent to medical treatment. (Āyār.
318) Purging, emetics, anointing the body, bathing, and massage are not permitted for him; he has fully understood the cleansing of the teeth. (Āyār. 319)
Abstaining from the dharmas of the village, the Brahmin wanders about, speaking little;
once in the cold season, the Blessed One meditated in the shade and remained seated.
During the summer, he practiced heat-exposure and sat in the *utkuṭuka* posture, enduring the scorching heat. (Āyār. 320)
Or even here with coarse food—barley-gruel, flour-mash, and groats—the Blessed One practiced these three for eight months.

Standing constantly on his haunches, he should watch for those who have returned [from their alms-round]:
whether it be a Brahmin, a śramaṇa, a village beggar, a guest, a dog-cooker, a rat-catcher, or even a dog standing before him. (Āyār. 327–328)
Avoiding the interruption of livelihood and eschewing what is improper for them, the Blessed One exerted himself gently; not causing harm, he sought his food. (Āyār.
329) Whether it was meat-broth or dried meat, cold lumps of rice, or old groats—

Seated on his seat, free from agitation, he meditates—upward, downward, and across—observing equanimity and remaining firm in his vow. (Āyār. 330–331)

Free from passions and devoid of possessiveness, uninfatuated with sounds and forms, even while practicing as a *chadmastha* (one still under the veil of ignorance), he should not indulge in negligence even for a moment.
The Blessed One remained seated until the one who was free from deceit had attained final liberation.

First Chapter: The Search for Alms-food.

If that monk or nun, having entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms, should know that the food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy—is mixed with living beings, small creatures, seeds, or green plants; or if it has been sprinkled with cold water, or covered with dust; then such food, drink, soft food, or delicacy, whether in the hand of another or in the vessel of another, considering it to be unwholesome and unfit for acceptance, should not accept it even if it is available.

If he should receive food unexpectedly, he should take it and go to a secluded place. Having gone to a secluded place—in a grove, or in a dwelling—where there are no insects, no living beings, no seeds, no greenery, no mud, no water, and no webs of worms, fungi, or earth-ants; having repeatedly sifted it and repeatedly purified it, he should then, being restrained, eat or drink it. But if he should not be able to eat or drink it, he should take it and go to a secluded place. Having gone to a secluded place—on a burnt piece of ground, or on a heap of bones, or on a heap of dross, or on a heap of husks, or on a heap of cow dung, or on any other such kind of bare ground—he should repeatedly inspect it and repeatedly sweep it, and then, being restrained, he should discard it.

When a monk or a nun has entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms-food, and they perceive that the beds or medicinal herbs are entirely green, uncrushed, not cut into pieces, not cut off at the top, or if they see a young cucumber that has not been fully ripened, thinking it is impure and not fit for acceptance, they should not accept it even if an opportunity for gain arises.

When that monk has entered [the village], he should, if there are medicinal herbs which he knows to be unripe, uncooked, split, cut across, or severed, or if he sees a fresh gourd that has been thoroughly roasted, considering it pure and acceptable, he may accept it when an opportunity arises.

If that monk or nun, having entered among householders, should know that there is flattened rice, or rice with much dust, or parched grain, or flour, or rice, or rice-gruel, or rice fried by oneself—considering it to be unwholesome and not in accordance with the rules of alms-seeking, he or she should not accept it, even if it is available.

If that monk or nun, having entered the family of a householder, should know that there is flattened rice or even rice, or rice-gruel, or rice-cakes—which have been fried once, or twice, or three times, and which are pure and acceptable—they may accept them. When that monk or nun wishes to enter the family of a householder for the purpose of alms, he or she should not enter or exit the family home for the purpose of alms together with one belonging to another sect or a householder, whether that person is a regular attendant or not.

Whether that monk or nun is going out or entering the external study ground or the dwelling ground, they should not go out or enter the external study ground or dwelling ground together with a non-believer or a householder—whether one who is permitted to accompany them or one who is not permitted.

Whether that monk or nun is traveling from village to village, they should not travel from village to village together with a non-believer or a householder—whether one who is permitted to accompany them or one who is not permitted.

When that monk or nun has entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms-food, they shall not give or cause to be given food, drink, solid food, or delicacy to one belonging to another sect or to a householder, whether that person is a regular recipient or not.

If that monk or nun, while staying [in a residence], should know that food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy—has been prepared specifically for a fellow ascetic, having procured it by harming living beings, creatures, souls, or sentient beings; or if it has been specially intended, purchased, borrowed, taken by force, given without being relinquished, or brought from outside; whether it has been brought forth or not brought forth, prepared for one's own sake or not for one's own sake, consumed or unconsumed, tasted or untasted—if such food, drink, soft food, or delicacy is impure (aphāsuya), they should not accept it.
In this same way, four discourses (*ālāvaga*) should be recited concerning many fellow monks, one fellow nun, or many fellow nuns.

When that monk or nun has entered [the village], if he or she should know: "This food—whether solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy—has been specifically intended for many ascetics, brahmins, guests, beggars, or mendicants, having been selected one by one; and it has been prepared by harming living beings, creatures, souls, or sentient beings," then he or she shall not accept it.

When that monk or nun has entered [the village], if they should know that food, drink, solid food, or delicacy has been prepared for many ascetics, brahmins, guests, craftsmen, or beggars, and is being offered—such food, drink, solid food, or delicacy, if it has not been placed within the threshold, has not been brought out, is not intended for oneself, and has not been tasted—if they consider it unwholesome and unfit to be sought, they should not accept it even if it is available. However, if they should know it thus: "It has been placed within the threshold, it has been brought out, it is intended for oneself, it has been tasted, and it has been consumed"—if they consider it wholesome and fit to be sought, they may accept it if it is available.

If that monk or nun, desiring to enter a householder’s family for the sake of alms, should know of those families where food is given regularly, where the first portion of food is given regularly, where a full share is given regularly, or where a half-share is given regularly—such families which are regular and fixed—he should not enter them nor leave them for the sake of food or drink. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that he is restrained in all things, self-controlled, and ever vigilant. Thus I say.

If that monk or nun, having entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms, should know: "Food, drink, soft food, or sweet food is being distributed from a single pot—or being distributed from two pots, three pots, or four pots—on the eighth-day fast days, or on the half-monthly, monthly, two-monthly, three-monthly, four-monthly, five-monthly, or six-monthly festivals, or at the beginning of a season, at the junction of seasons, or during the change of seasons; or it is being distributed from the mouths of jars, or from *kalovāī* vessels, or from stored accumulations"—then such food, drink, soft food, or sweet food, if it has not been prepared with a separation of persons (*apurisantarakaḍa*) and so forth, until it is not yet consumed, being impure (*aphāsuya*) and unfit for consumption (*anesaṇijja*), he or she should not accept it.

But if he should know thus: "This was prepared by another person, brought out from outside, intended for oneself, already consumed, and enjoyed; it is pure and acceptable," then, considering it to be so, he may accept it if it is available.

When that monk or [nun] has arrived [at a house for alms], he should recognize those families which are such as: noble families, wealthy families, royal families, kṣatriya families, Ikṣvāku families, Harivaṃśa families, Ārṣika families, Vaiśika families, Gaṇḍāka families, Koṭṭāka families, village-guardian families, or Bokkāsāliya families; or in other similar families that are not despised and not censured—therein he may accept pure and permissible food, whether it be solid food, drink, chewable food, or delicacies.

If a monk or a nun, having entered a householder's family for the sake of alms, should know this: that food, drink, solid food, or delicacy is being served at gatherings, or at distributions of alms, or at festivals of Indra, Skanda, Rudra, Maṅguda, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Stūpas, Caityas, trees, mountains, caves, wells, tanks, lakes, rivers, ponds, oceans, or mines—or at various other such diverse great festivals—where many ascetics, Brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars are seen being served from a single cooking pot, or where it is seen being served from two [pots], or even from stores and hoards; then such food, drink, solid food, or delicacy, if not prepared with a separation of space (i.e., not set aside specifically), they should not accept. But if he should know thus: "That which was to be given has been given to them," and if he sees people eating there—the householder’s wife, sister, son, daughter, daughter-in-law, wet-nurse, slave, servant, or female laborer—he should first address them: "O lady" or "Sister, will you give me some portion of this food? If, while he is speaking thus, another brings and gives him food, drink, solid food, or delicacy; or if he himself obtains such food, drink, solid food, or delicacy, or another gives it to him, thinking it to be pure and acceptable, then, if it is available, he may accept it.

If a monk or a nun, having learned of a communal feast (*saṅkhaḍi*) within half a *yojana* range, should not set out for the journey with the intent of going to that feast. If a monk or a nun, having learned of a feast to the east, should go to the west without being drawn toward it; having learned of a feast to the west, should go to the east without being drawn toward it; having learned of a feast to the south, should go to the north without being drawn toward it; having learned of a feast to the north, should go to the south without being drawn toward it. Wherever that feast may be—whether in a village, a city, a town, a hamlet, a market-town, a capital, a port, a mine, a commercial center, a hermitage, a settlement, or a royal capital—they should not set out for the journey with the intent of going to that feast. An omniscient one would say: "This is a source of fault. For one who sets out with the intent of going to a feast, they might eat food that is procured by means of alms, or prepared specifically for them, or mixed with householders' food, or purchased, or borrowed, or taken by force, or given without permission, or brought from elsewhere and offered to them. Furthermore, for the sake of the monks, the uncontrolled (householders) might make large doors small, or make small doors large; they might make even sleeping places uneven, or make uneven sleeping places even; they might make windy sleeping places sheltered from the wind, or make sheltered sleeping places windy; or they might cut down and pull up green plants inside or outside the dwelling and spread them out as bedding.

This indeed has been declared by the Blessed One regarding bedding; therefore, a restrained *niyantha* should not, for the sake of a meal-preparation (*saṅkhaḍi*)—whether held before or after—resolve to go toward such a meal-preparation. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they are always self-controlled, patient, and disciplined in all things. Thus I say.

If one person, having attended a certain feast (*saṅkhaḍī*), having drunk from it, should either spit it out or vomit it, or if, after eating it, it does not digest properly, or if some other painful disease or affliction should arise in him, a Kevalin would say: "This is a cause for concern."

In this case, indeed, if a monk, while inspecting his lodging beforehand or afterwards for the sake of drinking intoxicants with householders, housewives, male wanderers, or female wanderers, should not find [privacy] and would thus fall into a state of social mixing in that very lodging; or if, being intoxicated and mentally deranged, he should approach a woman, a eunuch, or a child; or if someone should approach that monk and say: "O venerable ascetic, whether here in the grove or here in the lodging, at night or at twilight, having yielded to the ways of the village, we have come together in secret for sexual intercourse"—if he should consent to that very thing, [the Teacher says]: "This must not be done, having considered it; these are the sources of danger that exist and are present as obstacles. Therefore, that self-controlled Nigaṇṭha should not, for the purpose of going to such a feast, either before or after, resolve upon going to a feast."

If that monk or nun, having heard of or perceived some festive gathering (*saṅkhaḍi*), runs toward it with a mind full of longing, thinking "the gathering is certain," and is unable to obtain alms-food—whether sought from various families, or obtained by chance—from those other families there for the purpose of eating, he or she would be touching upon a state of deceit; therefore, one should not act thus. Instead, having entered there at the proper time, he or she should obtain alms-food—whether sought from various families or obtained by chance—and eat the food.

If a monk or a nun should know of a village, or even a capital city, where there is a communal feast (*saṅkhaḍī*), they should not, for the purpose of that feast, set out to go to that village or capital city. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger; for one entering a crowded and noisy communal feast, it may happen that his foot has previously been stepped upon by another's foot, or his hand moved against another's hand, or his foot struck by another's foot, or his head bumped against another's head, or his body jostled by another's body; or he may have been struck with a staff, a bone, a fist, a clod of earth, a stone, or a potsherd; or he may have been splashed with cold water, or covered with dust, or made to consume what is unfit for consumption, or have received what was being given to others. Therefore, a restrained Nirgrantha should not, for the purpose of such a communal feast, set out to go to such a crowded and noisy place.

If that monk or nun, having entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms, should know that food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacies—is both acceptable and unacceptable; then, with a mind possessed by doubt and with a state of being unpurified, even if such food is available, they should not accept it.

If that monk or nun, desiring to enter a householder’s family for the purpose of alms-gathering, should enter or exit that householder’s family for the purpose of alms-gathering with all their belongings; or if that monk or nun, while exiting or entering the dwelling-ground or the study-ground outside, should exit or enter the dwelling-ground or the study-ground outside with all their belongings; or if that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should travel from village to village with all their belongings.

If that monk or nun should perceive that there is heavy rain falling, or see that heavy mud is being accumulated, or see that dust is being raised by a great wind, or see that crawling or flying mobile creatures are swarming together, then having perceived this, he should not enter or exit a householder’s family for the sake of alms with all his belongings; nor should he enter or exit the dwelling ground or the study ground outside, nor travel from village to village.

If that monk or nun should know families where there are Kshatriyas, or kings, or chieftains, or royal officials, or those belonging to the royal lineage—whether they are going out or coming in, whether they are settled or have assembled, whether they are inviting or not inviting—to food, drink, soft food, or delicacies that are impure and unfit for acceptance, then even if such things are available, he or she should not accept them, considering them to be impure and unfit for acceptance. Thus I say.

When a monk or a nun has entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms-food, and should he perceive that there is meat or fish, or a heap of meat or a heap of fish, or a gift being sent, or a present, or a *hiṅgola*, or a *saṃmela*—and should he see it being carried along a path that has many living beings, many seeds, many herbs, much dew, much water, and many insects, fungi, mud, clay, and spiderwebs; and that many ascetics, Brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars have arrived or will arrive there, making it a place of crowded activity where there is no freedom for coming and going, nor freedom for reciting, questioning, rehearsing, reflecting, or contemplating the meaning of the Dharma—then, having understood this, he should not set out with the intention of going to such a communal feast (*saṅkhaḍi*), whether it be one held before or after [the meal].

When a monk or a nun has entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms, and should they perceive that there is meat or fish being carried away, and that the path between [the houses] contains few living beings, up to few cobwebs, and that many ascetics, brahmins, and others will not be approaching; and that the livelihood for one who possesses wisdom is restricted regarding going out and coming in, or regarding recitation, questioning, reviewing, reflection, and contemplation on the Dharma—having understood this, he should not, for the purpose of alms, set out toward such a communal feast, whether it be a feast held before or after [the meal].

If that monk or nun, desiring to enter a householder’s family for the sake of alms, should perceive that milch cows are being milked, or should perceive food, drink, solid food, or delicacies being prepared, and should know that it has not yet been offered, then perceiving this, he should neither go out nor enter the householder’s family for the sake of alms. Having understood this, he should move aside to a secluded spot; having moved aside, he should stand where there is no noise and no visibility. But if he should perceive that the milch cows have been milked, or should perceive that the food, drink, solid food, or delicacies have already been prepared, and should know that it has already been offered, then, perceiving this, he may indeed, with self-restraint, go out or enter the householder’s family for the sake of alms.

Some mendicants speak thus: "Whether staying in one place or traveling from village to village, this village is indeed small and crowded; it is not large. Therefore, O Venerable Ones, go for alms-round to the villages outside. There, certain people with whom a monk has had prior acquaintance or later acquaintance reside—namely, householders, housewives, sons of householders, daughters of householders, daughters-in-law of householders, nurses, male slaves, female slaves, laborers, or female laborers. To such families, whether known before or known after, I shall enter first for alms-round. Perhaps there I will obtain alms-food, or rice-gruel, or milk, or curds, or fresh butter, or ghee, or sugar, or oil, or honey, or liquor, or meat, or *saṅkuli* (a type of cake), or *phāṇiya* (molasses), or *pūya* (cakes), or *sahariṇī* (a sweet dish). Having eaten that beforehand and drunk it, and having thoroughly cleaned and wiped my bowl, I will afterwards enter or exit the householder's family for alms with the other monks. He should not act in this way. Instead, he should enter those places together with the monks at the proper time, and there, having received alms-food collected from various families—whether sought or obtained by chance—he should take his meal. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that which is consistent in all things, disciplined, and always self-controlled. Thus I say.

When that monk has entered [the village], he should know: if he sees the first portion of alms being lifted up, if he sees the first portion of alms being set down, if he sees the first portion of alms being carried away, if he sees the first portion of alms being distributed, if he sees the first portion of alms being consumed, or if he sees the first portion of alms being discarded; or if he perceives that before he arrives there will be theft or plunder, or that other ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, or beggars will already be rushing there in great haste—thinking, "Alas! Shall I too have to rush there?"—he should not, out of a sense of deceit, allow himself to be affected by such thoughts, nor should he act in this way.

When that monk has entered [the village] up to this point—should there be fields, ditches, walls, archways, bolts, or bolt-sockets in his path—he should proceed with restraint; he should not go in a straight line. A kevalin would say: "This is a danger. While proceeding there, he might stumble, slip, or fall. While stumbling, slipping, or falling there, his body might become smeared with feces, urine, saliva, mucus, vomit, bile, pus, dried excrement, or blood. Such a body he should not rub or wipe, nor scrub or scrape, nor press or rub it dry, nor heat or warm it on ground that is bare, nor on moist ground, nor on dusty ground, nor on a living stone, nor on a living clod of earth, nor on wood inhabited by living beings, containing eggs, containing creatures, or even containing webs. He should not rub or wipe it, nor scrub or scrape it, nor press or rub it dry, nor heat or warm it. Rather, he should first seek out grass, leaves, wood, or gravel that is free from dust. Having sought it, he should take it and move aside to a secluded spot. Having moved aside, on a clean spot such as a heap of ashes or another similar place, having inspected it repeatedly and wiped it repeatedly, he may then, with restraint, rub or wipe it, or even heat or warm it.

When that monk or nun has entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms, if he or she should perceive a stray bull on the path, or perceive a stray buffalo on the path; likewise, if he or she perceives a stray human, horse, elephant, lion, tiger, leopard, bear, hyena, jackal, fox, dog, wild dog, *kokantika*, or *cittācillaḍaya* on the path, then with due care and exertion, he or she should proceed with restraint; he or she should not go straight ahead. If, while proceeding with due care and exertion, there should be an obstacle in the way—such as a pit, a stump, thorns, a slope, a precipice, uneven ground, or a swamp—he or she should proceed with due care and exertion; he or she should not go straight ahead.

If that monk or nun sees that the door-post of a householder’s family has been blocked by a thorn-fence, they should not open it, enter, or exit without first having obtained permission from them, and without having inspected and swept it; rather, having first obtained permission from them, and having repeatedly inspected and swept it, they should then, being restrained, open it, enter, or exit.

When that monk, having gone for alms, should perceive that a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a village beggar, or a guest has already entered the dwelling, he should not stand in their company or in the doorway. [The Kevalin says: This is a source of fault—before seeing them, another might bring food, drink, solid food, or delicacies for their sake and offer it. Now, for monks, this is the previously taught rule, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction: that he should not stand in their company or in the doorway. Taking that [alms-food], he should go aside; having gone aside, he should stand in a place free from obstruction and free from company. If that other person, while he is standing in a place free from obstruction and free from company, brings food, drink, solid food, or delicacies and offers it, and he should say: "O venerable śramaṇa, this food, drink, solid food, or delicacy has been set aside for all people; eat it or distribute it," and if he, having accepted it, should remain silent, thinking, "Perhaps this shall be mine alone"—this touches upon the ground of deceit; he should not do so. Taking that [food], he should go there; having gone there, he should announce it beforehand: "O venerable śramaṇa, this food, drink, solid food, or delicacy has been set aside for all people; eat it or distribute it. When he speaks thus, the other might say: "O venerable śramaṇa, you yourself should distribute it. While distributing it there, he should not take for himself excessively, nor what is choice, nor what is abundant, nor what is savory, nor what is delicious, nor what is pleasant, nor what is smooth, nor what is dry; rather, being uninfatuated, unattached, unclinging, and not overcome by passion therein, he should distribute it very evenly. If, while he is distributing it, the other should say: "O venerable śramaṇa, do not distribute it; let us all eat or drink together at once," then while eating or drinking there, he should not take for himself excessively, nor what is choice, nor what is abundant, nor what is savory, nor what is delicious, nor what is pleasant, nor what is smooth, nor what is dry; rather, being uninfatuated therein, and so on, he should eat or drink with great equanimity.

When that monk (or nun), having entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms, should perceive that a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a village beggar, or a guest has already entered previously, he should not bypass them to enter or stand in their presence. Taking that into account, he should move aside; having moved aside, he should stand where there is no obstruction. But if he should know that [the food] has been refused or given, then, when they have turned back, he may indeed enter or stand in their presence with self-restraint. This is the complete rule of conduct, which one should always practice. Thus I say.

When that monk, while wandering for alms, should perceive that many creatures seeking food have gathered and settled for the sake of foraging—for instance, he perceives that flocks of chickens or swarms of pigs, or crows, have gathered and settled upon a heap of grain—he should, being self-restrained, move by taking a detour; he should not go straight.

When that monk has gone for alms, he should not stand repeatedly leaning against the door-frame of a householder’s family; he should not stand at the place where water is discarded by a householder’s family; he should not stand at the threshold of a householder’s family; he should not stand in the line of sight of a bathhouse or a latrine belonging to a householder’s family, nor where there is a doorway directly opposite; he should not, having repeatedly extended his arms, point with his finger at a householder’s family, nor gaze at a window, a wall-opening, a crack, or a water-cistern after repeatedly extending his arms, pointing with his finger, bending down, or looking up; he should not beg from a householder by repeatedly pointing with his finger; he should not beg from a householder by repeatedly shaking his finger; he should not beg from a householder by repeatedly threatening him with his finger; he should not beg from a householder by repeatedly making a snorting sound with his finger; he should not beg from a householder by repeatedly bowing to him; and he should certainly not speak harshly.

If he sees someone there eating—whether it be a householder or even a laborer—he should first address them, saying, "O long-lived one," or "Sister," "Will you give me some other kind of food from this? If, while he is speaking thus, the other person should wash or rinse their hand, bowl, ladle, or vessel with cold water or hot water, he should first address them, saying, "O long-lived one," or "Sister," "Do not wash or rinse this hand, bowl, ladle, or vessel with cold water or hot water; if you wish to give me, give it to me exactly as it is. If, despite his speaking thus, the other person should wash or rinse the hand, bowl, ladle, or vessel with cold water or hot water and then bring it to him to give, then he, considering such food, drink, chewable food, or delicacy to be impure and unfit for consumption because of that prior preparation (*pūrvakarma*), should not accept it, even if it is offered.

But if he should know this: "It has not been prepared beforehand," and so on, up to "moist with water"—if it is of such a kind, or with a hand moist with water, or even with a vessel, then food or drink, up to solid food or soft food, being unwholesome, he should not accept it.

But if he should know thus: "It is not moist with water, nor damp," and the rest is exactly as before; likewise with earth-dust, water-moisture, and dampness; with green moss, vermilion, realgar, antimony, salt; with red ochre, yellow ochre, white chalk, and Soraṭṭhika clay; with flour, husks, or mixed [substances]. But if he should know thus: "It is not unmixed, but mixed"—with such a mixed hand or [other utensil] up to the vessel, he may accept the food or [other items] up to the snack, provided it is pure and so forth.

When that monk, while staying [in his dwelling], should know this: that someone, for the sake of a monk and with an uncontrolled mind, has pounded, is pounding, or will pound *pihu* (flour), *bahuraya* (coarse meal), *bhajjiya* (fried grain), *manthu* (gruel), *cāula* (rice), or *cāulapalamba* (boiled rice), upon a stone slab containing living beings, down to a web of cobwebs; or has scattered, is scattering, or will scatter it; then such *pihu* or up to *cāulapalamba*, being unwholesome and considering it unfit for alms, he should not accept it even if it is offered.

When that monk, while staying [in a dwelling], should know: "This is salt from a pit or salt from a saline soil; and an uncontrolled person, for the sake of a monk, has broken, is breaking, or will break it with a sentient stone, a sentient clod of earth, on a termite mound, or on wood inhabited by living beings, containing eggs, containing small creatures, seeds, green sprouts, dew, moisture, as well as insects, fungi, water, mud, and spiderwebs"—or if they have relished, are relishing, or will relish it—then such salt from a pit or salt from a saline soil is not fit to be accepted, even if it is available; he should not accept it.

If that monk, while staying there, should know that food, drink, solid food, or delicacy has been placed near a fire—such food, drink, solid food, or delicacy being impure and unfit for acceptance—he should not accept it, even if it is available, thinking it is not in accordance with the rules of seeking. The Kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger; one who is uncontrolled, acting for the sake of a monk, might injure living beings of fire by pouring out, or pouring down, or stroking, or wiping, or lifting up, or turning over. Now, for monks, this is the previously taught principle, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction: that such food, drink, solid food, or delicacy placed near a fire—being impure and unfit for acceptance—he should not accept it, even if it is available. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun. Thus I say.

If a monk or a nun, having entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms, should know that food—whether solid, soft, chewable, or tastable—is placed upon a beam, a pillar, a couch, a gallery, a palace, a roof-terrace, or any other such place suspended in the air; then such food brought from a gallery (mālōhaḍa)—whether solid, soft, chewable, or tastable—is unwholesome. Thinking it to be "not fit for acceptance" (anēsaṇijja), even if it is available, he should not accept it. The Kevalin would say: "This is a source of fault (āyāṇa). One who is not self-restrained might, for the sake of a monk, bring down a stool, a plank, a ladder, or a winnowing-fan, set them up, and climb upon them."

If, while climbing there, he should stumble or fall; and while stumbling or falling, he should injure his hand, foot, arm, thigh, belly, head, or any other part of his body, or damage the collection of sense organs; or if he should strike, crush, scratch, pinch, collide with, overturn, or fatigue living beings, creatures, souls, or sentient beings, or cause them to move from one place to another—then such food brought on a garland, even if it is obtained, he should not accept.

If that monk, while staying [in a dwelling], should know that food, drink, chewable food, or delicacy has been brought from a heap or a pile by one who is not self-restrained, for the sake of the monks, having been turned up, turned down, or pulled out and brought forth to be given—such food or drink, knowing it to be "brought from a height" (mālōhaḍa), even if it is available, he should not accept it.

When that monk, while wandering for alms, should know that food—whether it be solid food, drink, chewable food, or delicacy—is smeared with clay, then even if such food is available, he should not accept it. A Kevalin would say: "This is a source of harm; for the sake of a monk who is not self-restrained, one who digs up food smeared with clay for his sake would initiate violence against the earth-body; likewise, he would initiate violence against the fire-body, air-body, plant-life, and mobile beings. Furthermore, by smearing it again, he would perform subsequent action (pacchākamma). Therefore, monks, this has been previously taught [this is the resolve, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction]: that when such food smeared with clay is available, one should not accept it.

If that monk or nun, while staying [in a dwelling], should know that food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy—is placed upon the earth-body (puḍhavikāya), then such food, being impure and unfit for consumption, they should not accept.

If that monk or nun, while staying [in a dwelling], should know that food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy—is placed upon the water-body (āukāya), then such food, being impure and unfit for consumption, they should not accept even though it is available, considering it to be unobtainable through proper means (anēsaṇijja).

If a monk or a nun, having entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms, should know that food—whether hard, soft, chewable, or tastable—is placed upon a fire, they should not accept it even if an opportunity arises. A Kevalin would say: "This is a source of fault—if one who is uncontrolled, for the sake of a monk, were to move the fire, shift it, take it out, or bring it forth and offer it. Now, for monks, this has been previously taught: this is the resolve, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction—that such food, up to that which is placed upon a fire, being impure, should not be accepted.

If that monk or nun, while staying [in a house], should know that food, drink, chewable food, or delicacy is very hot, and that someone, for the sake of the monks, might blow upon it or fan it with a winnowing basket, a whisk, a palm-leaf fan, a leaf, a branch, a twig, a peacock feather, a peacock-feather fan, a cloth, a corner of a cloth, or with the hand or the mouth; then he should first speak thus: "O long-lived one," or "O sister," "do not blow upon or fan this food, drink, chewable food, or delicacy, which is very hot, with a winnowing basket or [any of the aforementioned items] up to the mouth. "If you wish to give it to me, give it to me just as it is. If, despite his speaking thus, the other person should blow upon or fan it with a winnowing basket or [other items] and then bring it and offer it, such food or [the rest] being unwholesome (aphāsuya), he should not accept it.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, if they should know that food, drink, solid food, or delicacy is placed upon a vegetable body (vanaspatikāya), then such food, or [any of the others] up to delicacies, even if obtained, they should not accept.

[If that monk or nun, having entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms, should know that there is food, drink, soft food, or solid food established upon a body of mobile beings—such food, up to being established upon a body of mobile beings, being unwholesome and unfit according to the rule—they, considering it so, should not accept it even if it is available.]

Whether it be a monk or a nun, if they should know that a certain kind of drink—such as water from a well, water from a pond, rice-water, or any other such kind of drink—is freshly washed, not yet sour, not yet overflowed, not yet digested, and not yet transformed, and considering it to be impure and unfit for consumption, they should not accept it even if it is offered. However, if they should know that it has been washed for a long time, is sour, has overflowed, is digested, and is transformed, and considering it to be pure and fit for consumption, they may accept it if it is offered.

If that monk or nun, while staying there, should recognize a kind of beverage, such as sesame-water, husk-water, barley-water, fermented rice-gruel, sour gruel, or pure water—or any other such kind of beverage—they should first address [the host], saying: "O long-lived one" or "Sister, will you give me any of these kinds of beverages from this? If the other person, being thus addressed, should say: "O venerable ascetic, take this very beverage yourself with your bowl," or "Pour it out for me and take it," or "Set it aside and take it"—then such a kind of beverage, if it is pure and available, he may accept it himself, or if another should give it to him, he may accept it.

If that monk, or [nun], should know that a kind of drink has been poured out or set down upon ground that is not free from living beings, up to: covered with vegetation, and if an unrenunciant, for the sake of the monks, having mixed it with water containing living organisms, or with moisture, or with alkaline water, or with fermented liquid, or with cold water, should bring it and offer it; such a kind of drink, being unwholesome, he should not accept even if it is offered. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun, [that they are restrained in all things, self-controlled, and always disciplined—thus I say].

When a monk or a nun has entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms, and should they know that there is a kind of beverage such as mango juice, emblic myrobalan juice, wood-apple juice, citron juice, grape juice, pomegranate juice, date juice, coconut water, bamboo-shoot juice, jujube juice, or tamarind juice—or any other similar kind of beverage—that contains seeds, husks, or grains; and if an uncontrolled person, for the sake of the monks, having squeezed it with a stone, a cloth, a hair-strainer, or having filtered it, should bring it and offer it; then such a kind of beverage, being impure and unfit for acceptance, they should not accept it even if it is offered, considering it to be unacceptable.

When that monk, having gone on his alms-round, arrives at incoming travelers' lodgings, park-houses, the families of householders, or hermitages, and repeatedly smells the scents of food, the scents of drink, or fragrant scents—there, out of a longing for them, being infatuated, greedy, attached, and obsessed, he should not inhale the scent, thinking, "What a fragrance! What a fragrance!"

If that monk, while staying [in a dwelling], should know that there is lotus root, or lotus stalk, or water-lily tuber—or anything else of a similar kind—that is raw, not processed by fire, and not suitable, he should not accept it.

If that monk or nun, while staying [in a dwelling], should know that there is long pepper or powdered long pepper, black pepper or powdered black pepper, ginger or powdered ginger, or anything else of a similar kind, raw and not processed by fire—[considering it] impure, unfit for alms, and not to be accepted—even when such is available, they should not accept it.

If that monk or nun, while staying [in a dwelling], should know of a hanging cluster of fruit—such as a cluster of mangoes, or a cluster of hog-plums, or a cluster of palmyra fruits, or a cluster of *jhijjhirī*, or a cluster of *surabhi*, or a cluster of *sallai*—or any other such hanging cluster of fruit that is raw, not yet processed by a knife, impure, and not fit for alms, then even if it is offered, they should not accept it, considering it thus.

If that monk or nun, while staying [in a dwelling], should know it to be a growth of sprouts—namely, the sprout of an *āsottha*, or the sprout of a *naggōha*, or the sprout of a *pilukhu*, or the sprout of a *nīpūra*, or the sprout of a *sallaï*, or any other such growth of sprouts—that is raw, not transformed by fire, unwholesome, and unfit for alms, they should not accept it.

If that monk, while staying [in a residence], should know that it is a fruit that has become worm-eaten—namely, a mango that has become worm-eaten, or a jambu-fruit that has become worm-eaten, or a wood-apple that has become worm-eaten, or a pomegranate that has become worm-eaten, or a bilva-fruit that has become worm-eaten, or any other such fruit that has become worm-eaten, raw, not transformed by fire, and unfit [to be accepted]—he should not accept it.

When that monk or nun has entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms, and should they know that there is a preparation of flour-mash, such as flour-mash of *udumbara*, or flour-mash of *nyagrodha*, or flour-mash of *pilukhu*, or flour-mash of *aśvattha*, or any other such preparation of flour-mash that is raw, improperly cooked, containing seeds, and impure—then, even if it is available, they should not accept it.

When that monk, having gone for alms, should know that there is rice-porridge, or flour-cakes, or honey, or liquor, or clarified butter, or whey, or old molasses, and that living beings have been born therein, have grown therein, have increased therein, have not departed, and have not transformed; that living beings are still present therein—considering it impure and unfit for collection, he should not accept it, even if it is offered.

When that monk, while staying there, should know that it is sugar-cane, or *anka*-karelu, or kaseruka, or *siṅghāḍaka*, or *pūtiāluka*—or any other such raw food that has not been transformed by fire [and is thus unfit and improper], he should not accept it, even if it is offered.

When that monk, having arrived [at a dwelling], should know that it contains a blue lotus, a blue lotus stalk, a lotus root, a lotus fiber, a water-lily, or a water-lily bud, or anything else of a similar nature—[raw, not processed by fire, unwholesome, and not to be sought for alms]—then, considering it thus, he should not accept it even if it is offered.

When that monk or nun has entered a householder’s family, he or she should know: if there are seeds from the tip, seeds from the root, seeds from the trunk, or seeds from the joint; or those produced from the tip, produced from the root, produced from the trunk, or produced from the joint—except for the top of a *takali* palm, the head of a *takali*, the top of a *nāliēri* palm, the top of a date palm, or the top of a *tāla* palm—or any other such raw thing not yet processed by an instrument, [considering it unwholesome and unfit for alms], even if it is available, he or she should not accept it.

If that monk, while staying [in a dwelling], should know: "This is sugarcane, or sugar-cane, roasted, mixed, burnt, or with its tips cut off; or a kandalī sprout, or anything else of a similar kind—raw, not yet transformed by fire"—then, being impure, he should not accept it.

If that monk, while staying [in a dwelling], should know: "This is garlic, or garlic leaf, or garlic stalk, or garlic bulb, or garlic shoot; or anything else of a similar kind—raw, not yet transformed by fire"—then, being impure, he should not accept it.

When that monk, having arrived [at a village], should know that there is *atthiya* (a type of tuber), or *kumbhipakka* (food cooked in a pot), or *tinduga* (the fruit of the *tinduka* tree), or *vēluga* (the fruit of the *velu* tree), or *kāsavanāliya* (a type of grain), or any other such raw food that has not been processed by fire—then, even if it is available, he should not accept it.

If that monk, being present, should know that it is rice, or rice in a pot, or rice in a basket, or husked rice, or rice flour, or sesame seeds, or sesame flour, or sesame cakes—or anything else of a similar kind—that is raw, not yet processed by fire, unwholesome, and not fit for alms, then even if it is obtained, he should not accept it, considering it thus.
This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun, [that they are restrained in all things, self-controlled, and ever vigilant]. Thus I say.

In this world, indeed, in the east, west, south, or north, there may be certain faithful householders, or even female laborers, who have previously thought thus: "These venerable ascetics are possessed of virtue, possessed of vows, possessed of qualities; they are self-restrained, fully controlled, celibate, and have desisted from the practice of sexual intercourse. It is not permissible for them to eat or drink food, drink, soft food, or delicacy that has been prepared specifically for them (*āhākammiya*). However, this food—whether it be solid food or anything up to all these things—which was prepared for our own sake, we shall now offer to the ascetics. Furthermore, we ourselves shall later consume solid food or anything up to [all these things] for our own sake. Having heard and reflected upon such a proclamation, if such food—whether it be solid food or anything up to [all these things]—is impure and unfit to be sought, he should not accept it, even if it is available, thinking it to be so.

Whether that monk or nun is staying, residing, or traveling from village to village, if they should know of a village, or [a town, a market-town, a hamlet, a fort, a city, a port, a mine, a commercial center, a hermitage, or a settlement], or a capital city—within this village, or even within this capital city—there are certain people who dwell as long-standing associates or later acquaintances of a particular monk; namely, householders or [even down to female laborers]. To such families, he should not go out for alms or enter before the meal or after the meal. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of fault. For, having seen it beforehand, another person might prepare or cook food, drink, solid food, or delicacy for his sake. Now, for monks, this has been previously taught: this is the rule, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction—that one should not enter or exit such families before the meal or after the meal for the sake of food or drink. Having understood this, he should step aside to a secluded spot; having stepped aside, he should remain in a place that is unobserved and private.

If he should enter there at the proper time, and having entered, should seek and obtain alms-food by wandering for alms among various families—whether it be what is gathered from the community, sought, or received—and should take that food; and if another person, after he has already entered at the proper time, should prepare or cook food, drink, soft food, or solid food for him, and if he should remain silent and wait for it, thinking, "I shall reject it only when it has been brought," he would be touching upon a state of deceit. He should not act in this way. He should first speak out: "O long-lived one! or "O sister!", "It is not permissible for me to eat or drink food, drink, soft food, or solid food that is prepared specifically for me (āhākammiya). Do not prepare it; do not cook it. If, despite his speaking thus, the other person should still prepare food, drink, soft food, or solid food and, having brought it, offer it to him, then such food, drink, soft food, or solid food being impure (aphāsuya), even if it is obtained, he should not accept it.

When that monk or nun has entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms-food, and should he or she perceive meat or fish being fried, or see oil-cakes being prepared for a specific order, he or she should not approach and request it in an excessive manner, except on account of illness.

If that monk, having gone [for alms] and received a certain kind of food, eats what is fragrant and fragrant and discards what is foul and foul, he touches upon a state of deceit; he should not act thus. Whether it be fragrant or foul, he should eat everything and not discard anything.

If that monk, while staying [in a monastery], having received some kind of beverage, discards flower after flower and bitter substance after bitter substance, he touches upon deceitful conduct; he should not act thus. Whether it be "flower" or "bitter substance," he should consume all of it and should not discard anything at all.

If a monk or a nun, having received a great variety of food, leaves it aside without informing or asking permission of those fellow monks who are staying there—fellow practitioners who are sharing the same meal, who are agreeable, not excluded, and not far away—he incurs the fault of deceit. He should not act in this way. Instead, taking that food with him, he should go to them and, upon arrival, announce it beforehand: "O venerable recluses, I have this food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacies—which is of many varieties; please eat of it. If the other person says to him who speaks thus: "O venerable recluse, this is food—whether it be solid food up to delicacies—as much as will spoil [before we can finish], so much shall we eat or drink; if all of it will spoil, then we shall eat or drink all of it."

If that monk, or even a nun, should know that food, drink, solid food, or delicacy has been prepared specifically for someone else and brought outside, and if they consider it not approved by others, not formally assigned, and impure—[even if it is available]—they should not accept it. But if they consider it approved by others, properly assigned, pure, and fit to be sought, and it is available, they may accept it. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun, [that they are always self-restrained, guarded, and disciplined in all things]. Thus I say.
