If one person, having received alms-food intended for the community, should give it away haphazardly to whomever they wish without first asking his fellow-monks, he touches upon a state of deceit; he should not act in this way. Taking that [alms-food] with him, he should go to them and say: "O venerable monks! I have fellow-monks who were my associates before or after—namely, an *ācārya*, an *upādhyāya*, a *pravartin*, an *sthavira*, a *gaṇin*, a *gaṇadhara*, or a *gaṇāvacchedaka*. I shall give [the food] to them in abundance. If another should say to him as he speaks thus: "By all means, O venerable one! Give as much as is appropriate," he should give as much as the other says; if the other says "all of this," he should give all of it.

If a certain individual, having received a pleasant variety of food, conceals it with coarse food, thinking, "Lest this be seen," and [thinking], "Whether it be myself, the teacher, or even the head of the community (gaṇāvacchedaka), nothing at all must be given by me to anyone"—this is a state of deceit; he should not act thus. He should go there taking that [food] with him. Having gone, he should first of all hold out his bowl with palms upturned and announce, "This indeed, this indeed," and he should not conceal anything. If a certain individual, having received some other kind of food, eats only the best and best portions and then consumes what is discolored or tasteless—this is a state of deceit; he should not act thus.

If that monk should know that there is a sugarcane stalk, or a cluster of sugarcane, or sugarcane juice, or sugarcane core, or sugarcane shoot, or sugarcane sprout, or a *śimbali* fruit, or a *śimbali* pod—wherein there might be a small amount of edible food that is largely of a nature to be discarded—he, considering such a thing as a sugarcane stalk up to a *śimbali* pod to be impure and unfit for acceptance, should not accept it even if it is offered.

If that monk, or [nun], should know that in the alms-bowl there is much bone, or meat, or fish, or many thorns, and that it contains little edible food and is mostly characterized by things to be discarded—then, considering such things as containing much bone, or meat, or many thorns to be impure and unfit for acceptance, he should not accept them even if an opportunity for gain arises.

If that monk, while wandering for alms, should be invited by another with much bone—whether with meat or fish—with the words: "O venerable ascetic! Do you desire to receive this meat with many bones? Having heard and reflected upon such an utterance, he should first speak out: "O brother! or "O sister! "It is not indeed permissible for me to receive meat with many bones. If you wish to give me, give me as much of the substance as there is; do not give the bones. If, while he is speaking thus, the other person, having brought it, should break off pieces of meat with many bones from within the bowl and offer them to him, then such a bowl—whether in the hand of another or in the vessel of another—being impure and unfit for acceptance, he should not accept it even if it is offered.

If he should receive [food] that has been forcibly taken, he should not say "it is edible" nor should he say "it is inedible. Taking it with him, he should go to a secluded spot; having gone to a secluded spot—whether in a grove or in a dwelling—where there are no insects and it is free from spreading growth, he should eat the meat or fish, remove the bones and thorns, and taking it with him, he should go to a secluded spot; having gone to a secluded spot—whether on a heap of ashes or elsewhere—he should repeatedly sweep the area and then, being restrained, properly dispose of it.

If that monk, while staying [in his dwelling], should have another person bring and place inside his alms-bowl either natural salt or refined salt, having first distributed it; if he should take such an alms-bowl from the hand of another or from the vessel of another—considering it to be unwholesome and not fit for acceptance, even though there is an opportunity for gain—he should not accept it.

If he should receive it by force, and he should perceive that the giver has not gone very far away, he should take it and go there himself. Having arrived, he should first announce it: "O long-lived one! or "Sister!", "Was this given to you knowingly, or unknowingly? If she should say, "It was certainly not given to me knowingly; it was given unknowingly," he should say, "Very well, O long-lived one, I shall now relinquish it; you may eat it or distribute it. When it has been approved and instructed by others, then, being restrained, he may eat it or drink it. But whatever he is unable to eat or drink, if there are fellow-monks (sādharmikas) staying there who share the same community, who are in agreement, and who are not to be excluded and are nearby, it should be offered to them. Wherever there are no fellow-monks, it should be disposed of exactly as one would do with food that has become stale. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun [who is composed in all things, self-controlled, and always striving]. Thus I say.

Some mendicants, while staying together, or living together, or wandering from village to village, having obtained a pleasant variety of food, [if] that mendicant becomes ill, [they might say: "Bring this for him; let that mendicant eat it. If that mendicant should not eat it, [the others might say: "You yourself should eat it. Then, thinking "I shall eat it myself," he should repeatedly misrepresent it by saying: "This is alms-food (piṇḍa), this is a morsel (loṇa); this is bitter, this is pungent, this is astringent, this is sour, this is sweet; indeed, nothing from this is suitable for the sick man. He touches upon a state of deceit. He should not do so; rather, he should describe it exactly as it is situated, according to what is suitable for the sick man: that which is bitter, he should call "bitter"; that which is pungent, he should call "pungent"; that which is astringent, he should call "astringent"; that which is sour, he should call "sour"; that which is sweet, he should call "sweet."

Some alms-collecting monks, while staying together, or living together, or wandering from village to village, having obtained a pleasing variety of food, [say]: "This monk is ill; come now, bring him some of this. If that monk should not eat it, one should bring it; [thinking] "I will certainly not eat it myself," one should set aside such grounds for attachment.

Now, a monk should know the seven ways of seeking alms-food and the seven ways of seeking drink. In this regard, this is the first way of seeking alms-food: if the hand is not smeared and the vessel is not smeared—with such an unsmeared hand or vessel, he may himself take food or even sweetmeats, or another may give them to him; if it is pure and [he considers it] acceptable, then, when there is an opportunity, he may accept it—this is the first way of seeking alms-food.

Furthermore, this is the second rule for the seeking of alms: if the hand is soiled or the vessel is soiled—and by such a soiled hand or vessel one should not oneself accept food, drink, soft food, or delicacy, nor should another give it to him—yet if he perceives it to be pure and acceptable, he may accept it when it is offered. This is the second rule for the seeking of alms.

Furthermore, this is the third rule for the seeking of alms-food: Here, indeed, in the east, west, south, or north, there may be certain faithful laypeople—whether householders or even female laborers—and in various kinds of vessels belonging to them, food may have been previously placed, such as in a platter, a pot, a pan, a bowl, or a cup. Now, if he should perceive that the hand is unsoiled while the vessel is soiled, or the hand is soiled while the vessel is unsoiled, then whether he is a carrier of an alms-bowl or one who uses his hands as a bowl, he should first inform [the giver], saying, "O long-lived one" or "O sister," "With this hand of yours which is unsoiled and with this vessel which is soiled, or with this hand which is soiled and this vessel which is unsoiled, having taken and picked up [the food] into this bowl or into your hand, please give it to me. Such a kind of food, whether he obtains it himself or someone else gives it to him, if it is pure and fit to be sought, he should accept it when it is available. This is the third rule for the seeking of alms-food.

Furthermore, this is the fourth rule for the seeking of alms-food: A monk—or a nun—should know that if there is *pihu* (flattened grain), or grain with much dust, or parched grain, or flour-mash, or rice, or rice-water, and if these have been placed in a bowl with little subsequent preparation and little modification, then such *pihu* or other items up to rice-water, whether he has obtained them himself or they are given to him by another, he may accept them if he considers them pure and fit to be sought, provided they are available. This is the fourth rule for the seeking of alms-food.

Now, furthermore, there is the fifth method of seeking alms-food: When that monk, having gone for alms, should know that the food has already been taken up—namely, in a shallow bowl, or in a *ḍiṇḍima* vessel, or in a basket—and if he further knows that it is "overflowing," with water-drops clinging to his hands, then such food, whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy, he should not seek it himself, nor should he accept it if another offers it, even while considering it pure and fit for consumption, provided that it is available. This is the fifth method of seeking alms-food.

Furthermore, this is the sixth method of seeking alms: that monk, or [nun], should know that a meal has been prepared—both that which was prepared for one’s own sake and that which was prepared for the sake of others—and having determined it to be wholesome and fit for consumption, he should accept it when it is available, provided it has been brought to the feet or brought to the hands. This is the sixth method of seeking alms.

Now, furthermore, is the seventh alms-gathering (piṇḍesaṇā): When that monk or [nun], being [on his alms-round], should know a kind of food consisting of discarded things (ujjhita-dhammiya), which many two-footed and four-footed beings—ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars—do not desire; such a kind of food consisting of discarded things he may himself seek or another may give him—[thinking it to be pure and acceptable]—if it is available, he should accept it. This is the seventh alms-gathering. These are the seven alms-gatherings. Now, furthermore, are the seven drink-gatherings (pāṇesaṇā).
In this regard, there are these first two ways of seeking alms-food (*pāṇesaṇā*): [the first is] when the hands are not mixed together and the vessels are not mixed together;
[the second is] when the hands are mixed together and the vessels are mixed together.
Furthermore, there is a third way of seeking alms-food: here indeed, in whatever direction—east, west, south, or north—there are certain faithful laypeople.

Furthermore, this is the fourth method of seeking food: when that monk, having gone for alms, should know a certain kind of drink, namely—sesame water, husk-water, barley water, fermented rice-gruel, sour gruel, or pure boiled water—and if this has been received in his bowl with little subsequent processing and little transformation, then such sesame water, husk-water, barley water, fermented rice-gruel, sour gruel, or pure boiled water he may himself seek or another may give him; being pure and acceptable, he may accept it.
Furthermore, there is the fifth method of seeking drink: that monk, having entered [the village], should know that the variety of drinks has already been taken up.
Furthermore, there is the sixth method of seeking drink: that monk, having entered [the village], should know that the variety of drinks has already been set aside.

Furthermore, there is the seventh method of seeking drink: that monk or nun, having entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms, should know that the variety of drinks consists of things that have been largely discarded.

Thus, when undertaking any one of these seven rules for seeking alms-food or the seven rules for seeking drinks, he should not speak thus: "These venerable ones have indeed entered upon a wrong course; I alone have rightly entered upon it. Rather, he should think: "Those venerable ones who, having undertaken these rules, dwell [in them], and I myself who, having undertaken this rule, dwell [in it]—all of us are established in the command of the Jinas, in mutual harmony, and thus we dwell. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun. Thus I say.
[The second chapter – Lodgings]

If that monk or nun should desire to seek out and enter a dwelling—whether it be a village, city, town, hamlet, market-town, capital, port, mine, district, hermitage, settlement, or royal capital—and should know that the lodging is a dwelling containing eggs, living beings, seeds, green plants, dew, water, and earth-mites, as well as cobwebs, then in such a dwelling they should not take up a standing posture, a bed, or a sitting place.

If that monk or nun should know a lodging to be free from insects, free from small creatures, and so on, up to free from webs; then, having inspected and swept such a lodging, they should, being well-restrained, prepare a place for standing, a bed, or a seat.

Furthermore, he should recognize a lodging (*uvassaya*) as follows: if, for the sake of a fellow-monk (*sāhammiya*), one has caused living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings to be harmed; if it is intended for that purpose, if it is purchased, if it is borrowed, if it is taken by force, if it is not given away, or if it is brought from elsewhere—and if such a lodging is prepared, whether it has been occupied by another person or not, or even if it has not been used [by others], he should not take up a standing posture, a bed, or a place for sitting there.

Furthermore, if he should know of a lodging where, for his sake, many fellow-monks have, for the purpose of providing for him, procured it by means of the destruction of living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings—whether it be purchased, borrowed, taken by force, given without permission, or brought from elsewhere—in such a lodging, whether it has been prepared by others or not, whether it is for one's own use or not, whether it has been occupied or not, or whether it has been used or not, he should not take up a standing place, a bed, or a sitting place.

Furthermore, if he should know a lodging (upassaya) to be one where, for the sake of a fellow-monk, living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings have been harmed; where it has been intended for that purpose, purchased, bartered, taken by force, given without permission, or brought from elsewhere, and thus prepared—then in such a lodging, whether it has been made accessible by another person or not, whether it has been occupied or not, he should not take up a standing place, a bed, or a sitting area.

Furthermore, he should recognize a lodging as follows: if, for the sake of many female fellow-monks, [a donor] has, with this intention, procured it by means of the destruction of living beings, plants, creatures, and sentient beings—whether it be purchased, bartered, taken by force, ungiven, or brought from elsewhere—and has thus prepared such a lodging, even if it is occupied by another person or has not yet been used, he should not take up a standing position, a bed, or a place of rest there.

If that monk or nun should know of a lodging where many ascetics, brahmins, guests, mendicants, and beggars have been specifically targeted—having repeatedly singled them out—and where living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings have been slaughtered for their sake, and where [food] has been purchased, bartered, seized, given away, or brought from elsewhere and prepared for them; in such a lodging, whether it has been occupied by others or not, whether it has been used or not, he should not take up a standing place, a bed, or a seat.

If that monk or nun should know that a lodging has been prepared specifically for many ascetics, brahmins, guests, beggars, or mendicants—where living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings have been killed, and which has not been used [by others]—he or she should not prepare a place, a bed, or a resting spot there. But if he or she should know it to be "prepared by another" (purisantarakaḍa) and so forth, and that it has been used [by others], then having inspected and swept it, he or she, being self-restrained, may indeed prepare a place, a bed, or a resting spot there.

If that monk or nun should know a lodging or dwelling-place to have been built, erected, roofed, plastered, leveled, smoothed, polished, or fumigated for the sake of a monk by one who is uncontrolled—such a dwelling, if it has not been made with an interval between persons, is not inhabited, and has not been used, they should not choose to take up a standing place, a bed, or a sitting place there. But if they should know it to have been made with an interval between persons and to have been used, then, having inspected and swept it, they may, being self-controlled, choose to take up a standing place, a bed, or a sitting place.

If that monk or nun should know of a lodging where uncontrolled people, for the sake of the monks, have made small doors large, as described in the *Piṇḍesaṇā* [chapter], up to the point of spreading out a bedding-cover; or where they have spread out a bedding-cover outside or in a low-lying place—in such a lodging, if it has not been prepared by others, is not established for them, is not used, and has not been resorted to, he should not choose a standing place, a bed, or a sitting place there. But if he should know it has been prepared by others and has been resorted to, then having inspected it and swept it, he may, being restrained, choose a standing place, a bed, or a sitting place.

If that monk or nun should know that a lodging is one where, for the sake of monks, an uncontrolled person has moved bulbs, roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds, or green plants from one place to another, or has thrown them outside, then in such a lodging—provided it is not prepared by another person—they should not choose a place to stand, a bed, or a sitting area. However, if they should know that it has been prepared by another person, is inhabited by them, used by them, and enjoyed by them, then having inspected and swept it, they may, being self-controlled, choose a place to stand, a bed, or a sitting area.

If that monk or nun should know that in a lodging or dwelling, someone who is not self-restrained, for the sake of a monk, has moved a bench, a plank, a ladder, or a winnowing fan from one place to another, or has thrown it outside—if such a dwelling is not secured by the presence of men, they should not occupy a standing place, a bed, or a sitting area there; however, if they should know that it is secured by the presence of men, then they may occupy it.

If that monk or nun should know of a lodging—namely, on a trunk, a bed, a platform, a palace, a flat roof, or any other such structure suspended in the air—they may, except for urgent or non-urgent reasons, choose to stand, lie down, or sit there. If they have already chosen it, they must not wash or rinse their hands, feet, eyes, teeth, or mouth with cold water or warm water. They must not discharge filth there, namely: feces, urine, spittle, mucus, vomit, bile, pus, blood, or any other part of the body. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger. If they discharge filth there, they might stumble or fall; while stumbling or falling, they might injure their hand, foot, arm, thigh, belly, head, or any other part of the body; or they might harm, wound, scratch, bruise, strike, crush, exhaust, or fatigue living beings, creatures, souls, or sentient beings; or they might move from one place to another, or deprive them of life. Therefore, this is the instruction previously given to monks: this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the teaching—that in such a lodging suspended in the air, one should not choose to stand, lie down, or sit.

If a monk or a nun should recognize a lodging as being shared with women, children, and domestic animals—such a lay-associated dwelling—they should not choose to stay there, nor take up a bed, nor a place for sitting or reclining. This is a source of danger for a monk living together with householders: he might suffer from indigestion, dysentery, or vomiting; or some other painful affliction or disease might arise. Then, out of compassion, an unrestrained person might anoint or smear the monk’s body with oil, ghee, butter, or fat; or they might rub it with a bath-powder, an alkali, lodhra, ointment, or flour; or they might scrub, massage, or rub it with cold water or warm water; or they might bathe him or sprinkle him; or, having prepared a fire-wood fire by means of wood that is "hard" (dāruṇā) or "wood-transformed" (dārupariṇāma), they might kindle or set it ablaze, and having kindled or set it ablaze, they might heat or burn his body. Now, this is the prior instruction, this is the teaching for monks: that in such a lay-associated dwelling, one should not choose to stay, nor take up a bed, nor a place for sitting or reclining.

This is a source of danger for a monk living in a layperson’s dwelling: here, indeed, householders, or housewives, or sons of householders, or daughters of householders, or daughters-in-law of householders, or nurses, or male servants, or female servants, or laborers, or female laborers, may mutually revile, bind, obstruct, or harm one another. Now, if a monk should harbor fluctuating thoughts, thinking, "Let these people revile one another or not; let them even go so far as to harm one another or not," then for such monks there is this previously enjoined resolve: that they should not, in such a layperson’s dwelling, take up a standing posture, a bed, or a sitting place.

This is a source of danger for a monk living together with householders: here, indeed, a householder might, for his own sake, kindle, rekindle, or extinguish a mass of fire. If the monk should entertain various thoughts—such as, "Let these people indeed kindle the fire or not; let them rekindle it or not; let them extinguish it or not"—then the monks have been previously instructed that this is their firm resolve: that in such a lodging belonging to a householder, he should not take up a standing place, a bed, or a sitting place.

This is a source of danger for a monk living together with householders: suppose he sees there in the householder’s home earrings, necklaces, gems, pearls, silver, gold, bracelets, armlets, triple-strand necklaces, pendants, long necklaces, half-necklaces, single-string necklaces, pearl strings, golden strings, or gem-strings; or suppose he sees a young girl adorned and decorated. Then the monk might fix his mind on various thoughts, saying, "She is like this," or "She is not like this," or he might express such thoughts in speech. Now, monks, this has been previously taught to you—this is the resolve, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction—that one should not, in such a residence, prepare a standing place, a bed, or a sitting place.

This is a danger for a monk living together with householders: there may indeed be householders’ wives, daughters, daughters-in-law, nurses, female slaves, or female servants, and it has been said of them before: “These are the venerable ascetics who possess virtue, possess vows, possess qualities, are self-controlled, restrained, celibate, and have desisted from the practice of sexual intercourse; it is not permissible for them to engage in the practice of sexual intercourse as a means of enjoyment. And she who should engage in sexual intercourse with them as a means of enjoyment would surely obtain a son—radiant, glorious, handsome, famous, beneficial in the future life, and worthy of being seen. Having heard and considered such a report, one among those faithful women might urge that ascetic monk toward the practice of sexual intercourse. Now, monks, this was previously taught [this is the vow, up to the instruction]: that in such a lodging belonging to a householder, one should not arrange a standing place, a bed, or a sitting place. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun, that they are equanimous in all things, self-restrained, and self-controlled. Thus I say.

Some householders are devoted to cleanliness (*śuci-samācāra*), whereas a monk is one who does not bathe and follows the practice of *moya* (the natural state). That odor may be unpleasant, foul-smelling, disagreeable, or even repulsive. What was his former practice may become his later practice, or what was his later practice may become his former practice; thus, regarding the requirements of a monk, he may perform them or he may not. Now, this is the previously taught rule for monks, up to this instruction: that in such a lodging, he should not prepare a place for standing, a bed, or a seat.

This is a source of danger for a monk living together with householders: suppose various kinds of food have been prepared there by a householder for his own sake; and then, for the sake of a monk, he should subsequently prepare or have prepared solid food, soft food, delicacies, or refreshments. If the monk should desire to eat, drink, or consume that, then for monks who have been previously instructed—this being their rule of conduct and so forth—he should not occupy a place, nor even stay, in such a lodging.

This is a source of danger for a monk living together with a householder: there may be various kinds of wood previously cut for the householder’s own use; then, for the sake of the monk, he might have such various kinds of wood split, or bought, or borrowed, or having fashioned them into a wooden structure, he might kindle or ignite a fire. In such a case, the monk might desire to warm himself, to cook, or to keep watch. Now, monks, this is the rule previously taught [and so on], that one should not occupy a place, nor even perform any activity, in such a lodging.

If that monk or nun, being pressed by the need for excrement or urine, should open the door-panel of a householder’s dwelling at night or at twilight, and a thief frequenting those pathways should enter, it is not permissible for that monk to say: "This thief is entering or is not entering; he is creeping in or is not creeping in; he is jumping over or is not jumping over; he is shouting or is not shouting; he has stolen this, he has stolen that; this belongs to him, this belongs to another; this is the thief, this is the accomplice, this is the killer, this one did it here. To suspect that an innocent monk is a thief is improper. Indeed, monks have been previously instructed: "This is the rule, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the teaching—that one should not occupy a place, a bed, or a resting spot in such a lodging."

If that monk or nun should know a dwelling-place to have grass heaps or straw heaps with eggs, living beings, seeds, sprouts, dew, mold, insects, fungi, water, mud, and cobwebs—such a dwelling-place they should not prepare for standing, for lying down, or for sitting. If that monk or nun should know a dwelling-place to have grass heaps or straw heaps without eggs, [without living beings, up to] without insects, fungi, water, mud, and cobwebs—such a dwelling-place, having inspected and swept it, they should then, being restrained, prepare it for standing, for lying down, or for sitting.
In guest-houses, or in park-dwellings, or in the households of householders, or in monastic residences, he should not speak thus whenever fellow-monks repeatedly visit him:

"Venerable sir, those who, having completed their summer retreat—whether for the winter or for the rainy season—continue to dwell in that very place, this, O long-lived one, is also an action that transgresses the proper time."

If, among those who have arrived at guest-houses, park-huts, the households of householders, or monastic dwellings, there are venerable ones who, having completed their seasonal retreat during the winter or the rainy season, do not observe the double or triple period of separation but instead reside there once again, then, O Venerable One, this is also an "act of remaining" (*uvaṭṭhāṇa-kiriyā*).

In this world, indeed, there are certain faithful people—whether to the east, west, south, or north—such as householders or even female laborers, for whom the sphere of proper conduct (*ācāra-gocara*) has not been well-heard. Having faith in it, having conviction in it, and taking delight in it, many ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and mendicants have had dwellings constructed for them here and there by householders. These include: assembly halls, sanctuaries, temples, community halls, pavilions, shops, market stalls, carriage-sheds, carriage-halls, workshops for ivory, reeds, leather, cane, wood, charcoal, timber, cemeteries, shrines, mountain retreats, cave-dwellings, or stone chambers; or even houses for the wealthy. When those venerable ones enter such assembly halls or even houses for the wealthy, O long-lived one, this too becomes an "excellent action" (*abhikkanta-kiriya*).

In this world, indeed, in the east, west, south, or north, there are certain faithful people—namely, householders or even female laborers—for whom the sphere of conduct (*ācāra-gocara*) has not been well-heard. Having faith in it, having conviction in it, and taking delight in it, many ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars are supported by those householders; for them, various dwellings are constructed here and there, such as guest-houses or even palatial residences. If venerable ones enter such guest-houses or palatial residences while they are not being offered [proper hospitality], then, O long-lived one, this is an "unexcelled action" (*anabhikrānta-kriyā*).

In this world, indeed, whether they be [people] from the east or even female servants, it has previously occurred to them thus: "These venerable ascetics are possessed of virtue and have desisted from the practice of sexual intercourse; it is not permissible for these venerable ones to dwell in a lodging that is 'procured by means of food' (āhākammiya). Whatever we have had built for our own sake—namely, beds and seats, or even houses—we shall relinquish all of those to the ascetics. Furthermore, after this, we ourselves will build [others] for our own sake, such as beds and seats, or even houses. Having heard and understood such a proclamation, if the venerable ones approach those beds and seats, or even houses, and having approached, engage in mutual hospitality, then, O long-lived one, this too is a "defiling action" (vajja-kiriyā).

In this world, indeed, there are certain faithful people—whether householders or even female laborers—in the east, west, south, or north. For them, the sphere of conduct (*ācāra-gocara*) is not well-understood. Yet, having faith in it, believing in it, and taking delight in it, many ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars are specifically sought out and designated; for their sake, householders have various dwellings constructed here and there, such as sitting-halls or even palatial residences. When venerable ones approach such sitting-halls or palatial residences and, having approached, engage with one another through mutual offerings, O long-lived one, this constitutes a "great sinful action" (*mahā-vajja-kiriya*).

In this world, indeed, there are certain faithful people—whether householders or even female laborers—in the east, west, south, or north. For them, the scope of proper conduct (*āyāra-gōyara*) has not been thoroughly heard. Having faith in that, having conviction in that, and being delighted by that, many ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars are supported; for their sake, householders have various dwellings constructed here and there, such as guest-halls (*āēsaṇa*) or even palatial residences (*bhavaṇagiha*). If venerable ones approach such guest-halls or palatial residences and engage with one another through mutual offerings, then, O long-lived one, this too becomes a blameworthy action (*sāvajja-kiriyā*).

In this world, indeed, whether toward the east, west, south, or north, there are some places where, for the sake of certain wandering ascetics who are weeping [for their own welfare], householders have constructed various dwellings. These include sitting-halls, and so forth, up to palatial residences. These are built with great violence against the earth-body, and so forth, up to great violence against the mobile-bodied beings, and through many kinds of evil deeds, such as: plastering, smearing, laying foundations, building doors, and closing them; or having cold water poured out, or having fire kindled. Those venerable ones who enter such sitting-halls, and so forth, up to palatial residences, and having entered, engage in dual-sided karma through various mutual offerings—this, O long-lived one, is also an act of great transgression.

In this world, indeed, there are certain faithful people—whether householders or even female laborers—in the east, west, south, or north. For them, the sphere of right conduct (*ācāra-gocara*) has not been well-heard. Having faith in it, having conviction in it, and being delighted by it, they have for their own sake had various dwellings constructed as householders. These include sitting-places, or even palatial mansions, involving great injury to the earth-body and so forth, up to great injury to the mobile-bodied beings, and through various kinds of evil deeds, such as: covering, plastering, laying foundations, and closing doors; or where cold water has previously been poured out, or where fire has previously been kindled. Now, those venerable ones who enter such sitting-places or even palatial mansions, and having entered, engage in work for one side with various offerings—this, O long-lived one, is an action that involves little fault. This, indeed, is the complete perfection for that monk or nun: that which is consistent with all goals, peaceful, and always disciplined. Thus I say.

Furthermore, that which is easily obtained, comfortable, and fit for alms-gathering is not necessarily pure with respect to these preliminary preparations (*pāhuḍa*), namely: covering, plastering, preparing the bedding and closing the doors, and the manner of seeking alms-food. That monk is devoted to his conduct, devoted to his standing posture, devoted to his sitting posture, and devoted to his bedding, seating, and seeking alms-food. There are monks who have declared themselves thus: upright, having entered upon the path of renunciation, and free from deceit—they are so described. Now, some preliminary preparations may have been previously removed, or they may have been previously set aside, or they may have been previously distributed, or they may have been previously consumed, or they may have been previously discarded. When explaining in this way, does he explain with equanimity? Yes, he does.

If a monk or a nun should know that a dwelling has small rooms and small doors, which are narrow and confined, then in such a dwelling, whether going out or entering at night or in the evening, they should go out or enter with their hand first and their foot afterwards; thus they should proceed with restraint. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger. Should there be anything belonging to ascetics or brahmins there—such as a sunshade, a bowl, a staff, a walking stick, a cushion, a tube, a cloth, a floor-covering, a hide, a leather case, or a leather scraper—if it is poorly tied, poorly placed, unstable, or moving to and fro, then a monk going out or entering at night or in the evening might stumble or fall. While stumbling or falling there, he might injure his hand, foot, arm, thigh, belly, head, or any other part of his body; or he might harm, wound, scratch, bruise, strike, collide with, crush, fatigue, or displace living beings, plants, souls, or creatures from one place to another, or even deprive them of life. Therefore, for monks, this is the previously taught rule, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction: that in such a dwelling, one should go out or enter with the hand first and the foot afterwards, proceeding with full restraint."

He should seek lodging after due consideration among incoming travelers, in garden-houses, in the households of householders, or in monasteries. He should request lodging from whoever is the master there or whoever has authority there, saying: "Indeed, O venerable one, we shall dwell for as long as it lasts and according to our needs, O venerable one, as long as [the dwelling] belongs to the venerable one, and until fellow-monks arrive; thereafter we shall depart."

Whether it be a monk or a nun, they should first ascertain the name and clan of the household with which they intend to dwell; thereafter, when that household invites them—or even if they do not invite them—to accept food, drink, soft food, or solid food, they should not accept it if it is unwholesome, thinking it to be "not fit for seeking," even though it may be available.

If that monk or nun should know a lodging to be shared with householders, crowded with people, and full of noise—where there is no freedom for going out or coming in, nor for reciting, questioning, reviewing, reflecting upon, or contemplating the Dharma—they should not choose to take up a standing posture, a bed, or a sitting place in such a lodging.

If a monk or a nun should know that a lodging has a path leading right through the middle of a householder’s family, such that it is connected to the road, then for one who is wise and mindful of the proper reflection, he or she should not choose to take up a standing posture, a bed, or a sitting place in such a lodging.

If a monk or a nun should know that in a certain lodging, householders or even female servants are mutually reviling, binding, obstructing, or harming one another, such that there is no possibility for entering or exiting, nor for the practice of meditation or reflection on the Dharma—having recognized this, he or she should not occupy a standing position or engage in any activity, up to and including lying down, in such a lodging.

If that monk or nun should know that in this very lodging, householders or even female servants are anointing or smearing one another’s bodies with oil, ghee, butter, or fat, he or she should not, while intent upon the Dharma, take up a standing posture or any other posture in such a lodging.

If a monk or a nun should know that in this very dwelling householder or even a female laborer are rubbing, scrubbing, massaging, or kneading one another’s bodies with bath-powder, *kakkā*, lodhra, cosmetic paste, scented powder, or *pauma*—if it is not for the sake of a religious discourse, they should not take up a standing posture, a bed, or a sitting place in such a dwelling.

If that monk or nun should know of a lodging where householders, or even female servants, are washing, bathing, sprinkling, or bathing one another’s bodies with cold water or hot water, he or she, mindful of the rule, should not occupy a place, or even stand, in such a lodging.

If a monk or a nun should know that in this very lodging there are householders, or even female servants, who have entered into secret union, or are engaged in secret conversation, and where there is no opportunity for coming and going, nor for reciting, questioning, rehearsing, reviewing, or reflecting upon the Dharma—then in such a lodging, he or she should not choose a place to stand, a bed, or a seat.

If that monk or nun should know a lodging or residence to have closely set rafters—such that it is not for one who possesses wisdom [to dwell there], up to [the point of] reflection—then in such a residence they should not take up a position, nor [should they perform] any of the other activities up to lying down.

If a monk or a nun should desire to seek out a bedding-mat, and if they should know that bedding-mat to contain eggs, living beings, seeds, green plants, dew, water, or earth with insects and moss—such a bedding-mat, considering it to be impure and unfit for use, they should not accept it, even if it is offered.

If that monk or nun should know a bedding or mat to be free from eggs, free from living beings, free from seeds, free from green plants, free from dew, free from moisture, free from mildew, fungi, water, mud, and spiderwebs—being heavy—and if, considering such a bedding or mat to be impure and unfit for use, there is an opportunity [to obtain another], they should not accept it.

If that monk or nun should know a bedding or mat to be free from insects, up to and including being free from living organisms, light, and not belonging to the Sangha (non-proprietary), then even if such a bedding or mat is available, they should not accept it.

If that monk or nun should know a bedding or mat to be free from insects, up to and including being free from living organisms, light, and belonging to the Sangha (proprietary), but not properly bound, then even if such a bedding or mat is available, they should not accept it.

If that monk or nun should know a bedding or mat to be free from insects, up to free from creeping things, light, borrowable, properly bound, and of such a kind—[considering it to be pure and acceptable]—then, when it is available, they should accept it.

Having avoided these aforementioned grounds for acquisition, a monk should know that he may seek a bedding (santhāraga) by means of these four postures (paḍimā). Herein, this is the first posture: that monk or nun, having specified it repeatedly, should seek a bedding, namely—of reed, of hard wood, of *jantu* grass, of *paraga*, of *mōraga*, of *taṇaga*, of *sōraga*, of *kusa* grass, of *kuccaga*, of *pippalaga*, or of straw. He should first examine it, saying, "O long-lived one" or "O sister, will you give me from this [store] any other bedding? If such [bedding] is obtained either by him himself or given to him by another, and considering it to be pure and acceptable, he should accept it when it is available—this is the first posture.

Now, the second vow: That monk or nun, having seen a bedding (santhāraga), should seek it from a householder, a householder’s wife, a householder’s sister, a householder’s son, a householder’s daughter, a daughter-in-law, a slave, a female slave, a laborer, or a female laborer. He should first address them: "O long-lived one," or "O sister," "Will you give me another such bedding from this [store]? Whether he obtains such bedding himself or someone else gives it to him—provided it is pure and acceptable—he should accept it. This is the second vow.

Furthermore, this is the third vow: that monk or nun should dwell wherever they may reside, provided it is furnished with such materials as follows—namely, mats of ikkaḍa, or kaḍhiṇa, or jantua, or paraga, or moraga, or grass, or sāraga, or kuśa, or kuccaga, or pippala, or straw; having obtained these, they should dwell there, and if these are not obtained, they should remain in the ukkuḍuka posture or in a sitting position. This is the third vow.

Furthermore, there is the fourth vow: that monk or nun should seek out a bedding-place exactly as it is found, such as a stone slab of earth or a wooden plank, or whatever is already spread out. Upon obtaining it, they should dwell there; if they do not obtain it, they should remain either in the squatting posture (ukkuḍua) or in a seated posture (nīsajjiya). This is the fourth vow. Thus, undertaking any one of these four vows, and so forth, until they dwell in mutual harmony with one another.

If that monk or nun should desire to return the bedding, and if he or she should know that the bedding contains eggs and so forth, up to being infested with living organisms, then such bedding as this should not be returned.

If that monk or nun should desire to return the bedding, and if he or she should know that the bedding is free from insects, free from living beings, and so on, up to free from earth, mud, spiders, and webs—then, having inspected it repeatedly, having wiped it repeatedly, having blown upon it repeatedly, and having shaken it repeatedly, he or she, being self-restrained, should indeed return it.

Whether that monk or nun is staying or residing, or traveling from village to village, they should first inspect the place for excrement and urine. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger—if a monk or nun, by night or at twilight, discharges excrement or urine on a place for excrement and urine that has not been inspected, they might stumble or fall. While stumbling or falling there, they might injure their hand or foot, or they might strike, crush, wound, bruise, collide with, overturn, or exhaust living beings, plants, souls, or creatures; or they might move them from one place to another, or deprive them of life. Therefore, this is the prior instruction for monks, this is the principle, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the teaching: that one should first inspect the place for excrement and urine.

If that monk or nun should desire to inspect the ground for a bed and bedding, except in the case of an *ācārya*, an *upādhyāya*, a *pravartin*, an elder (*sthavira*), a *gaṇin*, a *gaṇadhara*, a *gaṇāvacchedaka*, or one who is a child, an old man, a novice, an invalid, or one who is at the beginning, the end, or the middle; or on level or uneven ground; or in a windward or leeward direction, then being restrained, having inspected it repeatedly and having swept it repeatedly, he or she should, being restrained, spread out a bed and bedding that is largely pure.

If that monk or nun, having spread out a comfortable bed or bedding, should desire to mount that comfortable bed or bedding, then that monk or nun, while mounting the comfortable bed or bedding, should first repeatedly wipe his body and feet, including the head and the upper part of the body; then, being restrained, he should mount the comfortable bed or bedding. Having mounted it, then, being restrained, he should lie down upon the comfortable bed or bedding.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, while lying on a comfortable bed or bedding, they should not touch one another’s hand with their hand, foot with foot, body with body, or limb with limb. Without such contact, being restrained, they should lie down only on that comfortable bed or bedding. Furthermore, whether a monk or a nun, while breathing out or breathing in, coughing, sneezing, yawning, or releasing an upward wind or flatulence, they should first cover their mouth or nose with their hand; then, being restrained, they may breathe out, breathe in, cough, sneeze, yawn, or release an upward wind or flatulence.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, if there should be a bed that is level, or a bed that is uneven, or a bed with wind, or a bed sheltered from the wind, or a bed infested with dust, or a bed free from dust, or a bed infested with gadflies and mosquitoes, or a bed free from gadflies and mosquitoes, or a bed subject to disturbances, or a bed free from disturbances—in such beds being available, one should dwell in a more secluded lodging; one should not be attached to anything whatsoever. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they should always be self-controlled, steadfast, and disciplined in all things. Thus I say.

Indeed, when the rainy season has arrived and it has rained heavily, many living beings have come into existence, and many seeds have newly sprouted. On his way, there may be many creatures, many seeds, [many herbs, much dew, much water, many ant-hills, fungi, mud, and clay], continuous stretches where paths have not been traversed, and the routes are not known. Knowing this, he should not travel from village to village; rather, being self-restrained, he should enter upon the rainy-season residence.

If that monk or nun should know: "In this village, or [town, market town, hamlet, mountain settlement, port city, seaport, mine, provincial town, hermitage, or settlement], or even in this capital city—indeed, in this village up to this capital city—there is no large area for dwelling, no large area for study, no easy availability of seats, beds, couches, or bedding, and no easy availability of wholesome alms-food that is fit for seeking; and where many ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars have arrived and will continue to arrive, and where the way of life is overcrowded—such that there is no room for the coming and going of the wise, nor for their reflection upon the teachings"—having understood this, he or she should not enter the rainy-season residence in such a village, town, or even capital city.

If that monk or nun should know: "In this village, or even up to a capital city—indeed, in this village or up to that capital city—there is a large area for dwelling and a large area for study; where bedding, mats, couches, and straw-mats are easily obtained; where wholesome alms-food is easy to find and suitable for search; and where many ascetics, brahmins, guests, craftsmen, and beggars have not arrived nor will arrive," and where there is unobstructed movement for coming and going, and unobstructed [opportunity] for reciting, questioning, rehearsing, reviewing, and reflecting upon the study of the Dharma—having understood this, he or she, being self-restrained, may indeed enter the rainy-season residence in such a village or even up to a capital city.

If, however, he should know: "Four months of the rainy season have passed, and fifteen days of the winter period have been completed; meanwhile, the roads between here and there are full of living beings, even down to spiderwebs, and many ascetics—both those who have arrived and those who will arrive—are not present there," then having understood this, he should not travel from village to village. But if he should know: "Four months of the rainy season have passed, and fifteen days of the winter period have been completed; meanwhile, the roads between here and there are free of living beings, even down to spiderwebs, and many ascetics—both those who have arrived and those who will arrive—are present there," then having understood this, a self-controlled monk may indeed travel from village to village.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, while traveling from village to village, looking ahead the distance of a yoke’s length and seeing mobile living beings, he should step up with his foot, or step back with his foot, or step aside with his foot; if there is a way around, he should proceed only by that careful path, and should not go straight on. Thus, being restrained, he should travel from village to village.

Whether it be a monk or a nun traveling from village to village, if there be living beings, seeds, green plants, water, or mud in the way, he should proceed with restraint; he should not go straight across. Thus, with full restraint, he should travel from village to village.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, encounters on the way various kinds of frontier regions inhabited by barbarians—regions that are uncivilized, difficult to approach, difficult to instruct, where people wake up at improper times and consume food at improper times—if there is a favorable opportunity for wandering and the local population is well-disposed, he or she should not set out on a journey for the sake of wandering. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger. Those foolish people might think, "This is a thief; this is a spy; this has come from that place," and having said this, they might abuse the monk, bind him, restrain him, or even kill him; they might seize or steal his robe, bowl, blanket, or broom, or they might insult him. Now, monks, the previously taught resolve, reason, cause, and instruction is this: that one should not set out on a journey for the sake of wandering through such various frontier regions. Therefore, one should travel from village to village only when it is appropriate.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, encounters on the way a kingdom belonging to a king, a confederacy of kings, a crown prince, a frontier region, a hostile territory, or a rebellious realm, and there is a favorable opportunity for wandering due to the inhabitants being well-disposed toward the monastic life, he or she should not set out on a journey for the sake of wandering. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger. Those people are ignorant; [the consequences] are the same as before regarding the act of setting out on a journey. Therefore, a practitioner of self-restraint should travel from village to village only with proper caution.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter a wilderness on the way, and should he know that this wilderness will take one day, two days, three days, four days, or five days to cross—whether he can reach the other side or not—and that such a wilderness is impassable within a single day [while the inhabited regions are being traversed for the sake of dwelling], he should not set out on the journey for the purpose of wandering. A Kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger; there may be rain on the way, or living beings, or seeds, or green plants, or mud, or clay, which would cause him to stumble. Now, monks, the previously taught [resolve, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction] is that regarding such a wilderness that takes many days to cross... [he should not set out on the journey]; therefore, a restrained monk should indeed travel from village to village.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter water that must be crossed by boat, and if he should know of a boat such that—on account of a monk—it has been purchased or hired, or a boat has been transformed into another boat, or a boat has been moved from land into the water, or from water onto land, or a full boat has been baled out, or a light boat has been weighed down; then he should not board such a boat for the purpose of travel, whether it goes upstream, downstream, or across, for more than a *yojana* or half a *yojana*, or even for a shorter or longer distance.

If that monk or nun should know beforehand that a boat is crossing transversely, having known this, he or she should go aside; having gone aside, he or she should inspect the belongings; having inspected them, he or she should set aside the food-vessels; having set them aside, he or she should wipe the body, including the head and the upper garment, as well as the feet; having wiped them, he or she should renounce food with specific restrictions; having renounced it, having placed one foot in the water and one foot on the bank, he or she should then, being self-restrained, board the boat.

When that monk or nun is boarding a boat, he or she should not board at the front of the boat, nor at the rear of the boat, nor in the middle of the boat. He or she should not, repeatedly stretching out the arms, pointing with the fingers, bending down, or lifting up, gaze about. If another person on the boat should say to him or her: "O venerable ascetic, pull this boat up, or push it away, or throw it, or take hold of the rope and haul it along," he or she should not agree to that request; rather, he or she should remain silent.

If another person on board the boat should say to him who is on the boat: "O venerable ascetic, you are not able to pull up, push down, or tilt this boat, nor can you pull it by grasping the rope; bring us this rope of the boat, and we ourselves shall pull it up, push it down, tilt it, or pull it by grasping the rope," he should not accept that proposal, but should remain silent.

If another person on board the boat should say to him, who is also on the boat: "O venerable ascetic, please row this boat with a bamboo pole, a wooden paddle, a small oar, or a large oar that is either unanointed or smeared," he should not consent to that proposal; he should remain silent and wait. If another person on board the boat should say to him, who is also on the boat: "O venerable ascetic, please bail out the water from this boat with your hand, your foot, a vessel, a bowl, or a boat-bailer," he should not consent to that proposal; he should remain silent and wait.

If another person on board the boat should say to him who is on the boat: "O venerable ascetic, please plug this leak in the boat with your hand, or your foot, or your arm, or your thigh, or your belly, or your head, or your body; or cover it with a vessel, or with a cloth, or with mud, or with a leaf of *kuśa* grass, or with a *kuvinda* (a type of reed)," he should not acknowledge that request. He should remain silent. If that monk or nun sees water leaking through a hole in the boat, or sees the boat being covered in soot [by the water], he should not approach another person and speak thus: "O venerable householder! This water is leaking into your boat through a hole, or it is overflowing, or the boat is being fouled by soot. Having formed no such thought or speech beforehand, he should conduct himself without agitation, without distress, having gone to a secluded place, and should discipline himself in equanimity. Then, being restrained, he should cross the water by boat as is appropriate. This indeed is the complete perfection for that monk or nun: that in all things he is self-restrained, steadfast, and always exerts himself. Thus I say.

If another person on board a boat should say to one who is also on the boat: "O venerable ascetic! Please take this sunshade, or water-pot, or staff, or walking stick, or mattress, or tube, or cloth, or rug, or leather, or leather case, or leather-cutting tool; carry these various kinds of implements; and bring up for me a boy or a girl"—he should not accept that proposal, but should remain silent.

If another person, while on a boat, should say to one who is on a boat: "O venerable one! This ascetic is carrying a heavy load of goods on the boat; seize him by his arms and throw him into the water from the boat!"—having heard and reflected upon such a cry, if he is a wearer of robes, he should quickly loosen or untie them, or pull them up. But if he should know: "These fools are indeed of cruel deeds; they might seize me by my arms and throw me into the water from the boat," he should first say: "O venerable householder! Do not seize me by my arms and throw me into the water from the boat; I myself shall simply step down into the water from the boat. If, despite him speaking thus, the other should suddenly and forcibly seize him by his arms and throw him into the water from the boat, he should not be joyful, nor should he be dejected; he should not harbor fluctuating thoughts, nor should he rise up for the sake of killing or harming those fools. Being undisturbed and free from greed, withdrawing himself to a secluded place, and remaining composed, he should then proceed through the water with proper restraint.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, while wading through water, they should not let hand touch hand, foot touch foot, or body touch body. Not seeking such contact, they should wade through the water with full restraint. Whether it be a monk or a nun, while wading through water, they should not make a diving motion, lest this water should enter their ears, eyes, nose, or mouth; thus, they should wade through the water with full restraint.

If that monk or nun, while wading through water, should become exhausted, he or she should quickly adjust or clear out the robes, and should certainly not be attached to them. Furthermore, if he or she should know that there is a way across to reach the bank from the water, then being restrained, he or she may stand on the water's edge with a body that is wet or moist with water.

That monk or nun should not rub, wipe, stroke, scrub, massage, rub down, heat, or warm their body when it is wet with water or moist with moisture. However, if they should know: "My body is free from moisture; the stickiness of my body has been severed"—then such a body may be rubbed or warmed. Only then, being self-restrained, should he travel from village to village.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, while traveling from village to village, they should not travel from village to village by chatting and joking with others; rather, they should travel from village to village only with self-restraint.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter water that must be crossed by wading across, he or she should first wipe the body, including the head and the upper garment, as well as the feet. Having wiped them, he or she should renounce food with specific conditions (*sāgāra-bhatta*). Having so renounced it, and having placed one foot in the water and the other foot on dry land, he or she should then, being self-restrained, walk across the water to be waded through only as far as is necessary.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, when crossing water that flows knee-deep and is not yet dried up, they should not touch hand with hand, foot with foot, or body with body. Without such contact, being restrained, they should cross the knee-deep water that is not yet dried up.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, when crossing a stream by wading through the water, they should not, for the sake of bathing or for the sake of washing their clothes, immerse their body in very deep water. Rather, being restrained, they should cross the stream by wading through the water as it is. Furthermore, if they should know that there is a way across and they will reach the further bank, then, being restrained, they may stand on the riverbank with their body wet or dripping from the water.

That monk or nun should not rub or wipe their body when it is wet with water or moist with dew. However, if they should know: "My body is free from water; my body's moisture is gone"—then they may rub or [wip]e such a body, up to and including fanning it, and thereafter, being restrained, they may travel from village to village.

Whether it be a monk or a nun traveling from village to village, they should not travel by a wrong path for the sake of destroying vegetation with their feet covered in clay—cutting it repeatedly, tearing it up repeatedly, and splitting it repeatedly—thinking, "May this clay on my feet quickly carry away the vegetation. Such a course of action involves a state of deceit; therefore, one should not act thus. Instead, one should first examine a path that is free of vegetation, and then, being restrained, one should travel from village to village.

When that monk or nun is traveling from village to village, if there are in the way fields, ditches, walls, gateways, bolts, bolt-fastenings, pits, or caves, he, being restrained, should proceed with care; he should not go straight forward. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger. While proceeding there, he might stumble or fall. While stumbling or falling there, he should repeatedly cling to trees, shrubs, bushes, creepers, climbing plants, grass, thickets, or greenery to climb up. He should give notice to those travelers who come along the path, and then, being restrained, he should climb up by clinging [to them] and then proceed from village to village.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should see on the way chariots, carts, or wagons belonging to his own side or to the enemy's side, or a military force of various kinds stationed there, he should proceed with restraint; he should not go straight toward them. If someone from that army should say, "O venerable one, this ascetic is obstructing the army! Seize him by the arm and bring him here! and if that person should seize him by the arm and bring him there, he should neither be joyful nor dejected; he should not harbor a fluctuating mind, nor should he rise up for the sake of killing or harming those fools. Being undisturbed and free from greed, he should withdraw himself to a secluded place and remain in meditative composure; then, with restraint, he should continue his journey from village to village.

Whether it be a monk or a nun traveling from village to village, if they should encounter highwaymen along the way, those highwaymen might say this: "O venerable ascetics! How large is this village, or even up to a royal capital? How many horses, elephants, village servants, and people dwell here? Is it abundant in food and water, with many people and much livestock, or is it lacking in food and water, with few people and little livestock? One should not ask such questions; nor, whether asked or unasked, should one explain such matters. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that he or she should always be self-restrained, guarded, and disciplined in all things. Thus I speak.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should see in the way fields, or ramparts, or walls, or gateways, or bolts, or bolt-holes, or chasms, or caves, or watchtowers, or palaces, or underground dwellings, or tree-houses, or mountain-houses, or a tree that is a shrine, or a stupa that is a shrine, or assembly halls, or temples, or shrines, or meeting halls, or pavilions, or shops, or market stalls, or carriage-sheds, or carriage-halls, or workshops for straw, or workshops for reeds, or workshops for leather, or workshops for cane, or workshops for wood, or workshops for charcoal, or workshops for timber, or workshops for cemeteries, or workshops for sanctuaries, or workshops on mountains, or workshops in caves, or workshops on rock formations, or house-dwellings—he should not, stretching out his arms again and again, pointing with his fingers, bending down again and again, or lifting up again and again, gaze at them. Thus, being restrained, he should travel from village to village.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, encounters marshes, rivers, thickets, enclosures, forests, forest thickets, mountains, mountain thickets, pits, lakes, pools, streams, canals, lotus ponds, oblong ponds, small channels, or lakes and rows of lakes, he should not, repeatedly stretching out his arms, gaze [at them] as far as [the limit]. Then, being restrained, he should travel from village to village. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger; whatever creatures are there—beasts, cattle, birds, reptiles, lions, or water-dwellers, land-dwellers, or sky-dwellers—they might be startled, terrified, or seek a pen, a refuge, or protection, thinking, 'This ascetic is a thief. Therefore, monks, as previously instructed, until [the point where] he does not repeatedly stretch out his arms and gaze [at them], he should, being restrained, travel from village to village together with his teachers and preceptors."

Whether it be a monk or a nun, while traveling from village to village together with their preceptors (ācāryas) or teachers (upādhyāyas), they should not let hand touch hand, foot touch foot, body touch body, or limb touch limb of the preceptor or teacher. Without such physical contact, they should, being restrained, travel from village to village together with their preceptors or teachers.

If that monk or nun, while traveling together with teachers (ācāryas) or preceptors (upādhyāyas), should encounter highwaymen on the way, and those highwaymen should say, "O venerable ascetics, who are you? From where do you come? Where will you go? then whichever teacher or preceptor is there should speak or explain; while the teacher or preceptor is speaking or explaining, one should not interrupt their speech. Then, being restrained, one should travel for the sake of food and so forth.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, while traveling from village to village for the sake of alms-food, they should not travel from village to village for alms-food with one person’s hand grasping another’s hand, and so on, up to [grasping] the nose; rather, being restrained, they should indeed travel from village to village for alms-food.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village for the sake of alms-food, should encounter travelers on the way, and those travelers should say this: "O venerable ascetics! Who are you? Where have you come from? Where will you go? he who is there with a companion should speak or explain; while the companion is speaking or explaining, he should not speak an intervening word. Then, being truly restrained, he should travel from village to village.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter highwaymen on the way, and those highwaymen should say this: "O venerable ascetics, look here along the road; for instance, do you see a human being, a cow, a buffalo, a beast, a bird, a reptile, or a water-dweller? Tell us, show us! He should not tell them, nor should he show them; he should not acknowledge that recognition to them; he should remain silent or say, "I know not, I know not. Thus, being restrained, he should indeed travel from village to village.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter highwaymen on the way, those highwaymen might say to them: "O venerable ascetics! Look here at this path: do you see water-born bulbs, or roots, or bark, or leaves, or flowers, or fruits, or seeds, or green plants; or do you see water collected there, or fire placed there? Tell us! [The monk] should continue his journey [only after having informed them].

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter highwaymen on the way, and those highwaymen should say to them: "O venerable recluses! Look here at these things on the road—yoke-teams, or carts, or chariots, or armies of one's own kingdom, or of a foreign kingdom, or a military array of various kinds stationed there; tell us about it, show it to us! He should not tell them, he should not show them, nor should he acknowledge that knowledge to them; he should remain silent or say, "I do not know," even though he knows. Only then, being self-restrained, should he travel from village to village.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter wayfarers on the road, those wayfarers might say to them: "Venerable ascetics! Tell us how far it is from here to the village, or even to the capital city," and so they should continue their journey.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter wayfarers on the road, those wayfarers might say to them: "Venerable ascetics! Tell us the distance along the path from here to the village, or the town, or even to the capital city," and so they should continue their journey in the same manner.

Whether it be a monk or a nun traveling from village to village, if they see on the path ahead a stray bull, or a stray buffalo—likewise a human, a horse, an elephant, a lion, a tiger, a leopard, a bear, a hyena, a jackal, a cat, a dog, a wild dog, a jackal-dog, a *kokantika*, or any other dangerous beast (*vīyāla*)—they should not, out of fear of these, go by a wrong path; nor should they deviate from the path to a wrong path; nor should they enter a thicket, a forest, or a difficult pass; nor should they climb a tree; nor should they throw their body into a very deep pit; nor should they seek shelter in a fence, a refuge, an army, or a caravan. Without agitation and without fear, withdrawing themselves to a secluded spot, they should travel from village to village with composure and self-restraint.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter a forest on the way, and should recognize that forest as follows: "In this forest, indeed, many *āmōsaga* (robbers) are gathered for the purpose of seizing requisites," he should not, out of fear of them, go by a wrong path; rather, with full composure, he should travel from village to village only in a restrained manner.

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter thieves on the way, those thieves might say: "O venerable ascetics! Give us this food, or this garment, or this bowl, or this blanket, or this broom; set it down for us! He should not give it, nor set it down; he should not ask for it by repeatedly bowing, nor ask with palms joined in reverence, nor ask out of pity; rather, he should ask with a righteous request or remain silent. If those thieves, thinking "this is our own business," should revile him, or even kill him, or snatch away, steal, or despise his garment, bowl, blanket, or broom, he should not report it to the villagers, nor report it to the king, nor go to another person and say: "O venerable householder! These are indeed thieves who, thinking 'this is our own business' regarding their need for requisites, revile him or even destroy his property. He should not harbor such thoughts or speak such words in front of others, but should travel from village to village with few desires and in a state of composure. This, indeed, is the complete conduct for that monk or nun, which one should always practice, being restrained in all things and enduring with fortitude. Thus I say.
[The Fourth Chapter – The Origin of Speech]

Having heard and reflected upon these rules of proper conduct (*vaiyāvṛtya*), that monk or nun should recognize these improper conducts which have not been practiced before: those who utter speech out of anger, those who utter speech out of pride, those who utter speech out of deceit, or those who utter speech out of greed; whether they speak harshly knowingly or speak harshly unknowingly—one should avoid all this that is blameworthy by adopting a life of detachment (*viveka*). One should know what is permanent and one should know what is impermanent: whether food, drink, soft food, or hard food is obtained or not obtained; whether it has been eaten or not eaten; whether [the donor] has come or has not come; whether he is coming or is not coming; whether he will come or will not come; whether he has arrived here or has not arrived here; whether he is arriving here or is not arriving here; whether he will arrive here or will not arrive here. Having reflected thus, speaking with measured words, being equanimous and self-restrained, one should utter speech such as this: [The text continues with examples of appropriate speech regarding the arrival and departure of alms-givers.]

There is the singular expression, the dual expression, the plural expression; the feminine expression, the masculine expression, the neuter expression; the internal expression, the refined expression, the unrefined expression, the refined-and-unrefined expression, the unrefined-and-refined expression; the past expression, the present expression, the future expression; the perceptible expression, the imperceptible expression. Thinking, "I shall speak a singular expression," one should speak a singular expression, and so on, up to: thinking, "I shall speak an imperceptible expression," one should speak an imperceptible expression. Whether it be a woman's form, a man's form, or a neuter's form—having reflected upon this or that, or something else, one who speaks with determination, being restrained and equanimous, should utter speech. Thus, having transcended these sources [of transgression].

Now, a monk should know the four types of speech, namely: the first type of speech is truth; the second is falsehood; the third is both truth and falsehood; and that which is neither truth nor falsehood nor both truth and falsehood—this is called the fourth type of speech.

This I say: all those Arhats, Blessed Ones—those of the past, those of the present, and those of the future—all of them have spoken, do speak, or will speak these very same four kinds of speech; they have explained, do explain, or will explain them; and all of these are declared to be insentient, yet possessed of color, odor, taste, and touch, subject to decay, and characterized by changeability.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, if they should know this: speech that was previously non-speech becomes speech while being spoken; once the moment of speech has passed, the speech that has been spoken is no longer speech.

That monk, moreover, should know: whatever speech is truthful, whatever speech is false, whatever speech is both true and false, and whatever speech is neither true nor false—such speech that is blameworthy, involving action, harsh, bitter, cruel, rough, causing influx [of karma], causing cutting, causing piercing, causing torment, causing destruction, and harmful to living beings—he should not speak it intentionally.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know: whatever speech is true and subtle, and whatever speech is not false, such speech—blameless, non-action-inducing, not harsh, not bitter, not cruel, not rough, not causing concealment, not causing cutting, not causing piercing, not causing affliction, not causing violence, not involving the destruction of what has not come to be, and appropriate—such speech they should utter.

Whether that monk or nun is addressing a man, or he has already been addressed, if he does not respond, they should not speak thus: "Ho! or "Go! or "Vasula! or "Of bad faction! or "Dhaḍadāsa! or "Dog! or "Thief! or "Spy! or "Deceiver! or "Liar! or "These are your parents. Desiring to avoid such speech—which is blameworthy, involving action, and so forth, up to being harmful to living beings—they should not speak in such a manner.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, when addressing a man, or when he has been addressed, if he does not respond, they may speak thus: "O so-and-so," or "O venerable one," or "O long-lived one," or "O lay follower," or "O devotee," or "O righteous one," or "O lover of Dharma. Desiring such speech that is blameless and, as far as possible, free from harm to living beings, they may speak it.

When that monk or nun is addressing a woman, and she does not respond when addressed, he should not speak to her thus: "O hōlē! or "O gōlē! or "O vasulē! or "O kupakkhē! or "O dhaḍadāsī! or "O sāṇē! or "O thief! or "O spy! or "O liar! or "O speaker of falsehood!"—or saying, "These are your names" or "These are your parents. Desiring such speech, he should not utter any kind of speech that is blameworthy, up to and including that which involves harm to living beings.

If that monk or nun, while addressing a woman who does not respond when addressed, should speak thus: "O lady," or "Sister," or "Blessed One," or "Lay-devotee," or "Female lay-follower," or "Virtuous one," or "Lover of Dharma"—he may, if he so desires, speak such speech that is blameless and so forth.

That monk or nun should not speak thus: "Nabhodeva," or "Gajjadeva," or "Vijjudeva," or "Pavuṭṭhadeva," or "Nivuṭṭhadeva"; nor should they say, "May it rain, or may it not rain; may the crop ripen, or may it not ripen; may the night become light, or may it not become light; may the sun rise, or may it not rise; may that king be victorious, or may he not be victorious. An enlightened one should not utter such speech.

If that monk or nun should speak of "the sky," or "one wandering in secret," or "one who is deluded," or "one who has fallen," or "a cloud," or "a cloud that has rained its strength"—this indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that being composed in all things, being steadfast, one should always strive. Thus I say.
