Whether it be a monk or a nun, even if they should see various deformed physical conditions, they should not speak of them in this way: namely, “a tumor, a tumor,” or “a leper, a leper,” or “one with a skin disease, one with a skin disease,” or “one suffering from consumption, one suffering from consumption,” or “one who is blind, one who is blind,” or “one who is squint-eyed, one who is squint-eyed,” or “one with a withered arm, one with a withered arm,” or “one who is hunchbacked, one who is hunchbacked,” or “one with a distended belly, one with a distended belly,” or “one who is mute, one who is mute,” or “one with a swollen face, one with a swollen face,” or “one who is sickly, one who is sickly,” or “one who is trembling, one who is trembling,” or “one who is a cripple moving on a stool, one who is a cripple moving on a stool,” or “one with elephantiasis, one with elephantiasis,” or “one whose hands have been cut off, one whose hands have been cut off,” or “one whose feet have been cut off, one whose feet have been cut off,” or “one whose nose has been cut off, one whose nose has been cut off,” or “one whose ears have been cut off, one whose ears have been cut off,” or “one whose lips have been cut off, one whose lips have been cut off. Whatever other such persons there may be, and whatever such speech is uttered that would cause young men to be disturbed, desiring their own welfare, one should not utter such speech.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, if they should see various types of forms, even then they should speak of them thus: "He is radiant, he is radiant," or "He is brilliant, he is brilliant," or "He is graceful, he is graceful," or "He is famous, he is famous," or "He is handsome, he is handsome," or "He is well-proportioned, he is well-proportioned," or "He is pleasing, he is pleasing," or "He is beautiful to behold, he is beautiful to behold"—whatever such [forms] there may be that, when described by such descriptions, do not cause pride in men; of those [forms], one may desire to speak using such descriptions.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, if they should see various types of structures, such as: fields or boundaries, walls, gateways, bolts, bolt-holes, pits, caves, gabled houses, palaces, underground dwellings, tree-houses, mountain-houses, or a tree made into a shrine, a stupa made into a shrine, assembly halls, sanctuaries, temples, meeting halls, pavilions, market-houses, market-sheds, carriage-houses, carriage-sheds, workshops for weaving reeds, workshops for weaving grass, workshops for basket-making, workshops for leather-work, workshops for wood-work, workshops for charcoal, workshops for timber, workshops for cremation grounds, workshops for sacred sites, workshops for mountains, workshops for caves, workshops for rock-shelters, or residential houses—even then, regarding these, one should not speak thus: "Well done," or "Very well done," or "Excellent work," or "It is auspicious," or "It ought to be done. One should not utter such speech that is blameworthy, and so forth.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, if they should see various kinds of structures, such as fields or even palatial residences—nevertheless, regarding them, they may speak thus: "This was made through labor," or "this was made with blame," or "this was made with effort"; or they may say of it, "it is beautiful, it is beautiful," or "it is worthy of being seen, it is worthy of being seen," or "it is handsome, it is handsome," or "it is well-proportioned, it is well-proportioned"—they may speak such speech that is blameless and so forth.

If that monk or nun sees food, drink, solid food, or delicacy that has been prepared, they should not speak thus: "It is well-prepared," or "It is very well-prepared," or "It is excellently prepared," or "It is auspicious," or "It is worthy of being made. Such speech, which is blameworthy and so forth, they should not utter.

If that monk or nun, having seen food, drink, solid food, or delicacy that has been prepared, should speak thus: "It was made through exertion," or "it was made with fault," or "it was made with effort," or "it is excellent, it is excellent," or "it is abundant, it is abundant," or "it is flavorful, it is flavorful," or "it is agreeable, it is agreeable"—such speech, being blameless, up to not causing harm to living beings, he or she may desire to speak.

If that monk or nun sees a human, a cow, a buffalo, a deer, a domestic animal, a bird, a reptile, or an aquatic creature with its body fully grown, he or she should not speak thus: "It is fat," or "It is plump," or "It is round," or "It is fit for slaughter," or "It is fit for cooking. Desiring such speech, which is blameworthy and leads to the injury of living beings, he or she should not speak it.

If that monk or nun should see a human being, or even a water-dweller, with a fully developed body, they may speak thus: "one with a fully developed body," or "one with a well-nourished body," or "one with firm skeletal structure," or "one with abundant flesh and blood," or "one with many perfectly complete sense faculties. Such speech, which is blameless and, up to the point of not causing harm through untruth, they may utter when they so desire.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, upon seeing various kinds of cows, they should not speak thus: "These cows are for milking," or "for taming," or "for breeding," or "for carrying loads," or "fit for chariots. Desiring such speech, which is blameworthy and leads to the injury of living beings, one should not speak it.

That monk or nun, having seen various kinds of cattle, may speak thus: "a young bull," or "a cow," or "a milch cow," or "a heifer," or "an old one," or "a large one," or "one fit for breeding"—such speech that is blameless, up to being non-destructive, they may desire to speak.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, upon seeing gardens, mountains, forests, or large trees, they should not speak thus: "These are fit for palaces," or "fit for houses," or "fit for gateways," or "fit for walls," or "fit for bolts, boats, water-tubs, stools, cangabēras, ploughs, hoes, pestles, hubs, drums, seats, beds, vehicles, or dwellings. Desiring to avoid speech of this kind—which is blameworthy and leads to the injury of living beings—they should not speak such words.

If that monk or nun sees pleasure groves, parks, forests, or large trees, they may speak thus: "They are noble," or "they have long trunks," or "they are massive," or "they have spreading branches," or "they have hollows in their branches," or "they are pleasing," or "they are beautiful to behold," or "they are handsome," or "they are well-proportioned. Such speech, which is blameless and free from harm to living beings, they may utter with desire.

If that monk or nun sees forest fruits in great abundance, even so they should not speak thus: "They are ripe," or "they are fit to be eaten raw," or "they are ready to be plucked," or "they are soft," or "they are succulent. Desiring such speech, which is blameworthy and leads to the injury of living beings, one should not speak it.

If that monk or nun, seeing mango trees with abundant fruit, should speak thus: "They are not yet covered [with leaves]," or "they have many fruits that have not yet ripened," or "they are abundant," or "they are in great quantity"—such speech, being blameless and not involving false accusation, he or she may, if desired, speak.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, seeing medicinal plants that have grown in abundance, they should not speak of them in such a way, namely: "They are ripe," or "They are soft," or "They are tender," or "They are fit for eating," or "They are fit for roasting," or "They are fit for much chewing. Desiring [to remain pure], they should not utter such speech which is blameworthy and, ultimately, harmful to living beings.

If that monk or nun, seeing medicinal plants that have grown abundantly, should speak thus: "They are grown," or "they are abundant," or "they are firm," or "they are flourishing," or "they are in bud," or "they have flowered," or "they have spread"—such speech, being blameless and so forth, up to not involving falsehood or injury, he or she may desire to speak.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, when they hear various kinds of sounds, they should not speak of them in such a way, namely: "this is a good sound" or "this is a bad sound. Such speech, which is blameworthy and so forth, they should not utter. Whether it be a monk or a nun, when they hear various kinds of sounds, they may speak of them in this way: "a good sound is a good sound" or "a bad sound is a bad sound. Such speech, which is blameless and so forth, they may utter.

Thus are forms—whether black, or blue, or red, or yellow, or white; odors—whether pleasant-smelling or foul-smelling; tastes—whether bitter, or pungent, or astringent, or sour, or sweet; tangibles—whether hard, or soft, or heavy, or light, or cold, or hot, or smooth, or rough.

That monk or nun, having vomited forth anger, pride, deceit, and greed, should speak after due reflection, speaking with determination, speaking without haste, speaking with detachment, and speaking with equanimity, being restrained in speech. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that he or she should always be equanimous toward all things, self-controlled, and disciplined. Thus I say.
[The fifth chapter – The Search for Clothing]

If that monk or nun should desire to seek a robe, and should know that robe to be of one of these kinds—namely, made of jaṅgīya, bhaṅgīya, sāṇaya, pottaga, khōmiya, or tūlakaḍa—then a Niggaṇṭha who is young, in the prime of life, strong, free from physical ailments, and of firm constitution, may wear one such robe, but not a second. A Niggaṇṭhī may wear four *saṅghāḍīs*: one two-cubit wide, two three-cubit wide, and one four-cubit wide. If she is unable to manage with such robes, then afterwards she may sew them together one by one.
That monk or [nun] should not, for the sake of obtaining cloth, resolve to travel more than half a *yojana* beyond the boundary.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that a certain cloth has been intended for a fellow-monk; even if it is available, they should not accept it. Likewise for many fellow-monks [intending it] for one fellow-nun, or many fellow-nuns [intending it] for one fellow-monk; it is exactly as in the case of the search for alms-food (*piṇḍesaṇā*), provided there is an intermediary.

If that monk or nun should know that a garment has been intended specifically for them by many recluses, brahmins, guests, beggars, or mendicants, having selected it one by one, and that such a garment—whether it has passed through another person's hands or not, whether it has been brought outside or not, whether it is for one’s own sake or not, whether it has been used or not, or whether it has been enjoyed or not—if they consider it to be impure and unfit for acceptance, they should not accept it, even if it is offered.

If that monk or nun should know that a robe has been intended for many ascetics—having procured it by means of harming living beings and so forth, having purchased it, and having brought it there—they should, considering such a robe as not having passed through human hands and as unfit for consumption, not accept it even if it is offered. However, if they should know that it has passed through human hands, has been taken outside [the monastery], and is fit for consumption, they may accept it, considering it so, provided it is available.

If that monk or nun should know that a robe has been purchased, washed, dyed, rubbed, polished, smoothed, or fumigated for the sake of a non-recluse who intends it for a monk, they should not accept such a robe if it has not been mediated by a person. However, if they should know that it has been mediated by a person, taken outside, intended for oneself, used, and enjoyed—considering it pure and acceptable—they may accept it, provided it is available.

If that monk or nun should know of certain garments of various kinds that are of great value—such as those made of antelope skin, fine cloth, auspicious fine cloth, silk, kāya-cloth, linen, cotton, woven silk, malaya-cloth, pannunna-cloth, *aṃśuka*-cloth, Chinese silk, country-dyed cloth, *abhila*-cloth, *gajjala*-cloth, *phāliya*-cloth, *kōyava*-cloth, woolen blankets, or shawls—or any other such garments of great value, [considering them to be unobtainable and not fit for acceptance], they should not accept them even when an opportunity arises.

If that monk should recognize such garments made of wool or fur, namely: those from the *udda* antelope, or the *pēsa*, or the *pēśala*; or skins of black antelopes, blue antelopes, or white antelopes; or golden ones, those made of gold, gold-patterned, gold-embroidered, gold-flecked, or gold-sprinkled; or tiger skins, various tiger skins, or ornaments and variously decorated ornaments; or any other such garments made of wool or fur—considering them to be unwholesome and unfit for alms, he should not accept them even if they are offered.

Having thus avoided these sources of danger, a monk should know that there are four postures for seeking clothing. Herein, this is the first posture: A monk or a nun should seek clothing by specifying its type, namely: woolen, hempen, made of hemp-cloth, cotton, silk, or made of bark-fiber. Such clothing, whether he seeks it himself or someone else gives it to him, he may accept it if he considers it pure and fit for use, provided it is available—this is the first posture.

Furthermore, this is the second vow: that monk or nun, having seen a cloth, should seek it thus—[from] a householder, or a householder’s wife, or a householder’s sister, or a householder’s son, or a householder’s daughter, or a daughter-in-law, or a wet-nurse, or a male slave, or a female slave, or a laborer, or a female laborer. He should first address them: "O long-lived one," or "Sister," "Will you give me from this [stock] any such cloth? If he should seek it himself, or if another should give it to him, and if it is pure and he considers it acceptable, he may accept it when it is available. This is the second vow.

Furthermore, this is the third practice: that monk or nun, if they should know a garment—namely, an undergarment or an upper garment—and it is of such a kind, whether they have sought it themselves or another has given it to them, thinking it to be pure and acceptable, they may accept it if there is an opportunity for gain. This is the third practice.

Furthermore, this is the fourth vow: if a monk or a nun should seek a garment that has been discarded according to the rule—a garment which many other ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars do not desire—such a discarded garment they may either seek themselves or receive from another; if it is pure, they may accept it. This is the fourth vow.

Regarding these four vows (*pratimā*), when adopting any one of them, he should not speak thus: "These venerable ones have indeed entered upon a wrong path; I alone have correctly entered upon it. Those venerable ones who, having adopted these vows, live their lives, and I myself who, having adopted this vow, live my life—all of us are established in the teaching of the Jinas, in mutual harmony, and thus we live. If, while he is seeking alms according to this practice, another should say: "O long-lived ascetic! Come after a month, or ten days, or five days, or tomorrow, or the day after tomorrow; then, O long-lived one, we shall give you some kind of garment," having heard and reflected upon such an announcement, he should first of all respond: "O long-lived one" or "Sister! "It is not permissible for me to accept such an appointment. If you wish to give me [a garment], give it right now. If, as he speaks thus, the other should say: "O long-lived ascetic! Follow us, then we shall give you some kind of garment," he should first of all respond: "O long-lived one" or "Sister! "It is not permissible for me to accept such an appointment. If you wish to give me [a garment], give it right now. If, as he speaks thus, the other should lead him away and say: "O long-lived one" or "Sister! We shall bring this garment for the ascetic; however, we shall later procure the garment by harming, killing, or destroying living beings, creatures, souls, and entities for our own sake," having heard and reflected upon such an announcement, and considering that such a garment is unwholesome and not to be sought, even if it is obtained, he should not accept it.

If another person, acting as a guide, should say: "O long-lived one," or "O sister," "I shall bring a garment; having rubbed it with bath-powder, or with *kakka*, or with *lodhra*, up to *padma* [fragrant substances], and having rubbed it thoroughly, we shall give it to the ascetic"—having heard and understood such an announcement, he should first of all say: "O long-lived one," or "O sister," "Do not rub this garment with bath-powder, or [with *kakka*, etc. up to rubbing it thoroughly; if you wish to give it to me, give it to me exactly as it is. If, while he is speaking thus, the other person should nevertheless bring it after having rubbed it with bath-powder, or [with *kakka*, etc. up to rubbing it thoroughly, then such a garment is unwholesome (*aprāsuka*) and he should not accept it.

If another person should say to him, "O long-lived one! or "O sister!", "I shall wash this garment with cold water or hot water, and having washed or rinsed it, I shall give it to the ascetic"—having heard and understood such an announcement, he should first of all address them: "O long-lived one! or "O sister!", "Do not wash or rinse this garment with cold water or hot water; if you wish to give it to me, give it to me just as it is. If, despite his speaking thus, the other should still wash or rinse it with cold water or hot water and then give it to him, he should, considering such a garment to be unwholesome and unfit for use, not accept it even if it is offered.

If another person should say to him, "O long-lived one! or "Sister!", "I shall bring this cloth, or bulbs, or roots, or bark, or leaves, or flowers, or fruits, or seeds, or green vegetables, having cleaned them, and I shall give them to the ascetic"; having heard and understood such a sound, he should first of all address them: "O long-lived one! or "Sister!", "Do not wash or rinse this cloth with cold water or hot water. If he desires to give it to me, give it to me exactly as it is. While he is speaking thus, if the other person should still wash it with cold water or [hot water], even though there is no gain [for the monk], he should not accept it.

If another person should say to him, "O long-lived one" or "O sister! Bring this cloth; having cleaned away the bulbs or even the green plants, we shall give it to the ascetic," then having heard and understood such an announcement, he should first speak out: "O long-lived one" or "O sister! Do not you clean away these bulbs or even the green plants; it is not permissible for me to accept a cloth of this kind. If, despite his speaking thus, the other person should give it after cleaning away the bulbs or even the green plants, then such a cloth is unwholesome and he should not accept it.

If someone else should cast a garment over him, he should first look at it—saying, "O long-lived one! or "Sister!", "I shall inspect this garment belonging to you from end to end. A kevalin would say: "This is a source of acquisition (ādāna)—there might be earrings, strings, gems, pearls, silver, gold, bracelets, armlets, rings, pendants, necklaces, half-necklaces, single-strand necklaces, pearl necklaces, golden necklaces, or jewel necklaces; or there might be living beings, seeds, or green plants. Therefore, for monks, as previously taught—this being the resolve, this the reason, this the cause, this the instruction—they should first inspect the garment from end to end.

If that monk or nun should know a cloth to be with eggs, [with living beings, with seeds, with grass, with fungi, with water-creatures, with water, with mud, with spiderwebs], and with hanging cobwebs—such a cloth, considering it to be unwholesome and not fit for alms, even if it is obtained, they should not accept it.

If that monk or nun should know a garment to be free from insects, free from small animals, free from seeds, free from green plants, free from dew, free from eggs, free from ant-hills, fungi, water-creatures, mud, and spiders’ webs; yet if it is full of threads, unstable, non-permanent, not durable, and while being dyed it is not pleasing—then such a garment, being unwholesome, they should not accept.

If that monk or nun should know a garment to be free from insects, up to and including being free from cobwebs—sufficient, firm, durable, fit for wear, and suitable for dyeing—and if they consider such a garment to be pure and acceptable, they may accept it when it is available.

That monk or nun, thinking "this is my new cloth," should not, on that account, rub or scrub it with abundant country soap-powder or [other substances]. That monk or nun, thinking "this is my new cloth," should not, on that account, wash or rinse it with abundant country cold water or [other liquids].

That monk or nun, thinking "my robe has a foul odor," should not scrub or rub it with a bath-powder mixed with much water, nor should they wash it with cold water mixed with much water. That monk or nun, thinking "my robe has a foul odor," should not [wash it] with cold water mixed with much water.

If that monk or nun should desire to wash or dye a garment, they should not wash or dye such a garment on ground that is bare, nor on moist ground, nor on dusty ground, nor on a stone with life, nor on a clod of earth with life, nor on wood inhabited by living beings, nor where there are eggs, nor where there are living creatures, nor where there are seeds, nor where there are sprouts, nor where there is moss, nor where there is mildew, nor where there is mold, nor where there is dust, nor where there is spiderwebs, nor where there are algae, water-moss, mud, or ant-hills, nor where there are continuous threads of cobwebs; [in such places] they should not wash or dye it.

If that monk or nun should desire to dry or warm a cloth on a pillar, a house-rafter, a peg, a water-pipe, or any other such thing produced from the open air that is poorly fixed, poorly placed, unstable, and shaky, he or she should not dry it nor warm it.

If that monk or nun should desire to dye or bleach a cloth, they should not dye or bleach such a cloth on a wooden block, a wall, a stone, a brick, or any other similar object produced from the open air that is poorly fixed, poorly placed, unstable, and movable.

If that monk or nun should desire to wash or dye a garment, they should not wash or dye such a garment on a shoulder, a bed, a platform, a palace, a flat roof, or any other such place suspended in the air.

Taking that [garment], he should go to a secluded spot. Having gone to a secluded spot, on a clean piece of ground—such as a heap of ashes, a heap of bones, a heap of dregs, a heap of chaff, a heap of cow dung, or any other such place—he should repeatedly inspect it and repeatedly sweep it, and then, being self-restrained, he may dry the garment in the sun or have it dried. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun, which they should always practice, being composed in all things, steadfast, and self-controlled. Thus I say.

That monk or nun should seek garments that are not to be sought after; they should wear garments that have been already accepted, but they should not wash them, nor dye them, nor wear garments that have been washed and dyed. Without concealing them while moving between villages, wearing simple clothing—this indeed is the proper conduct for one who wears garments. That monk or nun, desiring to enter a householder’s family for the sake of alms, should go out or enter the householder’s family for the sake of alms having taken up their entire robe.

When that monk or nun is going out or entering the external grounds for exercise or the grounds of the monastery, they should take all their robes and go out or enter the external grounds for exercise or the grounds of the monastery.

When that monk, while traveling from village to village, takes all his robes and travels from village to village, if he should perceive a heavy rain falling in that region, or perceive thick mud settling down, or perceive dust being raised by a great wind, or perceive crawling insects or other mobile creatures scattered about and falling in his path—having understood this, he should not, taking all his robes, go out or enter a householder’s family for the sake of alms; nor should he go out or enter the grounds for exercise or the grounds for meditation; nor should he travel from village to village.

If that monk or nun, being alone, should obtain a temporary robe for a moment at a time, and then return after having stayed away for one day, two days, three days, four days, or five days; he or she should not take such a robe for oneself, nor give it to another, nor lend it, nor exchange it for another robe, nor, having approached another, say: "O venerable ascetic, do you wish to wear or use this robe? Provided it is firm and intact, he or she should not cut it up piece by piece and redistribute it; rather, such a robe, along with its tag, should be returned to that very person, and he or she should not consent to keep it.

If a certain person, having heard and reflected upon such a proclamation, [sees] venerable ones who, having borrowed such garments that have been joined together for a moment—having stayed away for one day, two days, three days, four days, or five days—return and do not take those garments for themselves, nor give them to another, nor lend them, nor make them out on loan, nor exchange garment for garment, nor approach another and say: "O venerable ascetic, you desire to wear or use this garment; while it remains firm, do not cut it up and discard it part by part"; and if they hand over such garments with their seams intact to him alone, he does not approve of it, thinking: "Alas! I too, having borrowed a momentary garment, shall return after staying away for one day, two days, or even up to five days; otherwise, this will become mine alone. He should not touch upon such a state of deceit; he should not act in this way.

That monk or nun should not turn cloth that has color into colorless [cloth], nor turn colorless [cloth] into cloth that has color. Thinking, "I shall obtain another cloth," he should not give it to another, nor should he lend it; he should not exchange one cloth for another, nor should he go to another person and say: "O venerable ascetic! Do you desire my cloth to wear or to use? Nor, even if it is durable, should he cut it up repeatedly and discard it. If another person considers this cloth to be fire, and seeing that the other is a thief taking what is not given, he should not, out of concern for that cloth, go by a wrong path, nor cross from one path to another, nor enter a thicket, a forest, or a difficult pass, nor climb a tree, nor expose his body in a great flood, nor long for a fence, a shelter, an army, or a weapon. Without agitation and without distress, having withdrawn himself to a secluded place, he should maintain composure and then, being truly restrained, travel from village to village.

Whether it be a monk or a nun traveling from village to village, there may be a forest on their way. If they should know of that forest: "In this forest, indeed, many molesters (robbers) will be moving about in groups for the sake of seizing clothes," one should not, out of fear of them, take a wrong path; rather, one should continue traveling from village to village [by the proper route].

If that monk or nun, while traveling from village to village, should encounter thieves on the way, and those thieves should speak thus: "O venerable ascetics! Give us this garment; hand it over! he should neither give it nor hand it over. He should not beg by repeatedly bowing; he should not beg with joined palms; he should not beg out of pity; rather, he should beg with a righteous request, or he should pass by in silence. If those thieves, thinking "this is our own business," should revile him, bind him, obstruct him, or destroy him; or if they should snatch away the garment, carry it off, or insult him—then he should not report it to the village community, nor should he report it to the king, nor should he approach another and say: "O venerable householder! These are indeed thieves who, thinking 'this is our own business,' revile, bind, obstruct, destroy, snatch, carry off, or insult [the monks] for the sake of a garment. He should not travel about harboring such thoughts or speech before himself. Being undisturbed and free from agitation, he should withdraw himself to a secluded place and remain in meditative composure. Then, being truly self-restrained, he should travel from village to village. This indeed is the complete conduct of that monk or nun, which one should always practice, being composed and disciplined in all things. Thus I say.

[The Sixth Chapter – On Alms-Bowls] If that monk or nun should desire to seek an alms-bowl, he or she should know of such a bowl as follows: whether it be an alms-bowl made of gourd, or one made of wood, or one made of clay. Of such a kind of bowl, a Nirgrantha who is young, in the prime of life, strong, free from bodily ailments, and possessed of firm constitution, may carry one bowl, but not a second.
That monk or nun should not, for the purpose of seeking a bowl, travel more than half a yojana beyond the boundary.

If that monk or nun should know of such a drink—prepared specifically for a fellow member of the community, having procured it by harming living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings; prepared specifically for him, whether bought, bartered, borrowed, given as a gift, brought from elsewhere, or delivered—then, considering such a drink to be unwholesome and unfit for acceptance, whether it has been taken outside or not, whether it was intended for oneself or not, whether it has been consumed or not, or whether it has been tasted or not, he or she should not accept it, even if an opportunity for gain exists. Just as in the *Piṇḍesaṇā* (the section on alms-food), so should four discourses be recited; in the fifth, regarding many recluses, one should enumerate them one by one, and it is exactly the same.

If that monk or nun should know a bed or a seat to have been purchased, washed, dyed, scraped, polished, smeared, or fumigated for the sake of a monk by one who is not restrained—such a bed or seat, if it has not been placed between [the donor and the recipient], has not been brought outside, has not been made for oneself, has not been used, and has not been enjoyed, and considering it to be impure and unacceptable, he or she should not accept it even if it is offered. However, if he or she should know it to have been placed between, brought outside, made for oneself, used, and enjoyed—considering it to be pure and acceptable, he or she may accept it if it is offered.

If that monk or nun should recognize that there are various kinds of bowls of great monetary value—such as bowls made of iron, or bowls made of tin, or bowls made of copper, or bowls made of lead, or bowls made of silver, or bowls made of gold, or bowls made of pewter, or bowls made of *hārapuḍa* (a type of alloy), or bowls made of precious stones, or bowls made of bell-metal, or bowls made of conch-shell or horn, or bowls made of ivory, cloth, or stone, or leather bowls, or any other such various kinds of bowls of great monetary value—and considering them to be unwholesome and unfit for use, he or she should not accept them even when they are offered.

If that monk or nun should know that the alms-bowls are of various kinds and made of costly materials—such as those bound with iron, or even those bound with leather, or any other such bowls bound with costly materials—and considering them to be unwholesome and not fit for seeking, they should not accept them even if an opportunity for gain arises. Having thus avoided these sources of danger, if a monk should know how to seek an alms-bowl according to four practices (*paḍimā*), then indeed this is the first practice: that monk or nun should seek an alms-bowl by specifying it, namely: a gourd bowl, a wooden bowl, or an earthenware bowl; such a bowl he or she may either obtain himself/herself or [accept one offered], up to the point of accepting it. This is the first practice.

Furthermore, this is the second vow: that monk or nun, upon seeing a begging bowl, should seek it as follows—whether from a householder, a householder’s wife, a householder’s sister, a householder’s son, a householder’s daughter, a daughter-in-law, a wet-nurse, a male slave, a female slave, a laborer, or a female laborer—he should first address them, saying, "O friend" or "Sister," "Will you give me from here one of these bowls—whether a gourd bowl, a wooden bowl, or an earthen bowl? If such a bowl is obtained by him himself or given to him by another, and he considers it pure and acceptable, he may accept it when it is available. This is the second vow.

Furthermore, this is the third vow: that monk or nun, if they should know a bed to be one belonging to a *saṅgati* (an assembly) or a *vejayantī* (a royal pavilion), such a bed they should not themselves seek out, nor should they accept it—this is the third vow.

Furthermore, this is the fourth vow: that monk or nun should seek out a discarded alms-bowl—one which other many ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars do not desire; such a discarded alms-bowl he or she may himself seek out or accept—this is the fourth vow.

When undertaking any one of these four vows (paḍimā), one should not speak thus: "These venerable ones have indeed entered upon a wrong path; I alone have rightly entered upon it. Those venerable ones who, having undertaken these vows, live [their lives], and I myself who, having undertaken this vow, live [my life]—all of us are established in the teaching of the Jinas, in mutual harmony, and thus we live."

If, while he is seeking alms with this manner of seeking, another person should see him and say: "O venerable ascetic, come! Whether it be after a month, ten days, five days, or even today or tomorrow, O venerable one, we shall give you some kind of food"—having heard and considered such an invitation, he should first of all respond: "O venerable one" or "Sister," "it is not indeed permissible for me to accept such an invitation. [If the other says: "If you desire to give me, give it right now," and as he speaks thus, the other might say: "O venerable ascetic, follow me; then we shall give you some kind of food. He should first of all respond: "O venerable one" or "Sister," "it is not indeed permissible for me to accept such an invitation. [If the other says: "If you desire to give me, give it right now," and as he speaks thus, the other might lead him away and say: "O venerable one" or "Sister," "we shall give this food to the ascetic, and furthermore, we shall prepare the food ourselves for our own sake, having undertaken the destruction of living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings"—having heard and considered such an announcement, he should not accept such food, as it is impure and so forth.

If another person should say to him, "O long-lived one," or "Sister," [and offer]: "I shall massage you with oil, or ghee, or fresh butter, or fat; or likewise provide a bath and so forth; or likewise cold water, roots, and so forth."

If another person, acting as a guide, should say: "O venerable ascetic! wait for a moment while we prepare or cook food, drink, soft food, or solid food; then, O venerable one, we shall give you the alms-bowl along with the drink and the meal," [the monk] should first inform him: "O brother, or sister, it is not permissible for me to eat or drink food, drink, soft food, or solid food that has been prepared specifically for me (āhākamma). Do not prepare it; do not cook it. If you wish to give to me, give it in this manner [only]. If, despite his speaking thus, the other person prepares or cooks food and gives him the alms-bowl along with the drink and the meal, he—considering such an alms-bowl to be unwholesome and unfit for acceptance—should not accept it, even though it is available.

If another person should pour [oil] into his alms-bowl, he should first look [into it], saying: "O long-lived one" or "Sister, I shall inspect this very bowl of yours from inside out. A Kevalin would say: "This is a source of acquisition—there may be living beings, seeds, or green plants within the bowl. Now, for monks, this has been previously taught: this is the vow, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction—that one should first inspect the bowl from inside out. All the discourses regarding [the bowl] containing eggs should be recited just as in the section on the search for clothing (*vatthesaṇā*); the difference is that [it concerns] oil, ghee, butter, or fat, or bathing and so forth, up to: or on some other such bare ground; having repeatedly inspected and repeatedly wiped it, then, being restrained, he should indeed rub it.
This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they should always be self-controlled, harmonious, and steadfast in all things—thus I say.

When a monk or a nun has entered a householder’s family for the sake of alms, they should first look ahead, lift up their alms-bowl, wipe it, and remove any dust; then, being restrained, they may indeed enter or exit the householder’s family for the sake of alms. A Kevalin would say: "This is a source of danger—living beings, seeds, or green plants might be harmed inside the alms-bowl. Now, this is what has been previously taught to monks: this is the vow, this is the reason, this is the cause, this is the instruction—that having first looked ahead, lifted up the alms-bowl, wiped it, and removed the dust, one should then, being restrained, enter or exit the householder’s family for the sake of alms.

When that monk, having entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms, should find another person bringing cold water from inside a bowl, pouring it out, and offering it to him; he should not accept such a bowl from the hand of another or from the vessel of another if it is impure, and so forth. However, if it has already been accepted, he should immediately pour the water away. Taking the bowl, he should pour out the drink or set it down on ground that is moist with water.

That monk or nun should not rub, wipe, scrape, scrub, polish, heat, or warm an alms-bowl that is wet with water or damp with moisture. However, if they should know: "My alms-bowl is free from water; my alms-bowl is devoid of moisture"—then, being restrained, they may indeed rub it or warm it.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, wishing to enter the family of a householder for the purpose of alms, they should enter or exit the householder’s family with their alms-bowl. Likewise, when traveling from one village to another, whether to a place for study or a place for meditation, they should do so with their alms-bowl, as prescribed in the second section on the search for food (*vattesaṇā*), with the specific difference here being the alms-bowl. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they should be restrained in all things, self-controlled, and always exert themselves. Thus I say.
[The Seventh Chapter – The Observance of Acceptance]

"I shall become a śramaṇa, homeless, possessing nothing, without sons, without a wife, subsisting on what is given by others; I will not commit an evil deed"—having thus resolved, O Venerable One, I renounce all taking of what is not given. Having entered a village, city, hamlet, [mountain settlement, market town, port, seaport, mine, trading center, hermitage, inhabited place, or capital], he himself shall not take what is not given, nor shall he cause another to take what is not given, nor shall he approve of another who takes what is not given. Furthermore, regarding those with whom he has gone forth, whatever belongs to them—a water-strainer, a bowl, a staff, or even a leather-shoe—without first having received permission from them, and without having inspected or wiped it, he shall neither take it nor cause it to be taken. Only after first having received permission from them, and having inspected and wiped it, should he, being restrained, take it or cause it to be taken.

That monk or nun, having approached travelers' lodgings, monastery dwellings, the houses of householders, or hermitages, should seek formal permission (*oggahe*) by reflecting upon it thus: "Whoever is the master there, whoever is the authority there, let him grant permission. 'Truly, O venerable one, we shall dwell for as long as it lasts, as long as it is known [to be permissible], O venerable one! As long as it is within the permission of the venerable one, and for as long as our fellow-monks [remain]—until then we shall occupy the permission; beyond that, we shall depart. What then? Once permission has been so granted therein, whatever fellow-monks who are associated with the same communion and are agreeable should arrive, he should invite those fellow-monks of the same communion and agreement to share his own sought-after food—whether it be solid food, drink, chewables, or delicacies—but he must not invite them by repeatedly seizing portions intended for others."

"Let us take possession [of this dwelling] as long as those who arrive remain, for as long as we live, O venerable one, and for as long as the venerable one's possession lasts, and for as long as our fellow-monks remain; beyond that, we shall dwell elsewhere. Why is that? Because when the possession has been thus taken there, if other fellow-monks who share in the same alms-food and are agreeable should come, one should invite them to use whatever seats, stools, wooden planks, beds, or bedding one has oneself sought out; but one must not, on account of another, repeatedly snatch [the items back] and then invite them."

Regarding those who come as guests, and so forth—what then? When a formal request has been made there, whatever needles, awls, ear-cleaners, or nail-clippers belong to householders or their sons, and which have been borrowed for one's own personal use, one should not give them to another or lend them to another; rather, thinking "this is my own duty," one should take that object and go there. Having gone, one should first place it on the ground with palms turned upward, or having placed it on the ground, one should point it out, saying, "This is indeed it. One must certainly not hand it over from one's own hand into the hand of another.

If that monk or nun should know a dwelling place to be on ground that is bare, or on ground that is damp, or on ground that is dusty, or on a sentient rock, or on a sentient clod of earth, or on wood inhabited by living beings, or containing eggs, or containing small creatures, or containing seeds, or containing sprouts, or containing dew, or containing frost, or containing insects, fungi, water-moss, mud, or spiderwebs—then such a dwelling place they should neither occupy nor cause to be occupied.

If that monk or nun should know a dwelling place to be on a pillar, or on a house-lattice, or on a peg, or on a water-pipe, or on any other such thing produced in the open air that is poorly fastened, [poorly placed, unsteady, and shaky], they should not take possession of it, nor should they enter upon it.

If that monk or nun should know a dwelling place to be on a pillar, a wall, a stone, a brick, or any other such thing produced from the open air, which is poorly constructed, poorly placed, unstable, and movable, they should not take possession of it, nor should they occupy it.

If that monk or nun should know a dwelling place—whether on a pillar, a bed, a gallery, a palace, a flat roof, or any other such kind of structure produced in the open air—that is poorly fastened, poorly placed, unstable, and shaky, they should neither take possession of it nor occupy it.

If that monk or nun should know a dwelling place to be shared with householders, containing families, containing domestic animals, containing women, containing children, containing infants, and containing food and drink—[where there is no freedom for going out or coming in, nor for reciting, questioning, rehearsing, reflecting, or contemplating the Dharma]—then, having understood this, they should not take possession of or occupy such a lodging as it is shared with householders and contains families, children, infants, food, and drink.

If that monk or nun should know of a dwelling that lies right in the middle of a householder’s family on the way, such that it is connected to the path, and where there is no freedom for coming and going, nor freedom for reciting, questioning, reflecting, inspecting, or contemplating upon the Dharma—having known this, they should not take up or occupy a formal possession of such a lodging.

If that monk or nun should know of a lodging where householders, housewives, sons of householders, daughters of householders, daughters-in-law of householders, nurses, male slaves, female slaves, laborers, or female laborers are abusing, binding, obstructing, or harassing one another, and where there is no peace [of mind] up to the point of anxiety—having understood this, he or she should not take possession of or occupy such a lodging.

If that monk or nun should know of a lodging where householders, or even female servants, are anointing or smearing one another’s bodies with oil, ghee, butter, or fat, such that there is no possibility of entering or exiting, nor of reciting, questioning, rehearsing, reviewing, or reflecting upon the Dharma—having recognized this, he or she should not take up or occupy a formal agreement for such a lodging.

If that monk or nun should know of a lodging where householders, or even female servants, are rubbing, scrubbing, kneading, or massaging one another’s bodies with bath-powder, alkali, lodhra, cosmetic paste, scented powder, or clay; or if they are thinking of doing so—knowing this, he or she should not take up or occupy such a lodging.

If that monk or nun should know of a lodging where householders, or even their female servants, are washing or rinsing one another’s bodies with cold water or warm water, or sprinkling or bathing them; and where there is no exit or entrance for the wise, nor scope for the wise to engage in reciting, questioning, rehearsing, observing, or reflecting upon the Dharma—knowing this, he should not take up or occupy such a lodging.

If that monk or nun should know a dwelling place where householders, or even female servants, are staying together in seclusion, clinging to one another, engaging in sexual intercourse or whispering secret counsel, such that there is no possibility for the wise to enter or exit; [he or she should not occupy it].

If that monk or nun should know of a dwelling-place where there is a dense thicket, not suitable for the coming and going of the wise, nor even for the contemplation of the Dharma—having known this, they should neither take possession of nor occupy such a lodging.
This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they should always be self-controlled, harmonious, and restrained in all things. Thus I say.

In guest-houses, or in park-houses, or in the households of householders, or in monasteries, he should seek permission after due consideration. Whosoever is the master there, whosoever is the supervisor there, he should ask them for permission: "Truly, O venerable one, we would dwell here as long as it lasts and as long as it is permitted; O venerable one, as long as [the stay] belongs to the venerable one, and as long as it is for the sake of our fellow-monks, so long shall we occupy this space; beyond that, we shall depart. Furthermore, when the space has been thus occupied, whatever there may be belonging to the ascetics or the brahmins—whether an umbrella, a bowl, a staff, a walking stick, a *misi* (a type of mat), a *nāliya* (a water-strainer), a cloth, a *cilimilī* (a rug), a hide, a leather case, or a leather scraper—he should not take it from inside to outside, nor bring it from outside inside; he should not wake them from sleep, nor do anything unpleasant or offensive to them.

If that monk or nun should desire to go to a mango grove, they should ask permission from whoever is the owner there or whoever is in charge there, saying: "Please, O venerable one, grant us the use [of this place] so that we may dwell here as long as we wish. Now, when such use has been granted there, if the monk should desire to eat or drink a mango, he should recognize that the mango is with eggs, with young, with seeds, with sprouts, with flies, with maggots, with insects, with fungi, with water-organisms, with mud, or with spiderwebs; such a mango, considering it to be impure and unfit for use, he should not accept it even if it is available.

If that monk or nun should know that mangoes are free from insects, up to and including being free from sprouts, yet are cut unevenly or not cut at all—considering them to be unwholesome and unfit for seeking, they should not accept them even if an opportunity arises.

If that monk or nun should know that mangoes are free from insects, up to and including being free from sprouts, and are cut evenly or properly cut—considering them to be wholesome and fit for seeking, they should accept them if an opportunity arises.

If that monk or nun should desire to eat or drink mango-slices, mango-powder, mango-rind, mango-juice, or mango-seed-kernel, yet should know that the mango-slices or even the mango-seed-kernels contain living beings and are thus impure and unfit for consumption, they should not accept them, even if an opportunity for gain is present.

If that monk or nun should know that it is mango-skin or even mango-stone—provided it is not yet ripe, and free from insects, moss, water, mud, or spiderwebs—and that it has not been cut across [the stalk], nor severed [from the tree], and considering it to be impure and unfit for alms, they should not accept it, even if an opportunity for gain presents itself.

If that monk or nun should know that it is mango-juice, or even mango-syrup, free from insects and so forth, up to being free from living organisms and fibers, cut crosswise and separated [from the source], pure, and available for acceptance—then, such being the case, they may accept it.

If that monk or nun should desire to go to a sugarcane plantation, they should ask permission from the one who is the master there [or from those who have authority there]: "Please, O venerable sir, grant us permission; we would like to dwell here for as long as it is appropriate and as long as we have fully understood [the conditions]. We shall occupy this space as long as the venerable one has permission, and for as long as there are fellow-monks; beyond that, we shall depart. Once permission has been granted in that place, if the monk should wish to eat or drink sugarcane, yet he should know that the sugarcane contains eggs [or is otherwise inhabited], up to and including spiderwebs, then—considering such sugarcane to be impure and unfit for use—he should not accept it even if it is available. The same applies to what is cut too long; the same applies to what is cut across.

If a monk or a nun should desire to eat or drink sugar-cane, a stalk of sugar-cane, sugar-cane juice, a sugar-cane plantation, or a sugar-cane thicket, yet they should know that it contains eggs, living beings, seeds, green vegetation, dew, water, or is infested with insects, fungi, water-creatures, mud, or spiderwebs—then, considering it to be impure and unfit for consumption, they should not accept it even if it is offered.

If that monk or nun should know that the bedding contains internal insects, or even fragments of clay, or webs of clay-mud, and that it has not been cut across nor separated [from the ground], then considering it to be unwholesome and unfit for use, they should not accept it even if it is offered.

If that monk or nun should know that the bedding contains internal insects, or even fragments of clay, and that it is free from insects, or has been cut across and separated [from the ground], then considering it to be wholesome and fit for use, they should accept it if it is offered.
If that monk or nun should desire to go to a garlic grove, the same three sections [of the rule] apply, with the only difference being "garlic."

If that monk should desire to eat or drink garlic, or a garlic bulb, or a garlic stalk, or a garlic shoot, he should, if he knows it to be garlic—or anything up to a garlic shoot—containing eggs, living beings, seeds, herbs, dew, water-born organisms, insects, algae, mud, or spiderwebs; being thus impure and unfit for consumption, even if it is available, he should not accept it. The same applies to what is cut from above or cut across, until he may accept it [only when it is pure].

Whether it be a monk or a nun, when they have come to guest-houses, or monastic dwellings, or the households of householders, or hermitages, they should seek permission after due consideration. When such a place has been thus permitted, and while avoiding those potential dangers belonging to the householders or the sons of householders therein—provided the monk knows this—he should take possession of the site according to these seven postures. Now, herein is the first posture:

In approaching guest-houses, park-houses, the families of householders, or monasteries, he should seek permission after due consideration: "Whoever is the master there, whoever is in charge there, let him grant permission for the use [of the space]. Indeed, O venerable one, we shall dwell as long as it is appropriate and as long as it is permitted; O venerable one, for as long as the venerable one has possession, and for as long as our fellow-monks remain, so long shall we occupy the use; beyond that, we shall depart. This is the first vow.

Furthermore, there is a second vow: when a monk thinks, "I shall take formal possession (oggaha) for the sake of other monks, and I shall rely upon the formal possession already taken by other monks"—this is the second vow. Furthermore, there is a third vow: when a monk thinks, "I shall take formal possession for the sake of other monks, but I shall not rely upon the formal possession already taken by other monks"—this is the third vow.

Furthermore, there is the fourth vow: for that monk who thinks, "I shall not take possession of a dwelling for the sake of other monks, but I shall rely upon a dwelling already taken by others"—this is the fourth vow.

Furthermore, there is the fifth vow: for that monk who thinks, "I shall take possession of a dwelling for my own sake, and not for two, nor for three, nor for four, nor for five"—this is the fifth vow.

Furthermore, this is the sixth vow: that monk or nun, having entered upon a specific undertaking, should dwell there if such materials as are available are found—namely, a mat of reeds, or a mat of *kaṭhina* grass, or a mat of *jantuka*, or a mat of *paraga*, or a mat of *moraga*, or straw, or even as far as *pippala* leaves, or chaff; if these are obtained, he should dwell there, but if they are not obtained, he should remain in the *ukkuḍuka* posture or in a sitting position (*nēsanjī*). This is the sixth vow.

Furthermore, this is the seventh vow: that monk or nun should seek a dwelling-place exactly as it is provided, such as a stone slab or a wooden plank, exactly as it is found. Upon obtaining it, they should dwell there; if they do not obtain it, they should remain either in a squatting position or in a sitting posture. This is the seventh vow. Thus, from among these seven vows, one should adopt whichever is appropriate, just as in the case of the rules for seeking alms. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that being restrained in all things, and being self-controlled, one should always strive. Thus I say.
[The Eighth Chapter – The Sevenfold Array of Positions]

If that monk or nun should desire to take up a standing position, he or she may enter a village, town, hamlet, mountain settlement, port, city, seaport, mine, market town, hermitage, inhabited area, or capital city. Having entered such a village or even a capital city, if he or she should perceive that the place for standing is infested with eggs, living beings, seeds, green plants, dew, water, or with earthworms, cobwebs, fungi, water, mud, and spiders’ webs—that is, if it is of such a nature—he or she, considering it to be unwholesome and unfit for use, should not accept it even if it is available.
In this manner, it should be understood through the *sijjāgama* (the method of the bed) up until the point of "those produced by the rising [of the sun].

Having bypassed these sources of attachment, if a monk should desire to stand in four postures, herein is the first posture: "I shall indeed occupy an inanimate place; I shall lean against it with my body; I shall move about within it; I shall stand in a position with movement. This is the first posture.

Furthermore, there is this second vow: "I shall indeed resort to an inanimate object; I shall hang [my body] from it; I shall move my body about; yet I shall not remain in a position involving movement. This is the second vow. Furthermore, there is this third vow: "I shall indeed resort to an inanimate object; I shall not hang [my body] from it; I shall not move my body about; yet I shall not remain in a position involving movement. This is the third vow.

Furthermore, this is the fourth vow: "I shall indeed dwell in a mindless state; I shall not lean against anything; I shall not move my body; I shall not stand in a shifting position; having renounced my body and having renounced my hair, beard, body hair, and nails, I shall stand in a restricted posture"—this is the fourth vow.

Thus, when undertaking any one of these four vows (*pratimā*), one should not speak thus: "They have entered upon a wrong path," and so on, up to: "One should dwell with even greater resolve. One should not say anything at all. This indeed is the complete conduct for that monk or nun: that being self-restrained and self-controlled in all things, one should always exert oneself. Thus I say. [The Ninth Chapter – The Seventh Section on Seclusion (*Nisīhiyā*)]

If that monk or nun should desire to go to a convenient resting place (*nisīhiyā*), and if they should know that resting place to be with eggs, with small animals, with seeds, with grass, with water-weeds, with water, with mud, and with the webs of spiders—such a resting place being inconvenient, unfit for use, and considering it not to be right to accept even if it were obtained—they should not go there.

If that monk or nun should desire to go for the sake of a resting place (*nisīhiyā*), and should know that resting place to be free from eggs, free from living beings, and so on, up to being free from spiderwebs—such a resting place, considering it to be acceptable and fit for use, [should think]: "I shall take it if it is available."

In this same manner, it should be understood through the procedure for the bed (sijjāgama) up until [the section on] those born of the Udaya hell. Those who there, in groups of two, three, four, or five, intend to go toward the *nisīhiya* (place of seclusion), they should not embrace one another’s body, nor stroke it, nor kiss it, nor bite it with their teeth or scratch it with their nails, nor tear at it. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that he or she should always be self-controlled and steadfast in all things. One should consider this as beneficial—thus I say.

[Tenth Chapter – The Section on Excrement and Urine] If that monk or nun is pressed by the need for the act of voiding excrement or urine, and there is no availability of his own foot-wiping cloth, he or she may thereafter seek one from a fellow practitioner of the same faith.

That monk or nun, moreover, should recognize a spot of ground that is infested with eggs, living beings, seeds, green plants, dew, water, or the webs of insects; on such a spot of ground, he or she should not void excrement or urine.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that ground to be free from insects, free from living beings, and so forth, up to free from creeping plants; on such a ground as this, he or she may void excrement or urine.

If that monk or nun should know a sleeping place or a bare ground where, for the sake of a fellow-monk, living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings have been harmed or killed, or which has been intended for him, purchased, bartered, taken by force, appropriated, brought from elsewhere, or specially prepared—whether such a bare ground has been made ready by others or not made ready by others, whether it is for one's own use or not for one's own use, whether it has been used or not used, or whether it has been enjoyed or not enjoyed—in such a bare ground as this, he or she should not void excrement or urine.

If that monk or nun should know of a spot where many fellow monks have been designated for its sake, having mobilized living beings and so forth, having designated it, having purchased it, up to: having taken it by force, having received it as a gift, having brought it there, and having prepared it specifically for them; then, on such a spot—even if it has been made ready by others, or even if it has not yet been used—they should not void excrement or urine.

If that monk or nun should know of a spot where someone, for the sake of a fellow practitioner, having intended it and having procured it by harming living beings, has purchased [food] and even prepared it—such a spot, whether it has been made ready by another person or is one that has not yet been used—in such a spot he or she should not void excrement or urine.

If that monk or nun should know of a piece of ground where, for their sake, many fellow-monks have intended it by procuring it through the destruction of living beings, having purchased it, and so forth, up to having brought it there and prepared it as an intended site—then on such a piece of ground, whether it has been prepared by others or even if it has not been used [before], he or she should not void excrement or urine.

If that monk or nun should know of a spot where many ascetics, up to and including mendicants, have specifically designated it for their own sake by repeatedly selecting [the site], having harmed living beings, and having purchased it specifically for them—having brought such a designated spot to a shrine, whether it has been prepared by men, or even if it has been carried outside, or if it is not yet inhabited—in such a spot as this, he or she should not void excrement or urine.

If that monk or nun should know that a certain open space has been prepared specifically for many ascetics and brahmins—having intended it for living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings, and having had it built for that purpose—then in such a place, even if it has been made by others and has not been carried outside, they should not void excrement or urine. However, if they should know that it has not been made by others and has been carried outside, then in such a place they may void excrement or urine.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that if a spot of ground has been prepared for this purpose—whether made by oneself, caused to be made, or obtained by barter; whether covered, leveled, smoothed, smeared, plastered, or fumigated—or if it is of any such other kind, they should not void excrement or urine upon that spot of ground.

If that monk or nun should know the ground to be such: "In this place, indeed, householders or householders' sons are bringing bulbs or roots, or even green plants from the inside to the outside, or are bringing them from the outside to the inside," then on such a ground he or she should not discharge feces or urine.
That monk, or [nun], should know that if there is a place such as a pillar, a bench, a couch, a gallery, a watchtower, or a palace—on any such kind of place—he should not void excrement or urine.

If that monk or nun should know a sleeping place or a bare patch of ground to be: on ground not covered by another, on moist ground, on dusty ground, on clayey ground, on a variegated stone, on a variegated slab, on a mossy surface, or on a tree trunk inhabited by living beings, containing eggs, containing young ones, containing seeds, containing herbs, containing fungi, containing water, containing earthworms, or containing a network of insects, spiders, water-creatures, mud, and monkeys—or on any other such bare patch of ground—they should not void excrement or urine there.

If that monk or nun should know of such a bare ground: "In this place, indeed, householders or householders' sons have scattered, are scattering, or will scatter bulbs, roots, bark, [up to] fruits, or seeds," then on such a bare ground he or she should not discharge feces or urine.

If that monk or nun should know of a certain open space: "In this place, indeed, householders or householders' sons... have scattered, are scattering, or will scatter rice, or paddy, or mung beans, or black gram, or sesame seeds, or horse gram, or chickpeas, or barley, or wheat," then in such an open space as this, he or she shall not discharge feces or urine.

If that monk or nun should know a resting place or a bare ground that contains moldy fodder, or scattered grass, or creeping plants, or stumps, or thorny brambles, or deep pits, or caves, or difficult terrain, or even if it be level or uneven—on such a bare ground as this, they should not void excrement or urine.

If that monk or nun should know that the spot is a place for the breeding of humans, or a place for buffaloes, bulls, horses, chickens, quails, partridges, francolins, or grey partridges, or any other such place, he or she should not void excrement or urine there.

If that monk or nun should know a certain spot to be a place for hanging, or a place where vultures feed, or a place for climbing trees, or a place for falling from a precipice, or a place for consuming poison, or a place for falling into fire, or any other such spot, they shall not void excrement or urine there.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that if it is a piece of ground such as a monastery, a park, a grove, a thicket, a temple, an assembly hall, or a pavilion—or any other such kind of ground—they should not void excrement or urine there.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that if it is a piece of ground such as a watchtower, a rampart, a gate, or a city gateway—or any other such kind of ground—they should not void excrement or urine there.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that ground to be a place where there are triads, or crossroads, or junctions, or four-way intersections; on such a kind of ground, he or she should not void excrement or urine.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that ground to be a place where there are burning embers, or alkaline pits, or places where corpses are burned, or funeral mounds for the dead, or shrines for the dead; on such a kind of ground, he or she should not void excrement or urine.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that if it is a piece of ground such as one near a river-bank, or near a muddy place, or near a flood-prone area, or on a path for cattle, or any other such ground, they should not void excrement or urine there.

If that monk or nun should know a sleeping place or a bare ground to be among fresh clay pits, or among fresh cow-pen sites, or among places where cattle have fed, or among pits, or any other such kind of bare ground, he or she should not void excrement or urine there.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that if the ground is covered with castor plants, or with hemp plants, or with radishes, or with *hatthaṅkara* plants, or with any other such kind of ground, they should not void excrement or urine there.

That monk or nun, moreover, should know that if it is a piece of ground such as a grove of *asaṇa* trees, a grove of *saṇa* grass, a grove of *dhāyairī* trees, a grove of *kēyaï* trees, a grove of mangoes, a grove of *asōga* trees, a grove of *nāga* trees, a grove of *punṇāga* trees, or any other similar places consisting of leaf-shelters, flower-shelters, fruit-shelters, seed-shelters, or green-shelters, they should not void excrement or urine there.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, having taken up [excrement or urine] from his own vessel or another’s vessel, he should go with that to a secluded place—free from people, out of sight, where there are no drinking water sources and no spiderwebs—and in a garden or a dwelling, he should carefully void excrement and urine. Having gone with that to a secluded place—free from people, as far as being free of spiderwebs—in a garden or on a heap of ashes, or on some other such kind of ground that is devoid of living beings, he should then carefully void excrement and urine.
This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they should always be self-controlled, restrained, and vigilant regarding all objects of desire—thus I say.

[The Eleventh Chapter – The Section on Sounds] That monk or nun hears various kinds of sounds as they arise, such as the sounds of the *mṛdaṅga* drum, the sounds of the *nandī* drum, the sounds of the *jhallarī* cymbals, or other such diverse sounds of percussion; yet, for the sake of hearing with the ear, they should not resolve to go toward them.

If that monk or nun hears various kinds of sounds as they occur, such as the sounds of the lute, the harp, the *baddhīsaga*, the flute, the small drum, the gourd-lute, the *ḍhaṅkuṇa*, or other similar sounds of diverse kinds produced by stretched membranes, he or she should not resolve to go toward them for the purpose of hearing with the ear.

If that monk or nun hears various sounds as they arise, such as the sounds of cymbals, the sounds of bronze cymbals, the sounds of lattiya drums, the sounds of gōhiya drums, the sounds of kirakiriya drums, or other such diverse kinds of sounds like those of cymbals, he or she should not resolve to go for the sake of hearing them with the ear.

If that monk or nun hears various sounds as they occur, such as the sounds of conchs, flutes, lutes, kharāmukhīs, or whistling sounds, or other similar sounds of diverse kinds that are hollow and reach the ear, he or she should not resolve to go toward them.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, when they hear various kinds of sounds such as those from fields, embankments, lotus ponds, marshes, waterfalls, cascades, tanks, lakes, oblong ponds, canals, pools, oceans, rows of lakes, or rows of lakes and pools, or any other such diverse sounds, they should not resolve to go toward them for the sake of hearing with their ears.

If that monk or nun hears sounds from various places—such as marshes, thickets, dense forests, woods, forest ravines, mountains, mountain ravines, or other similar places of diverse kinds—he or she should not resolve to go there for the purpose of hearing those sounds with the ear.

If that monk or nun hears sounds as they occur, such as those from villages, cities, market towns, royal capitals, hermitages, ports, or settlements, or any other such various kinds of sounds, he or she should not resolve to go toward them for the purpose of hearing with the ear.

If that monk or nun hears various sounds as they occur, such as those from pleasure groves, gardens, forests, thickets of trees, temples, assembly halls, or pavilions, or any other such diverse sounds, he or she should not set out to go toward them for the purpose of hearing with the ear.

If that monk or nun hears sounds such as those arising from fortifications, watchtowers, ramparts, gates, or city-towers, or any other similar sounds of various kinds, he or she should not set out to go toward them for the purpose of listening with the ear.

If that monk or nun hears sounds such as those from crossroads, or from four-way junctions, or from market squares, or from places with four entrances, or other such various kinds of sounds, he or she should not, for the sake of hearing them with the ear, resolve to go there.

If that monk or nun hears various sounds such as these—namely, the sounds of buffaloes fighting, bulls fighting, horses fighting, elephants fighting, [cocks fighting, monkeys fighting, quails fighting, pigeons fighting, partridges fighting, or woodpeckers fighting], or the sounds of kapiñjala birds fighting, or other similar sounds of various kinds—he or she should not, for the sake of hearing them with the ear, plan a journey toward them.

If that monk or nun hears various sounds as they occur, such as—buffalo fights, bull fights, horse fights, elephant fights, cock fights, monkey fights, quail fights, pigeon fights, partridge fights, or francolin fights, or any other similar sounds of diverse kinds for the sake of hearing with the ear—they should not resolve to go there.

If that monk or nun hears sounds such as those occurring at places for the training of thoroughbreds, or places for the training of horses, or places for the training of elephants, or other similar sounds of various kinds, he or she should not set out to go toward them for the purpose of listening with the ear.

If that monk or nun hears various kinds of sounds, such as places for storytelling, places of honor and dishonor, or places where there is great sound of dancing, singing, instrumental music, stringed instruments, cymbals, clapping, and the beating of drums, or other similar sounds of diverse kinds, he or she should not set out to go toward them with the intention of hearing them with the ear.

If that monk or nun hears sounds such as quarrels, riots, disturbances, civil unrest, feuds, or rebellions against rival kingdoms, or any other such various kinds of sounds, he or she should not, for the sake of hearing them with the ear, plan a journey toward them.

If that monk or nun hears various sounds such as these—seeing a young girl, one who is being led away, adorned, decorated, and dressed up, or seeing a man being led out for execution, or hearing other such various kinds of sounds with the intention of listening through the ear—one should not resolve to go toward them.

That monk or nun, knowing of various kinds of great thoroughfares such as these—namely, those with many carts, or many chariots, or many foreigners, or many border-dwellers, or other similar kinds of various great thoroughfares—should not set out for the purpose of traveling along them for the sake of hearing sounds.

If that monk or nun should learn of various kinds of great festivals, such as: women or men, the elderly, the young, or those of middle age; adorned with ornaments; singing, playing instruments, dancing, laughing, enjoying themselves, or being intoxicated; or consuming and distributing abundant food, drink, chewables, and delicacies; or distributing and sharing them; or scattering them about; or throwing them away; or any other such various kinds of great festivals—for the sake of hearing sounds, he or she should not resolve to go there.

That monk or nun should not be attached to sounds of this world, nor to sounds of the other world; not to sounds heard, nor to sounds unheard; not to sounds seen, nor to sounds unseen; not to pleasant sounds, nor to lovely sounds; they should not be captivated, should not be impassioned, should not be greedy, should not be deluded, and should not be obsessed by them.
This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they should always be self-restrained and steadfast in all things. Thus I say.

[The Twelfth Chapter – The Section on Forms] If that monk or nun sees various forms as they happen to come before them— namely, those that are knotted, those that are woven, those that are stuffed, those that are joined together, those made of woodwork, those made of book-covers, those made of painting, those made of jewels, those made of ivory, or those made of leaf-cutting— or various other such diverse forms, whether woven or otherwise— he or she should not resolve to go toward them for the purpose of seeing them with the eye.

In this same way, it should be understood that all representations of sound are to be avoided, as are representations of form. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they should always be self-controlled, steadfast, and restrained in all things. Thus I say.
(The Thirteenth Chapter: The Section on the Avoidance of Actions Performed by Others.)

Regarding service performed by another—whether it be internal or external—one should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another should massage or rub one’s feet, one should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another should knead or rub one’s feet, one should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another should blow on or dye one’s feet, one should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another should anoint or smear one’s feet with oil, ghee, or fat, one should neither approve of it nor insist upon it.

If someone else should rub or scrub one's feet with lodhra, or with a decoction, or with powder, or with ointment—that he should not consent to, nor should he resolve to do so. If someone else should wash or rinse one's feet with cold water or warm water—that he should not consent to, nor should he resolve to do so. If someone else should smear or anoint one's feet with any kind of unguent—that he should not consent to, nor should he resolve to do so.

If another person were to fumigate or re-fumigate his feet with any kind of incense, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person were to extract a splinter or a thorn from his foot, or cleanse it, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person were to extract pus or blood from his foot, or cleanse it, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person were to rub or wipe his body, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person were to massage or knead his body with oil or ointment, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person were to smear or rub his body with lodhra, karka, powder, or cosmetic paste, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person were to wash or bathe his body with cold water or warm water, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it.

If someone else should smear or anoint his body with any kind of ointment, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If someone else should fumigate or re-fumigate his body with any kind of incense, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If someone else should rub or wipe a wound on his body, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If someone else should massage or rub a wound on his body, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If someone else should anoint or smear a wound on his body with oil, ghee, or fat, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it.

If another person were to sprinkle or rub a wound on his body with lodhra, kakkā, powder, or ointment, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it.
