If another person were to wash or rinse a wound on his body with cold water or warm water, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person were to cut or incise a wound, a boil, a carbuncle, a rash, or an ulcer on his body with any kind of surgical instrument, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person, having cut or incised a wound on his body with any kind of surgical instrument, were to extract pus or blood or cleanse it, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it.

If another person should rub or wipe a boil, a carbuncle, an abscess, or a fistula on his body, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person should massage or rub a boil, a carbuncle, an abscess, or a fistula on his body, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it.

If another person should smear or rub with oil, ghee, fat, or marrow upon a boil, an ulcer, a carbuncle, or a fistula on his body, he should neither consent to it nor approve of it. If another person should sprinkle or rub with lodhra, a medicinal paste, powder, or ointment upon a boil, an ulcer, a carbuncle, or a fistula on his body, he should neither consent to it nor approve of it. If another person should wash or rinse with cold water or warm water a boil, an ulcer, a carbuncle, or a fistula on his body, he should neither consent to it nor approve of it.

If another person should smear or besmear a boil, a carbuncle, a tumor, or an ulcer on his body with any kind of unguent, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person should fumigate or smoke a boil, a carbuncle, a tumor, or an ulcer on his body with any kind of incense, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If another person should cut or lacerate a boil, a carbuncle, a tumor, or an ulcer on his body with any kind of surgical instrument, he should neither approve of it nor insist upon it.

If another person should, with some kind of surgical instrument, cut or incise a boil, a carbuncle, a tumor, or an ulcer on his body; or, having cut or incised it with some kind of surgical instrument, should extract pus or blood, or cleanse it—he should not approve of that, nor should he insist upon it. If another person should extract or cleanse sweat or dirt from his body—he should not approve of that, nor should he insist upon it. If another person should extract or cleanse the impurity of the eyes, the impurity of the ears, the impurity of the teeth, or the impurity of the nails—he should not approve of that, nor should he insist upon it. If another person should clip or trim long hair, long body hair, long arm-hair, long pubic hair, or long anal hair—he should not approve of that, nor should he insist upon it. If another person should extract lice or nits from his head, or cleanse them away—he should not approve of that, nor should he insist upon it.

If someone were to have him lie down on a couch or a bed and then massage or rub his feet—that he should approve of that, nor should he make a rule of it. Thus, the subsequent section regarding the feet should be recited.

If another person were to have him lie down on a couch or a bed, or were to place upon him a necklace, a half-necklace, a breast-ornament, a necklet, a crown, a long pendant, or a golden thread—whether by arranging it or laying it down—he should neither approve of that nor insist upon it. If another person were to lead him out to or bring him into a grove or a garden, or were to rub or wipe his feet—he should neither approve of that nor insist upon it. In this same way, other mutual actions are to be understood.

If another person should provide medical treatment with pure speech and power, or if another person should provide medical treatment with impure speech and power; or if another person, for the sake of the sick, should dig up or pull out, or cause to be dug up or pulled out, bulbs, roots, bark, or green plants—whether containing life or not—that is neither to be approved nor to be insisted upon. Living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings experience painful sensations.
This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that they should always be restrained, harmonious, and self-controlled in all things. One should understand this thus—so I say.
[The fourteenth chapter: The Section on Mutual Activity]

If that monk or nun should engage in mutual services for one another—whether internal or secret—they should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. If they should rub or wipe one another’s feet, they should neither approve of it nor insist upon it. The rest is exactly as before. This indeed is the proper conduct for that monk or nun: that which is consistent with all that is desired, harmonious, and always practiced with self-restraint. One should consider this to be beneficial. Thus I say.
[The fifteenth chapter – Bhāvanā]

At that time, on that occasion, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra was under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī (*pañca-hatthuttara*). Under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī he descended from his previous existence and entered the womb; under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī he was transferred from one womb to another; under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī he was born; under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī, having shaved his head entirely and completely, he went forth from the household life into homelessness; under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī, absolute, complete, unobstructed, unimpeded, infinite, and supreme perfect knowledge and vision arose; and under the constellation Svāti, the Blessed One attained final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*).

The Blessed One, the Great Hero, the ascetic—after the *susama-susamā* eon had passed, the *susamā* eon had passed, and the *susama-dusamā* eon had passed, and after much of the *dusama-susamā* eon had elapsed, with seventy-five years, eight and a half months remaining of that [eon]—in the fourth month of summer, in the eighth fortnight, during the bright half of Āṣāḍha, on the sixth lunar day, when the moon was in conjunction with the constellation *Hastottarā*, he descended from the great celestial palace *Mahāvijaya Siddhārtha-puṣpottara-pravara-puṇḍarīka-diśā-avatithita-vardhamāna*, having completed a lifespan of twenty *sāgaropamas*. Having fallen from there through the exhaustion of his life-span, the exhaustion of his existence, and the exhaustion of his duration, he indeed entered the womb of Devānandā, a Brāhmaṇī of the Jālandharāyaṇa lineage, wife of the Brāhmaṇa Usabhadatta of the Kōḍāla lineage, in the settlement of Kuṇḍapura in Southern Māhaṇa, within the region of Bharaha in the southern half of Jambudvīpa, by means of his own self which had manifested as a lion.

The Blessed One, the Great Hero, was a śramaṇa who had attained the three types of knowledge: he knew, "I shall fall [from the body]," he knew, "I have fallen," but while falling, he did not know; for that time is indeed subtle as it is described.

Then, out of compassion for the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, the gods thought, "This is what must be done," and so, in the third month of the rainy season, in the fifth fortnight—namely, the dark fortnight of Āśvina—on the thirteenth day of that dark fortnight of Āśvina, when the moon was in conjunction with the constellation *Hastottarā*, and when eighty-two days had passed and the eighty-third day was underway, [the gods] removed the embryo from the womb of the Kṣatriya lady Triśalā of the Vāsiṣṭha lineage, wife of Siddhārtha the Kṣatriya of the Kāśyapa lineage, from the northern settlement of Kṣatriyakundapura, and transferred it into the womb of the Brāhmaṇa lady Devānandā of the Jālandharāyaṇa lineage, wife of the Brāhmaṇa Ṛṣabhadatta of the Kauṇḍinya lineage, in the southern settlement of Brāhmaṇakundapura; having thus removed the impure constituents and infused the pure constituents. They then took that embryo which was in the womb of the Kṣatriya lady Triśalā and transferred it into the womb of the Brāhmaṇa lady Devānandā in the southern settlement of Brāhmaṇakundapura.

The Blessed One, the Great Hero, was a śramaṇa who had attained the three types of knowledge: he knew that he was about to be transferred, he knew that he was being transferred, and he knew that he had been transferred, O venerable śramaṇa! At that time, on that occasion, after nine months and seven and a half nights of the full term had passed for the Kṣatriya lady Triśalā, in the first month of summer, in the second fortnight—namely, the bright fortnight of Caitra—on the thirteenth day of that bright fortnight of Caitra, when the moon was in conjunction with the constellation Hasta, she gave birth to the śramaṇa, the Blessed One, the Great Hero, healthy from her own health.

On the night that the Kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā gave birth to the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, healthy and free from ailment, on that very night there arose a great divine radiance of the gods, a gathering of the gods, and a tumultuous clamor of the gods, as the gods and goddesses belonging to the Bhavanavāsins, Vānamantarās, Jyotiṣkas, and Vimānavāsins descended and ascended. It was indeed a scene of intense commotion.

On the very night that the Kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā gave birth to the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, healthy and without illness, on that same night many gods and goddesses rained down a great shower of nectar, a shower of perfumes, a shower of powders, a shower of flowers, a shower of gold, and a shower of jewels.

On the very night that the Kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā gave birth to the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, healthy and without ailment, on that same night the gods and goddesses dwelling in the Bhavanapatis, Vānamantaras, Jyotiṣkas, and Vimānas performed the birth-rites for the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra and the consecration of a Tīrthaṅkara.

From the moment the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra entered the womb of the Kṣatriya lady Triśalā, from that time forward, that family increased exceedingly with vast quantities of bullion, gold, wealth, grain, gems, pearls, conch-shells, crystals, and corals.

Then, having learned of this matter, the parents of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, when ten days had passed, when [the period of impurity] had elapsed, and when they had become pure, prepared an abundant supply of food, drink, soft food, and solid food. Having prepared it, they invited their circle of friends, kinsmen, relatives, and associates. Having invited them, they distributed, scattered, and bestowed [gifts] upon many ascetics, brahmins, the poor, travelers, beggars, and white-robed mendicants; they offered gifts to the recipients and distributed wealth among them. Having distributed, scattered, and bestowed [gifts], and having offered wealth to the recipients, they fed their circle of friends, kinsmen, relatives, and associates. Having fed them, they caused this kind of name to be given [to the child].

"Since the time this prince was conceived in the womb of the Kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā, from that time forth this family has increased exceedingly with vast amounts of bullion, gold, wealth, grain, jewels, pearls, conch-shells, crystals, and corals; therefore, let this prince be named Vardhamāna."

Then the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, surrounded by five nurses—namely, the milk-nurse, the bath-nurse, the adornment-nurse, the play-nurse, and the lap-nurse—was carried from lap to lap; he grew up in due course upon a delightful floor of precious stones, like a *campaka* tree sprouting in a mountain cave.

Then the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra—possessed of full knowledge and experience, having turned away from childhood, free from agitation—dwelt thus while enjoying human pleasures characterized by five attributes: sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells, which are sublime and worthy of praise.

The Blessed One, the ascetic Mahāvīra, of the Kāśyapa clan, has these three names thus proclaimed: Vardhamāna, given by his mother and father; Śramaṇa, given in agreement with the world; and because he endured the formidable, terrifying, and dreadful hardship of nakedness, the gods gave him the name Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra.
The father of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was of the Kāśyapa gotra; he had three names, which were proclaimed as follows: Siddhārtha, or Śreyāṃsa, or Yaśasvin.
The mother of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was of the Vāsiṣṭha gotra; she had three names, which were proclaimed as follows: Triśalā, or Videhadinnā, or Priyakāriṇī.

The maternal uncle of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was Supāśva, of the Kāśyapa gotra; the eldest brother of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was Nandivardhana, of the Kāśyapa gotra; the eldest sister of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was Sudarśanā, of the Kāśyapa gotra; and the wife of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was Yaśodā, of the Kauṇḍinya gotra.

The daughter of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, of the Kāśyapa gotra, had two names given to her as follows: Anojjā or Piyadaṃsaṇā. The granddaughter of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, of the Kausika gotra, had two names given to her as follows: Sēsavantī or Jasavantī.

The parents of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, were lay disciples (*śramaṇopāsaka*) who had taken refuge in the Pārśva tradition. Having observed the conduct of a lay disciple for many years, and for the sake of protecting the six classes of living beings, they confessed, censured, reproached, and repented their faults; they undertook the appropriate higher virtues and penances (*prāyaścitta*), ascended a bed of *kuśa* grass, and renounced food. Having renounced food, through the final mortification of the body at the time of death, they consumed their bodies, and at the end of their lifespan, having passed away and cast off that body, they were reborn as gods in the Ācyuta heaven. Then, with the exhaustion of their life-span, the exhaustion of their existence, and the exhaustion of their duration, falling from there, they will—in the final breath—attain perfection, awaken, be liberated, reach final nirvāṇa, and make an end to all suffering in the region of Mahāvideha.

At that time, in that season, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra—the kinsman, the son of the Jñāta clan, born of the Jñāta lineage—Videha, bestowed by Videha, born of Videha, the glory of Videha—having lived for thirty years in the household with the intention of renunciation, and after his parents had passed away and attained the world of the gods, he fulfilled his vow. Abandoning gold, abandoning silver, abandoning forces, abandoning vehicles, and having scattered, distributed, and dispensed his wealth, grain, gold, jewels, treasures, essentials, and all property among the heirs, giving gifts and sharing them out, and having given alms for one year; then, in the first month of winter, in the first fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa (the dark half), on the tenth day of that dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon was in conjunction with the constellation Uttarā-phalgunī, he set his mind upon the Great Renunciation.
"In one year there will be the Great Renunciation of the Supreme Victor;
therefore, the bestowal of wealth proceeds from the eastern direction:
one crore and eight full hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. (Āyār. 514)
"From the time of sunrise until the evening meal is given.
(Āyār. 515) "Three hundred and eighty-eight million, and eighty-four thousand; this much is given in one year. (Āyār. 516)

The gods of the world-systems, wearing earrings of refined gold and possessing great power, awaken the Tīrthaṅkara in the fifteen lands of action (karmabhūmi). They are to be understood as being in the middle of the row of darkness in the Brahma and Kalpa heavens. (Āyār. 517)
In the world-system, there are eight classes of celestial palaces, incalculable in number.
These hosts of gods, O Blessed One, entreat the Supreme Victor, the Hero, who is beneficial to all living beings in the world: "O Arhat, establish the ford! Āyār. 518–519.

Then, having learned of the ascetic Blessed Mahāvīra’s intention to renounce the world, the gods and goddesses dwelling in the *bhavanapati*, *vānamantara*, *jyotiṣka*, and *vimānavāsin* realms, each with their own forms, their own garments, and their own insignia, mounted their respective celestial chariots (*yānavimāna*) with all their splendor, all their majesty, and the full assembly of their power. Having mounted their respective celestial chariots, they shed their gross matter-particles; having shed their gross matter-particles, they transformed them into subtle matter-particles; having transformed them into subtle matter-particles, they flew upward. Having flown upward, with that most excellent, swift, agile, rapid, and divine celestial gait, descending downward, crossing across countless islands and oceans in a horizontal direction, they arrived at Jambūdvīpa. Having arrived there, they went to the settlement of Uttarakhattiyakuṇḍapura. Having arrived there, they approached with the force of devotion to the north-eastern quarter of the settlement of Uttarakhattiyakuṇḍapura.

Then Śakra, the lord of gods and king of the gods, slowly lowers his celestial chariot; having slowly lowered the celestial chariot, he slowly descends from the celestial chariot; having slowly descended from the celestial chariot, he steps aside; having stepped aside, he undergoes a great transformation by means of a great *vaikriya* expansion; having undergone a great transformation by means of a great *vaikriya* expansion, he creates one large, beautiful, charming, and lovely divine throne, variegated with the patterns of various jewels, gems, and precious stones.

In the very center of that celestial hall (*devacchandaka*), he creates a great throne (*sihāsana*) with a footstool, adorned with various patterns of jewels, gems, and gold; beautiful, lovely, and of exquisite form. Having created it, he approaches where the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra is; having approached, he performs three circumambulations, keeping the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra to his right; and having performed the three circumambulations, he pays homage and reverence to the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra.

Having paid homage and reverence to the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, he took him and went to where the *devacchanda* (royal couch) was; having arrived, he had him sit very slowly upon the lion-throne facing the east. Having seated him, he anointed him with oils refined a hundred and a thousand times. Having anointed him, he rubbed him with fragrant medicinal pastes. Having rubbed him, he bathed him with pure water. Having bathed him, he smeared him with red *gośīrṣa* sandalwood paste, which cost a hundred thousand pieces of gold and was prepared with three types of *paṭola* and was cooled. Having smeared him, he had him put on a pair of fine silken garments (*paṭṭa*)—exquisite, produced in a noble city, praised by skilled men, as delicate as a horse's saliva, with its edges adorned with the work of skilled artisans, and marked with the swan-pattern. Having dressed him, he had him wear a necklace (*hāra*), a half-necklace (*addhahāra*), a breast-ornament (*urattha*), a neck-ornament (*nēvattha*), a single-string necklace (*ēgāvali*), a long hanging thread (*pālamba-sutta*), a silk band (*paṭṭa*), a crown (*mauḍa*), and jewel-garlands. Having adorned him, he decorated him like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) with floral wreaths that were knotted, woven, stuffed, and sewn together. Then, for a second time, he underwent a great manifestation of his supernormal power (*veuvviya-samugghāya*).

Having performed the act of mental concentration (*samōhaṇittā*), he creates a single great palanquin, moon-bright, carried by a thousand [beings]. It is adorned with the patterns of *īhāmṛga* (wild beasts), bulls, horses, men, sea-monsters, birds, monkeys, elephants, *ruru* deer, *sarabha*, *camara* oxen, leopards, lions, forest creepers, and lotus clusters; it is joined with pairs of *vidyādhara* couples engaged in amorous play; it is garlanded with thousands of rays, exquisitely fashioned, and possessed of thousands of shimmering forms; it is slightly swaying and glinting, captivating the eyes with its luster; it is set within lattices of pearls and pearl nets; it has strings of pearls hanging down like excellent molten-gold *lambūsa* ornaments; it is graced with necklaces and half-necklaces as decorations; it is exceedingly beautiful to behold, decorated with patterns of *pāṭala* creepers, *aśoka* creepers, and *kundala* creepers, and further adorned with various floral designs; it is auspicious, of lovely and radiant form, with its upper peaks encircled by multi-colored bells and banners of various gems; it is pleasing, worthy of being seen, and of beautiful appearance.
A palanquin was brought for the Supreme Victor, who is liberated from old age and death;
it was adorned with garlands of *mallika* flowers and divine blossoms of both water and land.
In the center of the palanquin was a divine throne fashioned from excellent jewels and precious materials. (Āyār. 521)
A magnificent lion-throne with footstools for the Best of Victors. (Āyār.
522) He whose crest-jewel is peerless, whose body is radiant, who wears excellent ornaments, and who is clothed in linen garments—the price of which is a hundred thousand. (Āyār. 523)
On the sixth meal, with a pure mental disposition and purified by his tints (*leśyā*), the Jina ascends the supreme palanquin.
Seated upon the lion-throne, Śakra and Īśāna stand on either side.
They are fanned with yak-tail whisks having handles variegated with jewels and gems.
Previously raised by humans whose hair stands on end from joy, they are subsequently carried by gods, asuras, garuḍas, and lords of nāgas. (Āyār. 525–526)
The gods carry him in front, while the asuras carry him on the right side;
others, the garuḍas and nāgas, carry him on the northern side.
Like a flowering grove or a lotus pond in the autumn season... (Āyār. 527)
Thus the expanse of the sky shone with the hosts of gods, as if filled with the weight of blossoms;

just as a grove of *siddhārtha* trees, or a grove of *kaṇikāra*, or a grove of *campaka* shines with the weight of blossoms, so did the expanse of the sky shine with the gods and nagas. (Āyār. 528–529)
With hundreds of thousands of excellent drums, kettledrums, cymbals, and conchs, a most delightful sound of musical instruments resounded in the sky and upon the surface of the earth. (Āyār.
530) There were four kinds of musical instruments—stringed, percussion, wind, and hollow—and they were of many varieties.
There the gods sport with many kinds of dances. (Āyār. 531)

At that time, in that season, during the first month of winter, in the first fortnight—the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa—on the tenth day, under an auspicious day, in the Vijaya muhūrta, when the moon was in conjunction with the constellation Uttaraphalgunī, while the shadow was moving eastward and the fourth watch (pauruṣī) had passed, having fasted for six meals without water, wearing a single garment, and seated in the moon-bright, thousand-wheeled palanquin, he was escorted by an assembly of gods, humans, and asuras. Being thus escorted, he proceeded through the very center of the settlement of Uttarakṣatriyakuṇḍapura; having proceeded, he went to the Nāga-ṣaṇḍa garden. Having arrived, he slowly and gently lowered the moon-bright, thousand-wheeled palanquin upon a patch of ground that was slightly elevated and smooth. Having set it down, he slowly and gently descended from the moon-bright, thousand-wheeled palanquin. Having descended, he slowly and gently sat down on a lion-throne facing the east and removed his ornaments and finery.
Then the god Vaiśramaṇa, kneeling at the knee of the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, received his ornaments and finery in a swan-patterned cloth.
Then the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra performed the tonsure with five handfuls of hair, right hand for the right side and left hand for the left.

Then Śakra, the lord of gods and king of gods, kneeling at the knee of the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, caught the hair in a diamond-studded vessel; having caught it, he said, "Permit me, O Venerable One," and withdrew it to the Ocean of Milk.

Then the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra, having performed the five-fisted hair-plucking (locanā) on the right with his right hand and on the left with his left hand, offered a salutation to the perfected ones (siddhas). Having done so, and having resolved, "All evil karma is not to be committed by me," he undertook the conduct of equanimity (sāmāyika-cāritra). Having undertaken the conduct of equanimity, he rendered the assembly of gods and the assembly of humans as if they were merely painted figures in a picture.
As soon as he undertook that conduct, the divine voices, human cries, and the sounds of musical instruments vanished instantly at the word of Śakra. (Āyār. 533)
"Having adopted the conduct that is beneficial to all living beings day and night, the gods, their hair standing on end with joy, listen with devotion. (Āyār.

534) Then, when the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra had adopted the *sāmāyika* conduct characterized by the subsidence of karmic matter (*khāyovasamiya*), the knowledge called mental-cognition (*manapajjavanāṇa*) arose within him; through this, he knew the mental states of rational, five-sensed, fully developed beings throughout two and a half continents and two oceans.

Then, having gone forth, the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra dismissed his circle of friends, kinsmen, relatives, and associates. Having dismissed them, he undertook this kind of vow: "For twelve years, with my body cast off and my person renounced, whatever hardships may arise—whether divine, human, or from the animal realm—I shall endure, tolerate, and bear them all with equanimity."

Then, having undertaken this kind of vow, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra—having renounced his body and abandoned all attachment to it—arrived at the village of Kumāra when but a single moment remained of the day. Thereupon, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, having renounced and abandoned his body, dwelt while cultivating his self through supreme speech, supreme conduct, supreme restraint, supreme exertion, supreme protection, supreme austerity, supreme observance of celibacy, supreme forbearance, supreme equanimity, supreme contentment, supreme vigilance, supreme steadfastness, supreme action, and through the supreme path of liberation consisting of the fruit of well-practiced conduct.

While he was living in this manner, whatever obstacles (upasargas) arose—whether divine, human, or animal—he, remaining undisturbed, unperturbed, and with a mind free from dejection, protected by the threefold restraint of mind, speech, and body, properly endured, forgave, bore, and patiently accepted all those obstacles as they arose.

While the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was wandering on this journey, twelve years had elapsed and he was in the course of the thirteenth year of his religious career. In the second month of summer, in the fourth fortnight—namely, the bright half of Vaiśākha—on the tenth day, during the auspicious day, at the hour of Vijaya, while the moon was in conjunction with the constellation Hastottarā, when the shadow was moving toward the east and the *pauruṣī* (the eighth part of the day) had passed, outside the city of Jambhikagrāma on the northern bank of the river Ujuvāliya, in the wood-cutter’s shed of the householder Sāmāga, with his knees raised and his body bent forward, having entered the enclosure of meditation, in the north-eastern quarter of the Veyāvatta shrine, not far from a *sāla* tree, while performing the austerity of the *godōhiyā* posture, sitting in the *ukkuḍuka* position, having fasted for six meals without water, and while engaged in pure meditation (*sukkajjhāṇa*), there arose in him the absolute, complete, untroubled, unobstructed, infinite, and unsurpassed supreme knowledge and vision (*kevalavarajñānadarśana*).

That Blessed One, the Arhat, the Victor, has become an omniscient Kevalin, a seer of all states of being; he knows the conditions of the world including its gods, humans, and asuras—namely, their coming and going, their staying, their passing away, and their rebirth; what they have eaten, drunk, done, and experienced; their public deeds and secret deeds; what they have spoken and declared; and even their mental thoughts. Knowing and seeing all these states of all living beings in the entire world, he dwells in this manner.

On the day when the absolute, complete, unobstructed, unimpeded, infinite, and supreme knowledge and vision (*kevalavarajñānadarśana*) arose for the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra—on that very day, the world became filled with gods and goddesses belonging to the realms of the *bhavanapati*, *vānamantara*, *jyotiṣka*, and *vimānavāsin* deities, who descended from above until it was completely crowded. Then the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, possessing the arisen knowledge and vision, having perceived himself and the world, first taught the Dharma to the gods, and afterwards to humans. Then the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, possessing the arisen knowledge and vision, explained, declared, and expounded the five great vows (*mahāvratas*) along with their refinements (*sabhāvanās*) and the six classes of living beings (*ṣaḍjīvanikāyas*) to the ascetics and *nirgranthas* headed by Gautama, as follows: the earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, the plant-body, and the mobile-body.

Venerable Sir, I renounce the first great vow: all killing of living beings—whether subtle or gross, mobile or immobile—I myself shall not commit the killing of living beings, nor shall I cause others to commit the killing of living beings, nor shall I approve of another who is committing the killing of living beings. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—by mind, speech, and body—I turn back from it, Venerable Sir; I repent, I loathe, I condemn, and I relinquish this self.

For him, there are these five meditations (*bhāvanā*). Therein, this is the first meditation: "That Nirgrantha is restrained in his movement (*iryā-samita*), not unrestrained in his movement. A Kevalin would say: "If that Nirgrantha were unrestrained in his movement, he might strike, or injure, or crush, or torment, or destroy living beings (*pāṇa*), creatures (*bhūta*), souls (*jīva*), and sentient beings (*sattva*). "That Nirgrantha is restrained in his movement, not unrestrained in his movement"—this is the first meditation.

Furthermore, this is the second meditation: that Nirgrantha thoroughly understands the mind; whatever mind is evil, blameworthy, involving action, causing influx [of karma], causing cutting, causing piercing, provocative, burning, involving the taking of life, and involving injury to living beings—such a mind he does not direct toward movement. That Nirgrantha thoroughly understands the mind; whatever mind is not evil—this is the second meditation.

Furthermore, this is the third cultivation: the Nigaṇṭha thoroughly understands speech; whatever speech is sinful, blameworthy, involving action, and so forth up to being harmful to living beings—such speech he does not utter. He who thoroughly understands speech is a Nigaṇṭha; this is the third cultivation regarding that which is sinless speech.

Furthermore, there is the fourth cultivation: a Nirgrantha who is restrained in the taking up, laying down, and setting aside of his requisites and belongings is not one who is unrestrained in the taking up, laying down, and setting aside of his requisites and belongings. A Kevalin would say: "If that Nirgrantha were unrestrained in the taking up, laying down, and setting aside of his requisites and belongings, he might strike, or [even] destroy, living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings; therefore, a Nirgrantha is restrained in the taking up, laying down, and setting aside of his requisites and belongings, and is not unrestrained in the taking up, laying down, and setting aside of his requisites and belongings. This is the fourth cultivation.

Furthermore, there is the fifth cultivation: that Nirgrantha eats food and drink that has been inspected, not food and drink that has not been inspected. A Kevalin would say: "If that Nirgrantha were to eat food and drink that has not been inspected, he might strike or harm living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings; therefore, that Nirgrantha eats food and drink that has been inspected, not food and drink that has not been inspected"—this is the fifth cultivation.

To this extent, O Venerable Sir, the first great vow of abstaining from taking life becomes truly touched by the body, guarded, fulfilled, proclaimed, established, and also accomplished according to the command. This is the first great vow: abstention from taking life.

Furthermore, O Venerable One, I renounce the second great vow: all false speech, which is a source of evil. Whether out of anger, greed, fear, or jest, I myself shall not speak falsely, nor shall I cause another to speak falsely, nor shall I approve of another who speaks falsely. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I turn back from that, O Venerable One; I confess it, I blame it, I censure it, and I relinquish this self.

For him, there are these five meditations (*bhāvanā*). Therein, this is the first meditation: A Nirgrantha speaks after due reflection; a Kevalin would say that one who does not speak after due reflection, a Nirgrantha, might utter a falsehood. A Nirgrantha speaks after due reflection, not without speaking after due reflection—this is the first meditation.

Furthermore, there is a second meditation: the Nigrantha thoroughly understands anger; he should not be prone to anger. The Kevalin says: one who is overcome by anger and is angry might speak a falsehood with his speech. The Nigrantha thoroughly understands anger; he should not be prone to anger—this is the second meditation. Furthermore, there is a third meditation: the Nigrantha thoroughly understands greed; he should not be prone to greed. The Kevalin says: one who is overcome by greed and is greedy might speak a falsehood with his speech. The Nigrantha thoroughly understands greed; he should not be prone to greed—this is the third meditation.

Furthermore, there is the fourth meditation: that Nirgrantha thoroughly understands fear, yet he should not be one who is terrified by fear. A Kevalin would say that if one who has attained fearlessness were to speak words of fear, he would be speaking a falsehood. That Nirgrantha thoroughly understands fear and is not terrified by fear—this is the fourth meditation.

Furthermore, there is the fifth cultivation: that Nirgrantha thoroughly understands laughter and does not become one who seeks to provoke laughter. A Kevalin would say: "One who is subject to laughter might, in a fit of laughter, speak a falsehood with his speech. That Nirgrantha thoroughly understands laughter and does not become one who seeks to provoke laughter—this is the fifth cultivation. To this extent, the second great vow of truthfulness is properly touched, guarded, fulfilled, proclaimed, maintained, and realized through practice; O Venerable One, the second great vow is the abstention from false speech.

Furthermore, O Venerable Sir, this is the second great vow: I renounce all taking of what is not given—whether in a village, a town, or a forest; whether it be little or much, small or large, animate or inanimate. Neither shall I myself take what is not given, nor cause others to take what is not given, nor approve of others taking what is not given, for as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means: through mind, speech, and body. For that, O Venerable Sir, I repent, I blame, I censure, and I relinquish myself.

For him, there are these five meditations (*bhāvanā*). Therein, this is the first meditation: A Nirgrantha takes possession [of a dwelling] after due consideration; he does not take possession without due consideration. A Kevalin would say: "He takes possession without due consideration"—this is the first meditation.

Furthermore, this is the second reflection: A Nirgrantha eats food and drink that have been formally requested; he does not eat food and drink that have not been formally requested. A Kevalin would say: "If that Nirgrantha were to eat food and drink that have not been formally requested, he would be consuming what has not been given. Therefore, that Nirgrantha eats food and drink that have been formally requested; he does not eat food and drink that have not been formally requested. This is the second reflection.

Furthermore, this is the third meditation: "When a Nirgrantha has taken formal possession (*oggaha*) of a place, he should be one whose habit is to take possession only to that extent. A Kevalin might say: "If a Nirgrantha has not taken formal possession of a place, he would be one whose habit is not to take possession; yet he might take what is not given. Thus, "when a Nirgrantha has taken formal possession of a place, he should be one whose habit is to take possession only to that extent"—this is the third meditation.

Furthermore, there is the fourth meditation: a Nirgrantha, having taken possession of a dwelling, should be one who repeatedly practices taking possession [of that which is rightfully his]. A Kevalin would say: "If a Nirgrantha, having taken possession of a dwelling, were not one who repeatedly practices taking possession, he might take what has not been given. Thus, "a Nirgrantha, having taken possession of a dwelling, should be one who repeatedly practices taking possession" is the fourth meditation.

Furthermore, there is the fifth cultivation: that Nirgrantha, regarding fellow-monks, takes possession [of things] after having consulted [them], not without having consulted them. A Kevalin would say: if that Nirgrantha, regarding fellow-monks, were to take what has not been given without having consulted them, he would be at fault; but since that Nirgrantha, regarding fellow-monks, takes possession after having consulted them and not without having consulted them—this is the fifth cultivation. To this extent, indeed, the third great vow becomes truly touched by the body, guarded, fulfilled, proclaimed, established, blameless, and even accomplished. This, O Venerable One, is the third great vow: abstention from taking what is not given.

Furthermore, O Venerable One, I renounce the fourth great vow: all sexual intercourse, whether divine, human, or pertaining to the animal realm. Neither shall I myself engage in sexual intercourse, nor cause others to engage in sexual intercourse, nor shall I approve of others engaging in sexual intercourse. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—by mind, by speech, and by body—I turn back from it, O Venerable One; I confess it, I blame it, I reproach it, and I relinquish this self.

For him there are these five meditations (*bhāvanā*). Therein, this is the first meditation: A *nirgrantha* should not, from time to time, engage in conversation with women. The Kevalin would say: "If a *nirgrantha* should repeatedly engage in conversation with women, he would fall away from the teachings proclaimed as peace, integrity, and absolute purity. Thus, "A *nirgrantha* should not, from time to time, engage in conversation with women"—this is the first meditation.

Furthermore, this is the second meditation: A Nirgrantha should not look at or gaze upon the captivating sensory forms of women. A Kevalin would say: "If a Nirgrantha looks at or gazes upon the captivating sensory forms of women, he will suffer a breach, a collapse, and a fall from the Dharma proclaimed by the Omniscient One. Thus, "A Nirgrantha should not look at or gaze upon the captivating sensory forms of women" is the second meditation.

Furthermore, this is the third reflection: A Nirgrantha should not recall former pleasures or former amorous sports with women. A Kevalin would say: "If a Nirgrantha were to recall former pleasures or former amorous sports with women, he would fall away from the state of being undisturbed, from being free from fragmentation, and from the Dharma known by the Kevalins. Therefore, a Nirgrantha should not recall former pleasures or former amorous sports with women. This is the third reflection.

Furthermore, this is the fourth meditation: that Nirgrantha who eats food and drink in moderation does not eat refined or exquisite flavors. An omniscient one would say: "That Nirgrantha who eats food and drink in moderation eats refined or exquisite flavors"—this would be a breach, a fragmentation, and a falling away from the teachings proclaimed by the Omniscient One. [But] that Nirgrantha who eats food and drink in moderation does not eat refined or exquisite flavors—this is the fourth meditation.

Furthermore, there is the fifth cultivation: A Nirgrantha should not resort to lodgings and seats that are crowded with women, animals, or eunuchs. A Kevalin might say: "If a Nirgrantha resorts to lodgings and seats crowded with women, animals, or eunuchs, he may suffer a breach, a disruption, or a fall from the Dharma proclaimed by the Omniscient One. Therefore, a Nirgrantha should not resort to lodgings and seats crowded with women, animals, or eunuchs. This is the fifth cultivation.

And thus, O Venerable Sir, the fourth great vow—abstinence from sexual misconduct—is truly touched, guarded, fulfilled, proclaimed, maintained, and accomplished through bodily action by means of this [practice]. Thus, O Venerable Sir, the fourth great vow is fulfilled.

Furthermore, O Venerable Sir, there is the fifth great vow: I renounce all possession—whether it be little or much, small or large, animate or inanimate. Neither shall I myself take possession, nor cause others to take possession, nor approve of others taking possession, for as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means: through mind, speech, and body. For that, O Venerable Sir, I repent, I blame myself, I censure myself, and I relinquish my soul.

For this [monk], there are these five meditations (*bhāvanā*). Among them, the first meditation is as follows: With his ear, the living being hears pleasant and unpleasant sounds; he should not be attached to pleasant and unpleasant sounds, he should not be impassioned by them, he should not be greedy for them, he should not be deluded by them, he should not become obsessed with them, and he should not undergo destruction. The Kevalin says: "If a Nirgrantha, while being attached to, impassioned by, greedy for, deluded by, or obsessed with pleasant and unpleasant sounds, undergoes destruction, he will suffer a breach, a collapse, and a fall from the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins."
It is not possible that sounds which have entered the range of hearing are not heard; however, whatever passion or aversion arises therein, the monk should avoid it.
That the soul, through the sense of hearing, hears sounds—whether pleasant or unpleasant—is the first reflection.

Furthermore, this is the second meditation: with the eye, the soul perceives forms that are pleasant and unpleasant; toward pleasant and unpleasant forms, it should not become attached, should not be impassioned, should not crave, should not be deluded, should not become infatuated, and should not fall into destruction. An omniscient one would say: "A Nirgrantha who becomes attached, impassioned, craves, is deluded, becomes infatuated, or falls into destruction because of pleasant and unpleasant forms, will fall away from the Dharma that is free from division, free from fragmentation, and proclaimed by the Omniscient One."
It is not possible to avoid a form that has come within the range of the eye; however, a monk should avoid the passion and hatred that arise toward it.
That the soul, through the eye, perceives forms—whether pleasant or unpleasant—is the second meditation (bhāvanā).

Furthermore, this is the third meditation: with the sense of smell, the soul smells pleasant and unpleasant odors; it should not become attached to, enamored of, greedy for, infatuated with, or obsessed by pleasant and unpleasant odors, nor should it fall into self-destruction. A Kevalin would say: "If a Nirgrantha becomes attached, enamored of, greedy for, infatuated with, or obsessed by pleasant and unpleasant odors, and falls into self-destruction, he will fall away from those teachings that are peaceful, undisturbed, and perfectly complete."
It is not possible not to smell a scent that has come within the range of the nose; however, whatever passion or aversion arises therein, the monk should avoid it.
"The soul smells pleasant and unpleasant scents through the sense of smell"—this is the corresponding meditative reflection (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, this is the fourth meditation: the soul experiences pleasant and unpleasant tastes through the tongue; one should not be attached to, enamored of, greedy for, infatuated with, obsessed by, or fall into the destruction [of the self] because of pleasant and unpleasant tastes. The Kevalin says: a Nirgrantha who is attached to, enamored of, greedy for, infatuated with, obsessed by, or falls into the destruction [of the self] because of pleasant and unpleasant tastes would fall away from the Dharma that is peaceful, free from fragmentation, and proclaimed by the Kevalins.
It is not possible for one who is indifferent to tastes to avoid those [tastes] that have come within the range of the tongue; however, a monk should avoid the passion and aversion toward them.
That the soul experiences pleasant and unpleasant tastes through the tongue is the fourth reflection (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, there is a fifth meditation: the living being experiences pleasant and unpleasant tactile sensations; regarding these pleasant and unpleasant tactile sensations, he should not become attached, should not be impassioned, should not be greedy, should not be deluded, should not be obsessed, and should not fall into self-destruction. The Kevalin says: if a Nirgrantha becomes attached, impassioned, greedy, deluded, obsessed, or falls into self-destruction because of pleasant and unpleasant tactile sensations, he will fall away from the teachings proclaimed by the peaceful, the undisturbed, and the omniscient ones.

It is not possible not to experience a tactile sensation that has come within range; however, whatever passion or aversion arises therein, the monk should avoid them. That a living being experiences pleasant and unpleasant tactile sensations through touch—this is the fifth meditation (*bhāvanā*). To this extent, the fifth great vow of non-attachment (*parigraha-viramaṇa*) is truly touched, guarded, fulfilled, proclaimed, maintained, and even accomplished in accordance with the command by means of the body. Venerable sir, this is the fifth great vow: abstention from attachment.

Thus, an ascetic endowed with these five great vows and twenty-five reflections, having properly touched, guarded, fulfilled, proclaimed, and followed through the command—according to what was heard, according to the rule, and according to the path—becomes one who has attained realization.
[The sixteenth chapter: Liberation] Beings enter into impermanent dwellings; one should perceive this unsurpassed suffering.

Having understood the bondage of the household, the fearless one should abandon violent undertakings and possessions. (Āyār. 541) Men provoke with words and attack with arrows that monk who has attained such a state, who is restrained in infinite ways, and who practices incomparable food-gathering—just as they would attack an elephant gone into battle. (Āyār. 542)

When reviled by such people, when harsh sounds and tactile sensations are directed toward him, the wise man should endure them with an undisturbed mind; he should not be shaken, just as a mountain is not moved by the wind.
Observing this, he should dwell with those who are skilled; for both mobile and stationary beings suffer from unpleasant pain.
The great sage is unblemished and endures all things; thus he is a true ascetic, established in meditative concentration. (Āyār.

544) The wise one has mastered the unsurpassed path of Dharma. For the sage who has subdued his thirst and is absorbed in meditation, his austerity, wisdom, and glory increase through his splendor like a flame of fire. (Āyār. 545)

The infinite Conqueror, the Protector, has proclaimed the Great Vows which lead to the state of security; the Great Teacher has uttered them, free from worldly attachment. He alone illuminates that splendor in the three directions.
A monk who is pure should wander without possessions; he should not be attached to women and should renounce honor.
Thus, the wise man is not dependent on this world nor on the next, and he is not shaken by the qualities of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa). (Āyār.

547) Likewise, for the monk who is liberated, who lives with full comprehension, who is steadfast and patient with suffering, the impurity previously accumulated is purified—just as the tarnish on silver is removed by fire. (Āyār. 548)
He who abides in this understanding at the right time, free from desire and having ceased sexual intercourse, moves like a serpent;
just as it sheds its old skin, that Brahmin is liberated from the bed of suffering.
That which they call a flood, a water that is shoreless, like the great ocean difficult to cross with one's arms—Āyār. 549.
And when one understands this, O wise one, he indeed is called a sage who has made an end. (Āyār.

550) Just as it is bound here by human beings, and just as their liberation is declared, so too the wise one who knows the binding and the liberation—he indeed is called a sage who has made an end. (Āyār. 551)

In this world and in the next, in both places, there is no bond whatsoever for him who is without support and without foundation; he, free from the cycle of rebirth, is liberated on the path of pure being—thus I say. (Āyāra 552)
